choices: A. Continue olanzapine and add metformin
questions.explanation: He has developed frank type 2 diabetes and dyslipidemia on the antipsychotic that, with clozapine, anchors the highest-risk end of the metabolic table. When diabetes or substantial weight gain emerges on an antipsychotic, consensus guidance is to move the patient to an agent at the low-risk end rather than to layer a second chronic medication on top of the cause — and aripiprazole shows up on the "lowest risk" side of nearly every side-effect row, with the cleanest metabolic profile of the group. Board pearl — diabetes risk in psychiatric patients already runs 2 to 4 times the general-population baseline before any drug is added, and ziprasidone is the other guideline-named low-metabolic switch, though its QT signal has to be checked first.  [Learning objectives: LO 045, 086, 087]

wrongExplanations.0: Adding metformin treats the consequence while the drug generating it continues at full dose. It is a defensible move when no acceptable alternative antipsychotic exists, but here several low-metabolic-risk agents are available, so it is second-best.
wrongExplanations.2: Clozapine sits beside olanzapine at the highest-risk end of the metabolic table and adds agranulocytosis, seizure, sialorrhea, and myocarditis risk. It is also reserved for treatment-resistant disease, and his psychosis is in full remission — this switch worsens the exact problem being solved.
wrongExplanations.3: Quetiapine is a "-pine" and sits in the middle-to-upper band for weight gain, glucose, and lipids, along with prominent sedation. Moving from one metabolically burdensome agent to another does not resolve a new A1c of 7.9%.
wrongExplanations.4: Risperidone carries less metabolic burden than olanzapine but is not at the low-risk end, and it brings frequent hyperprolactinemia and more EPS as a "-done." Aripiprazole is the cleaner metabolic landing spot.

questions.eli5: The medicine cleared his voices but also gave him diabetes and almost 40 extra pounds. Rather than adding a diabetes pill on top and leaving the cause running, switch him to the antipsychotic that is gentlest on weight and blood sugar.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old man with schizophrenia has completed an 8-week trial of risperidone at 6 mg PO daily and a 10-week trial of olanzapine at 20 mg PO daily, each at an adequate dose with adherence confirmed by pill counts and refill records. He continues to hear a voice telling him to step into traffic, and he has made two suicide attempts in the past 14 months, one of which required intubation. He has had no extrapyramidal symptoms. His BMI is 24 kg/m2, fasting glucose is 90 mg/dL, ECG shows a QTc interval of 410 ms, absolute neutrophil count is 4,800/mm3, aminotransferases are within normal limits, and serum creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL. His psychiatrist plans to start the antipsychotic with the strongest evidence for this specific situation. Which of the following must be monitored on a mandatory scheduled basis once that medication is started?
questions.explanation: Two inferential steps, and the drug is never named. Step one: two adequate-dose, adequate-duration trials with documented adherence and persistent symptoms defines treatment-resistant schizophrenia, and recurrent suicidal behavior points the same direction — clozapine is both the superior agent for treatment-resistant disease and the only antipsychotic FDA-approved to reduce recurrent suicidal behavior in schizophrenia and schizoaffective disorder. Step two: clozapine's unique risk is agranulocytosis in roughly 1 to 2% of patients, so mandatory ANC/WBC monitoring under a REMS program is the price of prescribing it, running weekly at first and stretching out with continued normal counts. Board pearl — the action thresholds escalate from increased monitoring frequency, to interrupting therapy with daily counts, to permanent discontinuation with no rechallenge once severe neutropenia occurs.  [Learning objectives: LO 045, 095]

wrongExplanations.0: Scheduled QTc surveillance is the monitoring burden associated with ziprasidone and thioridazine. His QTc is already normal at 410 ms, and QT is not what makes the agent indicated here uniquely restricted.
wrongExplanations.1: Serial aminotransferases are the monitoring signature of valproate's fatal hepatotoxicity risk, not of any antipsychotic, and his liver enzymes are already normal.
wrongExplanations.3: Serial creatinine and BUN belong to lithium, which is renally cleared and reabsorbed at the proximal tubule. His creatinine of 0.9 mg/dL is normal and the agent being started is an antipsychotic.
wrongExplanations.4: Prolactin rises with risperidone and paliperidone through tuberoinfundibular D2 blockade, but it is checked when symptoms of hyperprolactinemia appear rather than as mandatory scheduled surveillance — and the drug indicated here causes essentially no prolactin elevation.

questions.eli5: He has already failed two good medicine trials and keeps hearing a voice telling him to hurt himself, so there is really only one medicine left worth starting. That medicine can wipe out the white blood cells that fight infection, so his blood count has to be checked on a strict schedule.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia maintained on clozapine 500 mg PO daily has been on a non-smoking inpatient medical unit for 6 days for cellulitis of the leg. Before admission he smoked 2 packs of cigarettes daily. On day 6 he is difficult to arouse, is drooling onto his gown, and has a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting 45 seconds. He is afebrile, HR 104, BP 108/66, RR 14. There is no rigidity, no diaphoresis, and deep tendon reflexes are 2+ throughout with no clonus. WBC is 7,200/mm3 with an absolute neutrophil count of 4,100/mm3, serum troponin is undetectable, and ECG shows sinus tachycardia without ST-segment changes. Serum sodium is 139 mEq/L, glucose is 96 mg/dL, and CT of the head shows no abnormalities. He drinks no alcohol and has been started on no other new medication. His serum clozapine concentration is markedly higher than his outpatient baseline. What is the underlying cause of his current condition?
choices: D. Loss of CYP1A2 induction after smoking cessation
questions.explanation: The hydrocarbons in cigarette smoke — not the nicotine — are CYP1A2 inducers, and clozapine and olanzapine are the two antipsychotics that are CYP1A2 substrates. Six smoke-free days removed that induction → CYP1A2 activity fell → clozapine metabolism slowed → serum levels climbed, reportedly by about 50% → sedation, sialorrhea, and a dose-related seizure at an unchanged prescribed dose. This is the mirror image of the more familiar version, in which a stabilized patient resumes smoking after discharge and relapses despite perfect adherence. Board pearl — inducers risk efficacy loss and inhibitors risk toxicity, and roughly 95% of patients with psychotic disorders smoke, so both directions of this interaction are routine ward events rather than trivia.  [Learning objectives: LO 022, 070, 086, 087]

wrongExplanations.0: Agranulocytosis is clozapine's unique 1 to 2% hematologic risk, but his WBC is 7,200/mm3 with an ANC of 4,100/mm3 and he is afebrile — the counts are the explicit negative that closes this option.
wrongExplanations.1: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome requires rigidity, hyperthermia, and diaphoresis after antipsychotic dosing. He is afebrile, has no rigidity, and is not diaphoretic — all three legs of the triad are absent.
wrongExplanations.2: Alcohol withdrawal is a genuine cause of seizure on hospital day 6 in a newly abstinent patient, which is why it belongs in the option set — but he drinks no alcohol, and his tremor-free, non-diaphoretic, normotensive presentation lacks the autonomic hyperactivity of withdrawal.
wrongExplanations.4: Clozapine myocarditis classically appears within the first weeks of therapy with chest pain, dyspnea, tachycardia, and elevated cardiac markers. He is 6 days into an admission on long-standing therapy with an undetectable troponin and a bland ECG.

questions.eli5: Cigarette smoke speeds up the liver enzyme that clears his medicine. Six days in a hospital where he could not smoke slowed that enzyme back down, so the medicine piled up until he was drowsy, drooling, and had a seizure — without anyone changing his dose.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman has taken haloperidol for 9 years for schizophrenia, and her psychotic symptoms have been in remission for the past 6 years. At her annual visit her daughter points out that for the past 8 months her mother has been continuously chewing, smacking her lips, and pushing her tongue against the inside of her cheek, even while sitting quietly watching television. The movements briefly stop when she is asked to open her mouth and resume when her attention shifts. She is afebrile, has no tremor at rest, no cogwheel rigidity, no sustained muscle contraction, and denies any subjective urge to move. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in management?
choices: A. Add amantadine 100 mg PO twice daily
B. Add benztropine 1 mg PO twice daily
C. Reduce the haloperidol dose and switch to an atypical agent
D. Add propranolol 20 mg PO three times daily
E. Increase the haloperidol dose and reassess in 8 weeks
questions.explanation: Involuntary, repetitive orofacial movements — chewing, lip-smacking, tongue protrusion — appearing after years of antipsychotic exposure are tardive dyskinesia, the chronic member of the EPS family. It is the one EPS syndrome whose initial management is to withdraw or reduce the offending agent and switch to an atypical, with a VMAT2 inhibitor considered if that is not enough. Board pearl — anticholinergics are the reflex answer for dystonia and pseudoparkinsonism, but they do not help tardive dyskinesia and can worsen it, because TD is not driven by the same relative-cholinergic-excess mechanism; TD is often irreversible, which is why prevention and early dose reduction matter more than any rescue drug.  [Learning objectives: LO 022, 049, 051, 053, 095]

wrongExplanations.0: Amantadine is used for pseudoparkinsonism, and she has neither the resting tremor, the cogwheel rigidity, nor the bradykinesia that syndrome requires — those negatives are stated explicitly.
wrongExplanations.1: Benztropine is the classic answer for acute dystonia and drug-induced parkinsonism, and it is the trap here. Anticholinergics do not improve tardive dyskinesia and may make it worse, since TD is not generated by relative cholinergic excess.
wrongExplanations.3: Propranolol is first-line for akathisia, which requires subjective restlessness and an urge to move. She explicitly denies any urge to move and sits quietly through television.
wrongExplanations.4: Raising the dose transiently suppresses the movements by increasing D2 blockade, which makes it seductive, but it deepens the underlying receptor supersensitivity and worsens the long-term course — the exact opposite of the correct direction.

questions.eli5: After nine years on the same medicine her mouth started chewing and smacking on its own, even when she is just watching TV. The fix is to slowly lower or change the medicine that caused it — the anticholinergic pill that helps other movement side effects does not help this one.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with schizophrenia was started on risperidone 4 mg PO daily 9 days ago. His wife says he now shuffles when he walks, his face "has gone blank," and his hands shake when they rest in his lap. He is afebrile, HR 76, BP 126/80, RR 14. Examination shows cogwheel rigidity at both wrists, bradykinesia, decreased arm swing, and a 4-Hz resting tremor. There is no sustained muscle contraction of the neck or eyes, no diaphoresis, and no orofacial or lingual movement; he denies any subjective urge to move and answers questions promptly, and his limbs do not remain in positions into which the examiner places them. Serum creatine kinase is 110 U/L. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Bradykinesia, cogwheel rigidity, resting tremor, and masked facies appearing within days to weeks of a new antipsychotic is drug-induced pseudoparkinsonism — nigrostriatal D2 blockade producing a relative dopamine deficiency that reaches the same final common pathway as idiopathic Parkinson disease. Risperidone is a "-done," the atypical subgroup that behaves like a watered-down typical and potentiates EPS more than the "-pines," so even a modest 4 mg dose can do this. Board pearl — this stem is built as a rule-out exercise: every negative in it eliminates exactly one option on the list, which is how a seven-option movement-disorder set is meant to be worked.  [Learning objectives: LO 022, 049, 051, 053]

wrongExplanations.0: An acute dystonic reaction is a sudden, sustained muscle contraction such as torticollis or oculogyric crisis, arriving within hours to days. The stem states there is no sustained muscle contraction of the neck or eyes.
wrongExplanations.1: Akathisia is defined by subjective motor restlessness — the patient cannot sit still and feels compelled to move. He explicitly denies any urge to move.
wrongExplanations.2: Catatonia would show features such as waxy flexibility, in which limbs remain where the examiner places them, along with mutism or marked response latency. His limbs do not hold imposed postures and he answers questions promptly.
wrongExplanations.3: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome requires hyperthermia, diaphoresis, and lead-pipe rigidity with a markedly elevated creatine kinase. He is afebrile, is not diaphoretic, has cogwheel rather than lead-pipe tone, and his CK is 110 U/L.
wrongExplanations.5: Restless legs syndrome is a nocturnal urge to move the legs relieved by movement, not a daytime picture of rigidity, bradykinesia, and resting tremor — and he denies any urge to move at all.
wrongExplanations.6: Tardive dyskinesia is the chronic EPS syndrome, developing over months to years and presenting with choreoathetoid orofacial movements. He is 9 days into treatment with no orofacial or lingual movement.

questions.eli5: Nine days into a new medicine he walks stiffly, his face stopped moving, and his hands shake when they are just sitting still. That combination looks exactly like Parkinson disease, but the medicine caused it — which is why it gets the "pseudo" name.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man was brought to the emergency department 2 days ago by police for agitation and has received five doses of intramuscular haloperidol since arrival, the most recent 6 hours ago. He is now barely responsive to voice. Temperature is 40.1°C (104.2°F), pulse is 132/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 158/94 mm Hg. He is diaphoretic, and his limbs resist passive movement uniformly through the full range with a lead-pipe quality. Deep tendon reflexes are 1+ throughout with no clonus and no tremor. Serum creatine kinase is 18,400 U/L and WBC is 16,200/mm3; urine is dark with a dipstick positive for blood but no red cells on microscopy. He has received no serotonergic medication and no inhaled anesthetic, and urine toxicology screening is negative. What is the most appropriate initial step in management?
questions.explanation: Rigidity, hyperthermia, and diaphoresis after repeated antipsychotic dosing is neuroleptic malignant syndrome, and the rhabdomyolysis picture — CK of 18,400 U/L with heme-positive urine containing no red cells — confirms the severity. The first and most essential step is to discontinue the causative dopamine blocker; supportive care with cooling and intravenous fluids follows, and dantrolene or bromocriptine are added in severe cases after the offending agent is stopped. The sequencing is the whole point: giving an antidote while the drug driving the syndrome is still being administered treats around the cause. Board pearl — 1+ reflexes with no clonus and a 2-day course are the negatives that separate NMS from serotonin syndrome, which runs the opposite way with hyperreflexia, clonus, and onset within hours.  [Learning objectives: LO 021, 022, 095]

wrongExplanations.1: Benztropine treats acute dystonia and drug-induced parkinsonism. His rigidity is generalized and lead-pipe with hyperthermia and rhabdomyolysis, which is not a dystonic reaction, and an anticholinergic also impairs sweating and heat dissipation in a patient at 40.1°C.
wrongExplanations.2: Bromocriptine is a dopamine agonist used to restore the dopaminergic tone lost to the antipsychotic, and it is a legitimate part of NMS management — but it is added in severe cases after the offending agent is stopped, not instead of stopping it.
wrongExplanations.3: Cyproheptadine is the 5-HT2 antagonist used for serotonin syndrome, which requires hyperreflexia and clonus. His reflexes are 1+ with no clonus, and the stem states he has received no serotonergic medication.
wrongExplanations.4: Dantrolene blocks calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum and is genuinely useful for the rigidity and heat generation of severe NMS — but it is a supportive measure layered on top of stopping the antipsychotic, which remains the first and most essential step.
wrongExplanations.5: Switching to a lower-potency typical still blocks dopamine and will not resolve an episode that is being driven by dopamine blockade. Any antipsychotic continued during active NMS perpetuates the syndrome.

questions.eli5: Two days of repeated shots of an antipsychotic left him burning hot, stiff as a board, and sweating, with muscle breaking down into his urine. Before any antidote, you stop giving the drug that is causing it.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by police after he was found pacing in the middle of an intersection, shouting that surveillance drones were tracking him. In the department he paces the hallway, clenches his fists, leans into the faces of staff members, and shouts obscenities at a nurse. Verbal de-escalation, an offer of food, and an offer of a quiet room have all failed. He has refused all oral medication, including an orally disintegrating tablet, and no intravenous access has been established. He is afebrile, HR 118, BP 146/88, RR 20. He is not known to this hospital, no medical records are available, and no medication history is obtainable from him or from the officers. What is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
choices: C. Diphenhydramine 50 mg, haloperidol 5 mg, and lorazepam 2 mg IM
D. Olanzapine 10 mg orally disintegrating tablet, repeated once
F. Diphenhydramine 50 mg and benztropine 1 mg IM
questions.explanation: This is the classic acute-agitation cocktail known as the B-52: Benadryl 50 mg, Haldol 5 mg, and Ativan 2 mg given intramuscularly as needed. Each component earns its place — haloperidol targets the psychosis driving the behavior, lorazepam provides rapid sedation, and diphenhydramine covers the acute dystonic reaction that a first dose of a high-potency typical can produce in exactly this demographic. The buried constraint is the route: he has refused every oral form including a dissolving tablet and has no intravenous access, so intramuscular administration is the only workable option, and that single sentence eliminates four of the six choices. Board pearl — the escalating warning signs that justify this intervention are behavioral as much as verbal: inability to sit still, fierce eye contact, clenched fists, and tensed jaw.  [Learning objectives: LO 022, 095]

wrongExplanations.0: Chlorpromazine is a sedating low-potency typical that would blunt agitation, but it is offered by mouth and he has refused all oral medication. It also brings a heavy alpha-1 blocking burden and orthostatic hypotension in an undifferentiated patient with no medical history available.
wrongExplanations.1: Lorazepam alone is a reasonable sedative but is offered here by mouth, which he has refused, and monotherapy leaves the psychotic drive behind the behavior untreated.
wrongExplanations.3: An orally disintegrating olanzapine tablet is a genuinely good option for a cooperative agitated patient, which is why it is in the set — the stem specifically states he has refused oral medication including an orally disintegrating tablet.
wrongExplanations.4: Propranolol is first-line for akathisia, not for acute agitation, and it is oral. Nothing in this presentation suggests medication-induced restlessness; he has no known medication history at all.
wrongExplanations.5: Diphenhydramine plus benztropine is an intramuscular combination, so route is not the problem — but it is two anticholinergic agents with no antipsychotic and no benzodiazepine, so it treats a dystonic reaction he does not have while leaving the agitation entirely uncovered.

questions.eli5: He is too worked up to take anything by mouth and has no IV, so the medicine has to go in as a shot in the muscle. The standard shot mixes three drugs: one to calm the psychosis, one to settle him down, and one to prevent a muscle-locking side effect from the first.

questions.stem: An adult with schizophrenia who takes no antipsychotic medication at all has an approximate relapse rate of which of the following at 1 year?
questions.explanation: The unmedicated relapse figures are roughly 70% at 1 year and 90% at 2 years. Those numbers exist to be compared against the treated ones: approximately 20% per year on an oral antipsychotic, and approximately 5% per year on a long-acting injectable. Board pearl — the whole ladder is worth memorizing as one string, because it is the quantitative argument for long-acting injectables in a patient whose relapses track with missed doses, and it is far more persuasive to a patient than any qualitative statement about adherence.  [Learning objectives: LO 045, 063]

wrongExplanations.0: Approximately 5% per year is the relapse rate on a long-acting injectable antipsychotic — the best figure on the ladder, and the reason LAIs are favored in patients with adherence-driven relapse.
wrongExplanations.1: Approximately 20% per year is the relapse rate for a patient taking an oral antipsychotic, which is roughly four times the LAI rate and still far better than no treatment.
wrongExplanations.2: 40% does not correspond to any figure in this set; it is the plausible-sounding midpoint a reader picks when hedging between the treated and untreated numbers.
wrongExplanations.4: Approximately 90% is the unmedicated relapse rate at 2 years rather than at 1 year — the closest near-miss on the list, separated from the answer only by the time frame in the question.

questions.eli5: If someone with schizophrenia takes nothing at all, about seven out of ten get sick again within a year. Taking a daily pill drops that to about two in ten, and a long-acting shot drops it to about one in twenty.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man with schizophrenia is admitted for the third time in 18 months. Each admission has followed the same course: he stops taking oral risperidone 4 mg PO daily within 3 to 5 weeks of discharge, becomes convinced that his upstairs neighbor is pumping gas through the heating vents, and stops sleeping. Each time, his symptoms remit fully within 2 weeks of restarting the same dose of the same medication. He has never had extrapyramidal symptoms, akathisia, galactorrhea, or weight gain on risperidone, and he says he simply forgets doses when his work schedule changes. His BMI is 24 kg/m2, fasting glucose is 92 mg/dL, absolute neutrophil count is 5,100/mm3, and ECG shows a QTc interval of 408 ms. He states that he is willing to accept whatever treatment his physician recommends. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
choices: A. Add benztropine 1 mg PO twice daily
B. Increase the oral risperidone dose to 6 mg PO daily
questions.explanation: The buried clue is that he remits fully within 2 weeks every time the same dose of the same drug is restarted — the medication works, so this is an adherence problem, not a treatment-resistance problem. That single sentence redirects the entire question toward delivery rather than pharmacology, and the long-acting injectable is the intervention built for it: annual relapse rates run about 20% on oral therapy versus roughly 5% on an LAI. Paliperidone is risperidone's active metabolite, so he stays on the molecule already proven to work for him and already proven tolerable. Board pearl — the trap is that three hospitalizations in 18 months sounds like treatment resistance, but resistance requires failed adequate trials of two agents, and a drug that is not taken has never been given an adequate trial.  [Learning objectives: LO 045, 095]

wrongExplanations.0: Benztropine treats acute dystonia and drug-induced parkinsonism. He has explicitly never had extrapyramidal symptoms, so there is nothing for it to prevent or treat, and it does not address why he relapses.
wrongExplanations.1: Raising the dose of a medication he is not taking changes nothing about the interval between discharge and discontinuation, and it adds EPS and prolactin risk to a regimen he currently tolerates well.
wrongExplanations.2: Psychosocial rehabilitation is the right answer for the patient whose symptoms are controlled and who is adherent but socially non-functioning. His symptoms are not controlled between admissions, and the immediate failure point is a missed dose rather than a functional deficit.
wrongExplanations.3: Clozapine is reserved for treatment-resistant disease, which requires failed trials of two agents at adequate dose and duration. He has never failed a trial — he has interrupted one three times — and clozapine adds agranulocytosis monitoring, seizure risk, and heavy metabolic burden for no gain here.
wrongExplanations.4: Switching to olanzapine abandons an agent he tolerates well and responds to, adds the highest-tier metabolic risk, and still relies on him remembering a daily oral dose — the exact step that keeps failing.

questions.eli5: The medicine works every single time he takes it — he just forgets it a few weeks after going home. So the answer is not a stronger or fancier medicine, it is the same medicine given as a long-acting shot he cannot forget.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man is started on chlorpromazine. Three days later he becomes lightheaded each time he stands, and his blood pressure falls from 132/80 mm Hg supine to 98/62 mm Hg after 2 minutes of standing. Blockade of which of the following receptors is most likely responsible for this finding?
choices: B. Dopamine D2 in the nigrostriatal tract
C. Dopamine D2 in the tuberoinfundibular tract
questions.explanation: Orthostatic hypotension maps to α1-adrenergic blockade: α1 receptors mediate the reflex vasoconstriction that maintains blood pressure on standing, so blocking them → failure of that reflex → a symptomatic postural drop. Chlorpromazine is the prototypical low-potency typical, and the potency see-saw predicts this without knowing anything else about the molecule — low potency means low EPS but high anticholinergic, antihistaminic, and alpha-blocking burden. Board pearl — the receptor-to-side-effect map is worth memorizing as a five-line table: H1 gives sedation, α1 gives orthostatic hypotension, M1 gives dry mouth and blurred vision and urinary retention, nigrostriatal D2 gives EPS, and tuberoinfundibular D2 gives galactorrhea, amenorrhea, and gynecomastia.  [Learning objectives: LO 055, 083, 095]

wrongExplanations.1: Nigrostriatal D2 blockade tips the striatal acetylcholine:dopamine balance toward relative cholinergic excess and produces the extrapyramidal movement syndromes — dystonia, akathisia, pseudoparkinsonism, and tardive dyskinesia — not a postural blood pressure drop.
wrongExplanations.2: Tuberoinfundibular D2 blockade disinhibits prolactin release and produces galactorrhea, amenorrhea, and gynecomastia. It has no role in blood pressure regulation.
wrongExplanations.3: H1 antagonism produces sedation and contributes to weight gain. Chlorpromazine does block H1 heavily, which is why sedation is one of its signature effects, but sedation is not what makes blood pressure drop on standing.
wrongExplanations.4: M1 antagonism produces dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, and urinary retention, and can cause tachycardia. It does not impair the vasoconstrictive reflex that fails here.

questions.eli5: When you stand up, your blood vessels are supposed to squeeze so blood keeps reaching your head. This medicine blocks the switch that tells them to squeeze, so his blood pressure drops and he gets dizzy every time he stands.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man with schizophrenia has taken haloperidol for 4 months. His auditory hallucinations and his belief that his phone was reading his thoughts have resolved completely and have not returned. He now sits without spontaneous speech, answers questions in three-word phrases, shows almost no facial expression, and has stopped bathing or changing clothes unless prompted; his sister says he is noticeably more withdrawn than he was before the medication was started. He is afebrile, and examination shows no resting tremor, no cogwheel rigidity, no bradykinesia of the limbs, and no subjective urge to move. Which of the following best explains these findings?
choices: A. Insufficient D2 blockade in the mesolimbic tract at the current dose
B. D2 blockade in the already-hypodopaminergic mesocortical tract
C. D2 blockade in the nigrostriatal tract
D. D2 blockade in the tuberoinfundibular tract
E. 5-HT2A blockade in the mesolimbic tract
questions.explanation: Reason backward from the effect. Flat affect, alogia, avolition, and asociality are negative symptoms, and the mesocortical tract that governs cognition and motivation is already underactive in psychosis — so adding D2 blockade there worsens, or at best fails to help, exactly these symptoms. Haloperidol is a typical, meaning it blocks dopamine much more than serotonin and has essentially nothing extra to offer the mesocortical picture, which is why negative symptoms are described as untouched by typicals. Board pearl — atypicals, with their relatively greater 5-HT2A blockade, are historically the better option for negative symptoms and are the only agents that address cognitive symptoms at all, so this finding is an argument for changing class rather than raising the dose.  [Learning objectives: LO 047, 068, 083]

wrongExplanations.0: Insufficient mesolimbic blockade would present as persistent or returning positive symptoms — hallucinations and delusions. The stem states his hallucinations and delusions have resolved completely and have not returned.
wrongExplanations.2: Nigrostriatal blockade produces extrapyramidal findings, and drug-induced parkinsonism can genuinely masquerade as negative symptoms through masked facies and bradykinesia — which is why the stem explicitly excludes resting tremor, cogwheel rigidity, and limb bradykinesia.
wrongExplanations.3: Tuberoinfundibular blockade disinhibits prolactin and produces galactorrhea, amenorrhea, and gynecomastia. It has no relationship to affect, speech output, or motivation.
wrongExplanations.4: Haloperidol is a first-generation agent that blocks dopamine far more than serotonin, so meaningful 5-HT2A blockade is not part of its profile — and if anything, greater 5-HT2A blockade is associated with better rather than worse negative-symptom outcomes.

questions.eli5: The medicine turned down dopamine everywhere, including in the part of the brain that was already running too low. That is the part that supplies motivation, expression, and speech — so the voices stopped, but he went flat and quiet.

questions.stem: Information that would be most supportive of a secondary (organic) cause of a patient's new-onset psychosis rather than a primary psychotic disorder is that the patient:
choices: A. has a first-degree relative with schizophrenia.
B. smokes two packs of cigarettes daily.
C. has had two previous psychiatric hospitalizations for psychosis.
D. has had a marked decline in occupational functioning since the symptoms began.
questions.explanation: Prominent visual hallucinations are atypical for a primary psychotic disorder, in which auditory hallucinations dominate, so their presence should push the workup toward a secondary cause — substance-induced psychosis or psychosis due to a general medical condition. The other four options are all items from the list of history clues that favor a primary disorder, which is what makes them tempting: a family history of psychotic disorders, prior psychiatric hospitalization, prior antipsychotic treatment, marked postmorbid decline in function, and heavy smoking all argue for a psychiatric diagnosis rather than an organic one. Board pearl — a primary psychotic disorder is to some degree a diagnosis of exclusion, and an unremarkable physical examination is itself a useful pertinent negative supporting it.  [Learning objectives: LO 063]

wrongExplanations.0: A family history of psychotic disorders is one of the standard history clues favoring a primary psychotic disorder, since the heritable risk belongs to the psychiatric illness rather than to any organic cause.
wrongExplanations.1: Heavy smoking argues toward a primary disorder rather than away from it — roughly 95% of patients with psychotic disorders smoke cigarettes, which is why smoking status appears on the primary-disorder clue list.
wrongExplanations.2: Prior psychiatric hospitalizations for psychosis establish a recurrent psychiatric course, which is one of the strongest clues favoring a primary psychotic disorder.
wrongExplanations.3: Marked postmorbid decline in level of functioning is a listed feature of primary psychotic disorders, and it appears in the diagnostic criteria for schizophrenia itself.

questions.eli5: People with the psychiatric kind of psychosis usually hear things rather than see them. So when someone is mainly seeing things that are not there, doctors start looking for a medical cause instead — an infection, a drug, or something in the brain.

questions.stem: Raymond is a 47-year-old tax accountant who has been convinced for the past 3 years that the owner of the neighboring property is poisoning the soil along their shared fence line to force him to sell his house. He photographs the fence line every Saturday morning, has sent four certified letters, and has filed two complaints with the county, each of which was investigated and closed. He continues to work full-time and has filed every client return on schedule, has been married for 19 years, and golfs with the same three friends each weekend. He has never heard voices or seen anything others could not see, his speech is organized and goal-directed, his affect is full and reactive, and he shows no decline in self-care. He has never had a period of depressed or elevated mood. His wife describes him as "the most easygoing man in the world — until you mention that fence." The most likely diagnosis is
questions.explanation: Delusional disorder requires a plausible, non-bizarre fixed delusion with otherwise preserved functioning and no other prominent psychotic features — and a neighbor poisoning soil in a property dispute is entirely plausible, which is exactly what makes it non-bizarre. Everything outside the belief is intact: full-time work, a long marriage, a stable friend group, organized speech, reactive affect, and normal self-care. The wife's quote is the tiebreaker, because it establishes that the suspicion is encapsulated to one topic rather than a pervasive stance toward the world. Board pearl — the six delusion subtypes are persecutory, somatic, erotomanic, grandiose, jealous, and mixed, and the characteristic insight failure is limited to the delusion itself.  [Learning objectives: LO 063]

wrongExplanations.1: Paranoid personality disorder is a pervasive, lifelong pattern of distrust and suspiciousness across many relationships and situations, without a single fixed delusion. His wife's description places him at the opposite pole — easygoing about everything except this one belief.
wrongExplanations.2: Schizoaffective disorder requires major mood episodes concurrent with psychosis plus a period of at least 2 weeks of psychosis alone. He has never had a period of depressed or elevated mood at all.
wrongExplanations.3: Schizophrenia requires at least two of the core psychotic criteria along with decline in functioning. He has one symptom only, and his occupational, social, and self-care functioning are explicitly preserved across 3 years.
wrongExplanations.4: Schizotypal personality disorder involves odd beliefs and magical thinking, eccentric appearance and behavior, constricted affect, and social anxiety with few close relationships. His affect is full, his speech is organized, and he maintains a marriage and a regular social group.

questions.eli5: For three years he has believed one specific thing that could actually be true — that his neighbor is poisoning the dirt — and everything else about his life works fine. One fixed, believable false idea with normal functioning around it has its own name: delusional disorder.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 4-month history of episodes of pounding heartbeat, sweating, trembling, shortness of breath, and a sense that she is about to die. Each episode begins abruptly, peaks within about 3 minutes, and resolves within 15 minutes. She has had roughly two episodes weekly; three have awakened her from sleep and others have occurred while she was watching television at home. For the past 6 weeks she has stopped driving on the highway and has declined a promotion that would require travel, because she is preoccupied with when the next episode will strike. She denies fear of being watched or judged, and she reports no worry about her finances, her family, or her health between episodes. Temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), pulse is 76/min, and blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. Thyroid-stimulating hormone concentration, electrocardiogram, and urine toxicology screening are normal. On mental status examination, affect is anxious but full-range and thought process is linear. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A panic attack is a discrete surge of intense fear with abrupt onset that peaks within 30 seconds to 5 minutes and includes ≥4 of 13 symptoms — but an attack alone is not panic disorder, because attacks also occur in GAD, OCD, social phobia, and PTSD. Panic disorder requires recurrent attacks that are at least partly unexpected, PLUS ≥1 month of persistent worry about further attacks or a maladaptive behavior change. Her attacks are uncued (nocturnal, and while watching television at home), and the 6 weeks of avoidance and preoccupation satisfy the behavioral criterion. Board pearl — nocturnal attacks are nearly diagnostic of the uncued pattern, since there is no external situation present to cue them.  [Learning objectives: LO 036]

wrongExplanations.0: Agoraphobia requires fear across multiple situations united by the theme that escape or help might be unavailable. Her avoidance of highway driving is a downstream consequence of the attacks rather than a primary fear of being trapped, and no other agoraphobic situations are described. DSM-5 unlinked agoraphobia from panic disorder, so it must stand on its own criteria.
wrongExplanations.1: Generalized anxiety disorder requires excessive, difficult-to-control worry about multiple everyday domains for more than 6 months. She explicitly reports no worry about finances, family, or health between episodes — that stated negative is what closes this option.
wrongExplanations.2: Illness anxiety disorder centers on persistent preoccupation with having a serious illness despite reassurance and minimal somatic symptoms. Her fear is of the attacks themselves recurring, not of an undiagnosed disease, and her somatic symptoms are prominent rather than minimal.
wrongExplanations.4: Social anxiety disorder requires the fear to be of scrutiny and negative evaluation by others. She specifically denies fear of being watched or judged, and several attacks occurred alone at home or during sleep.
wrongExplanations.5: A specific phobia is cued reliably by one discrete object or situation. Attacks that awaken her from sleep cannot be cued by any external stimulus, which rules out a phobic pattern.

questions.eli5: Her panic episodes come out of nowhere — some even wake her up at night — and now she spends her time dreading the next one and avoiding the highway. Attacks that arrive with no trigger, plus a month of worrying about them, is what makes it panic disorder rather than just panic attacks.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of chest tightness, palpitations, shortness of breath, and lightheadedness. He states this is his third such episode in 2 months, that each begins abruptly, and that a physician at an urgent care center told him after the first one that he was 'just having panic attacks.' Tonight's episode began 50 minutes ago and has not let up. He has no history of cardiac or pulmonary disease, takes no medications, and does not use tobacco, alcohol, or illicit drugs. Temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F), pulse is 194/min and regular, respirations are 22/min, blood pressure is 104/68 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation is 99% on room air. Lungs are clear and there is no calf tenderness or asymmetric swelling. Urine toxicology screening is negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
choices: E. Screening with the GAD-7 questionnaire
questions.explanation: The prior label of 'panic attacks' is the dramatic decoy; two buried clues override it. A true panic attack peaks within 30 seconds to 5 minutes and resolves in minutes — this episode has run 50 minutes without letting up — and a regular rate of 194/min is far outside what anxiety produces. MI, angina, pulmonary embolism, and arrhythmia must be excluded before anything is called 'just panic,' and a sustained regular narrow-complex tachycardia at this rate points to supraventricular tachycardia. A 12-lead ECG is immediate, noninvasive, and the only listed test that captures the rhythm while it is still present. Board pearl — patients routinely misremember attacks as far longer than they were, so a genuinely documented long episode with an extreme heart rate should move you off the psychiatric label.  [Learning objectives: LO 050, 099]

wrongExplanations.0: A Holter monitor records over the following 24 hours and would miss the arrhythmia occurring in front of you right now. Ambulatory monitoring is for capturing intermittent events between episodes, not for a patient who is symptomatic at a rate of 194/min.
wrongExplanations.1: Pulmonary embolism belongs on the differential, but his lungs are clear, oxygen saturation is 99% on room air, and there is no calf tenderness or asymmetric swelling — and CT angiography is a contrast study that should not precede a 30-second bedside test that will likely give the diagnosis.
wrongExplanations.3: Thyrotoxicosis can mimic panic and is worth checking, but a send-out laboratory test does not address a patient in a sustained tachycardia at 194/min during this visit.
wrongExplanations.4: The GAD-7 is a screening instrument for generalized anxiety disorder, not a diagnostic step, and administering a questionnaire to a patient in an active tachyarrhythmia accepts the psychiatric label that the vital signs are arguing against.

questions.eli5: Someone already told him these were panic attacks, but a real panic attack peaks in a few minutes and this one has lasted almost an hour with his heart at 194. Before calling it anxiety, you get a heart tracing while it is still happening.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old high school teacher comes to the office because of a 4-year history of intense fear of being scrutinized and judged. He teaches five class periods daily and reports sweating, trembling, and a racing heart in every one of them; he has twice left mid-lesson. The same fear occurs at weekly faculty meetings, at parent conferences, at restaurants where he might be seen eating, and at family gatherings, and he has declined all social invitations for the past 2 years. He states that he wishes he could take part in these things. He denies obsessions, compulsions, and unexpected attacks occurring outside social situations. He has no cardiac or pulmonary disease, does not use alcohol or illicit drugs, and takes no medications. Pulse is 72/min and blood pressure is 120/78 mm Hg; physical examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term pharmacotherapy?
choices: A. Alprazolam as needed before each class
B. Atenolol as needed before each class
C. Hydroxyzine as needed for anxiety
D. Propranolol as needed before each class
questions.explanation: The decisive variable is exposure frequency, not the diagnosis. This is generalized social anxiety disorder — the fear spans teaching, meetings, conferences, eating in public, and family gatherings — and he faces it five times every school day. For chronic, daily exposure, serotonergic therapy is the core treatment: an SSRI, or buspirone, paired with CBT and assertiveness training. Board pearl — the exam reading rule is daily fear gets an SSRI, date-night fear gets a beta-blocker. Questions of this type deliberately list both a serotonergic and an as-needed option and test whether you noticed how often the patient is actually exposed.  [Learning objectives: LO 036, 048, 081]

wrongExplanations.0: Alprazolam has the shortest half-life and the highest abuse potential of the benzodiazepines, and dependence can develop in as little as 2 weeks. Dosing it before each of five daily classes is scheduled use dressed up as as-needed use, which is exactly the pattern benzodiazepines are meant to avoid.
wrongExplanations.1: Atenolol shares propranolol's problem here and is additionally more cardioselective and less useful for the somatic tremor and sweating of performance anxiety.
wrongExplanations.2: Hydroxyzine is a reasonable as-needed anxiolytic with no abuse potential, but it is sedating — a genuine hazard for someone teaching all day — and it does not treat the underlying disorder, only blunts episodes.
wrongExplanations.3: This is the trap. Beta-blockers are the correct answer for the circumscribed, performance-only subtype, where exposure is occasional. His fear extends well beyond performance into restaurants and family gatherings, and he encounters it five times daily, so the episodic strategy fails on both counts.

questions.eli5: Propranolol is the famous answer for stage fright, but that works when you face the fear once in a while. He faces it five times every single day and outside work too, so he needs a daily medicine that treats the whole condition.

questions.stem: On the GAD-7 questionnaire, which of the following total score thresholds is generally taken to indicate a probable diagnosis of generalized anxiety disorder warranting further clinical evaluation?
questions.explanation: A GAD-7 total of 10 or greater is the accepted cut point suggesting probable generalized anxiety disorder that warrants confirmatory clinical evaluation. Board pearl — scores of 5, 10, and 15 serve as the rough severity anchors for mild, moderate, and severe once the diagnosis is under consideration, so 10 does double duty as both the screening threshold and the moderate anchor. Do not confuse the GAD-7 with the PHQ-9, which screens for depression, or with the MMSE and MoCA, which are scored out of 30 and assess cognition.  [Learning objectives: LO 036]

wrongExplanations.0: 5 is the anchor for mild anxiety severity, not the threshold suggesting a probable diagnosis; screening at this level would flag a large proportion of the general population.
wrongExplanations.2: 12 is not one of the established anchors or cut points for this instrument.
wrongExplanations.3: 15 is the anchor for severe anxiety. Using it as the diagnostic threshold would miss the moderate range in which most patients who warrant evaluation actually score.
wrongExplanations.4: 18 is not an established threshold and sits near the instrument's ceiling of 21, so it would identify only the most extreme presentations.

questions.eli5: The GAD-7 is a short anxiety questionnaire. A score of 10 or higher is the line where a doctor should stop and look more carefully for generalized anxiety disorder.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman with generalized anxiety disorder has taken sertraline for 10 weeks, titrated to 200 mg PO daily (dose range 25 to 200 mg PO daily). Her worry, irritability, and muscle tension have improved substantially but she continues to describe restlessness and difficulty falling asleep on most nights, which interferes with her work as a dispatcher. She has a history of alcohol use disorder in sustained remission for 3 years and attends weekly mutual-support meetings; she asks whether there is 'something to take the edge off,' noting that a walk-in clinic once gave her alprazolam and it 'worked instantly.' She takes no other medications. Pulse is 74/min and blood pressure is 116/72 mm Hg; physical examination and serum studies including thyroid-stimulating hormone are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in pharmacotherapy?
choices: D. Increase sertraline above 200 mg PO daily
questions.explanation: Two constraints do the work. First, she is already at sertraline's maximum dose, so there is no room to escalate. Second, she has alcohol use disorder in remission, which makes any benzodiazepine a poor choice given cross-dependence and abuse potential. Buspirone is a 5-HT1A partial agonist with no sedation and no addictive potential, and it is a listed option for generalized anxiety disorder both as monotherapy and as an add-on to a baseline antidepressant for further anxiety control. Board pearl — a partial response to a maximally dosed antidepressant calls for augmentation, not abandonment of an agent that is clearly working.  [Learning objectives: LO 036, 048, 081]

wrongExplanations.1: Alprazolam has the shortest half-life and highest abuse potential in its class, and her request framed around how fast it worked is itself a caution flag in a patient with a substance use history. Benzodiazepines are intended for short-term, as-needed use, not for ongoing residual anxiety.
wrongExplanations.2: Diazepam is long-acting with active metabolites that accumulate, and it carries the same cross-dependence problem with her alcohol use disorder. Its recognized role is alcohol withdrawal taper, not maintenance anxiolysis.
wrongExplanations.3: 200 mg daily is the top of sertraline's approved range, so this option asks for a dose that does not exist on the label and adds adverse-effect risk with no expected additional benefit.
wrongExplanations.4: Cross-tapering to another SSRI discards a substantial, documented partial response to reach for a same-mechanism agent. Paroxetine additionally has the shortest half-life and the worst discontinuation syndrome in the class.

questions.eli5: Her antidepressant is already maxed out and mostly working, so the answer is to add something rather than change it. Because she is in recovery from alcohol, the calming pills she is asking for are off the table, and buspirone eases anxiety without being habit-forming.

questions.stem: The patient described above is started on the selected agent and her as-needed alprazolam is discontinued. She returns 4 days later and states, 'This new pill does absolutely nothing — it is like taking water.' She confirms she has taken every dose as prescribed and has had no nausea, sedation, or other adverse effects. Which of the following best explains her experience?
choices: A. She has developed pharmacodynamic tolerance to the new agent within 4 days
B. Residual alprazolam is displacing the new agent from a shared binding site
C. She is experiencing benzodiazepine discontinuation syndrome that masks the new agent
D. A serum concentration should be drawn to confirm that dosing is adequate
E. The agent has no activity at the GABA-A receptor and requires 4 to 6 weeks to work
questions.explanation: Buspirone is a partial agonist at the 5-HT1A serotonin receptor and has no activity at the GABA-A receptor, which is exactly why it produces no sedation, no euphoria, and no dependence. It is also why it does nothing acutely: like an antidepressant, it needs roughly 4 to 6 weeks to produce its anxiolytic effect. Board pearl — the phrase patients use after switching off a benzodiazepine is almost verbatim 'it is like water,' because they are comparing a drug with no immediate subjective effect against one that worked within 30 minutes. Set that expectation before the switch, or the patient stops the medication before it can work.  [Learning objectives: LO 081]

wrongExplanations.0: Tolerance requires receptor or signaling adaptation over repeated exposure and could not develop to a therapeutic effect that has not yet appeared. There is nothing to become tolerant to at day 4.
wrongExplanations.1: Alprazolam acts at the benzodiazepine site on the GABA-A receptor while buspirone acts at 5-HT1A — different receptors entirely, so no competitive displacement is possible.
wrongExplanations.2: Discontinuation syndrome would produce active symptoms such as rebound anxiety, insomnia, tremor, or in severe cases seizures. She describes the absence of any effect, not the presence of new ones, and reports no adverse effects at all.
wrongExplanations.3: Buspirone is not dosed to a serum concentration; unlike lithium or valproate, it has no established therapeutic drug-monitoring range, and a level would not explain a delayed-onset mechanism.

questions.eli5: Her old anxiety pill worked in half an hour, so the new one feels like nothing. The new one works on a completely different switch in the brain and needs about a month to build up before she feels any benefit.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the office by his mother because he has refused to board the school bus on 11 of the past 14 school days. He tells his mother that 'bad men' will break into the house and take her while he is gone, and he telephones her from the school nurse's office to confirm she is unhurt. On school mornings he reports stomachaches and headaches that resolve completely once he is allowed to stay home, and on weekends he has no complaints. He sleeps in his mother's doorway several nights per week. His mother notes that she herself was 'exactly the same way' as a child. He speaks freely with the physician, makes appropriate eye contact, reciprocates conversation, and plays cooperatively with his younger sister; his teachers describe him as talkative and socially engaged in class when he does attend. Developmental milestones were met on time. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Every element points at separation itself: worry that harm will befall an attachment figure, reluctance to leave home, school refusal, sleeping near the parent, and somatic complaints that appear on school mornings and vanish when he is allowed to stay home — the classic feigned illness pattern. Separation anxiety disorder affects about 4% of school-aged children, is more common in girls, and runs in families, often in close-knit ones where a parent's own separation anxiety is copied by the child; his mother's remark is that familial clue. Board pearl — treatment starts by identifying the trigger and using therapy plus family therapy, with a serotonergic antidepressant added only alongside behavioral work, never as the sole intervention.  [Learning objectives: LO 035]

wrongExplanations.0: Autism spectrum disorder requires social communication deficits plus restricted, repetitive behaviors. He makes eye contact, reciprocates conversation, plays cooperatively, and is described as socially engaged at school — the explicit negatives that close this option.
wrongExplanations.1: Generalized anxiety disorder requires excessive worry across multiple domains for more than 6 months. His worry has a single theme, and he is symptom-free on weekends when no separation is required.
wrongExplanations.2: Selective mutism is a consistent failure to speak in one specific setting despite normal speech elsewhere, lasting at least 1 month. He speaks freely with the physician and is described as talkative in class.
wrongExplanations.4: A specific phobia is fear of a discrete object or situation such as an animal, heights, or injections. School buses and school itself are the route of separation here, not the feared object; he fears what will happen to his mother in his absence.

questions.eli5: His stomachaches only show up on school mornings and disappear the moment he gets to stay home, and what he is actually scared of is that something will happen to his mom while he is away. Being afraid of being apart from a parent, not of school itself, is separation anxiety disorder.

questions.stem: A second-year medical student is hungry midway through a 2-hour lecture but remains seated. Afterward she explains that she stayed partly because gathering her belongings and finding her seat again would have been inconvenient for her, but mostly because standing up and walking out would have disrupted her classmates and been disrespectful to the lecturer. In Freud's structural model, the second consideration is best attributed to which of the following?
questions.explanation: Freud's structural model has three parts. The id is the raw, unfiltered drive — here, the impulse to get up and get food immediately. The ego supplies primitive, practical restraint that lets a person function in society, which is the first reason she gives: leaving and returning would be inconvenient for her. The superego adds the fine-tuned social and moral layer on top of that, which is the second reason: leaving would disturb others and disrespect the lecturer. Board pearl — the split to hold onto is that the ego restrains for practical reasons and the superego restrains for moral and social ones; defense mechanisms are the unconscious tools the ego uses to keep conflict among these three from overwhelming the person.  [Learning objectives: LO 061]

wrongExplanations.0: The id is the unfiltered drive itself — the hunger pushing her to leave right now. It is what the other two structures are restraining, not the source of restraint.
wrongExplanations.1: The ego accounts for her first reason, the practical inconvenience of leaving and returning. It provides basic reality-testing restraint but not the moral weighing of how her exit would affect other people.
wrongExplanations.3: The unconscious is a level of awareness in Freud's topographic model, not a structure in the structural model, and it does not describe a moral restraint on behavior.
wrongExplanations.4: The preconscious likewise belongs to the topographic model and refers to material accessible to awareness but not currently in it — it is not an agency that restrains action.

questions.eli5: One part of her wanted food right away. Another part said leaving would be a hassle for her. The part that said it would be rude to the teacher and the class is the superego, the moral rule-follower.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman comes to the office 3 weeks after she was pulled from a burning apartment building in which two of her neighbors died. Since the fire she has had nightly dreams of smoke filling a hallway, intrusive images of the stairwell that arrive without warning during the day, and a startle response so pronounced that a slammed door made her drop a full tray at work. She has refused to re-enter any building with an interior stairwell and now takes a 40-minute detour to avoid the block where the fire occurred. She describes feeling 'behind glass,' as though events are happening at a distance, and she has been unable to recall how she got out of the building. She reports no hallucinations and no fixed false beliefs. She has no psychiatric history, does not drink alcohol, and urine toxicology screening is negative. Vital signs are within normal limits and physical examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: She has genuine Criterion A trauma exposure — actual death and threatened death — plus intrusion (nightmares, intrusive images), avoidance (stairwells, the block), arousal (exaggerated startle), and dissociation (derealization described as being behind glass, plus inability to recall her escape). The buried clue is the clock: at 3 weeks she sits inside the 3-day to 1-month window that defines acute stress disorder. Board pearl — acute stress disorder is the anxiety-chapter equivalent of brief psychotic disorder, sharing PTSD's symptom domains on a compressed timeline; if these same symptoms persist past 1 month, the diagnosis converts to PTSD without any change in what the patient is experiencing.  [Learning objectives: LO 060, 098]

wrongExplanations.1: Adjustment disorder can follow any identifiable stressor, but it is diagnosed only when the presentation does not meet criteria for another specific disorder. She has full trauma-related symptomatology after Criterion A exposure, so the more specific trauma diagnosis takes precedence.
wrongExplanations.2: Brief psychotic disorder requires at least one core psychotic symptom — delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, or grossly disorganized behavior. She explicitly reports no hallucinations and no fixed false beliefs. Derealization is a dissociative symptom with intact reality testing, not psychosis.
wrongExplanations.3: Generalized anxiety disorder requires excessive worry about multiple everyday domains for more than 6 months. Her symptoms are tethered entirely to one event 3 weeks ago.
wrongExplanations.4: Major depressive disorder requires depressed mood or anhedonia plus additional neurovegetative symptoms for at least 2 weeks. Neither core symptom is described; her presentation is intrusion, avoidance, arousal, and dissociation.
wrongExplanations.5: PTSD requires that symptoms persist for more than 1 month. At 3 weeks she has not reached that threshold, which is the single criterion separating these two diagnoses.

questions.eli5: Three weeks after escaping a deadly fire she has nightmares, jumps at loud noises, avoids stairwells, and feels like she is watching life through glass. Under one month, this exact picture is called acute stress disorder.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman comes to the office 7 months after she was pulled from a burning apartment building in which two of her neighbors died. Since the fire she has had nightly dreams of smoke filling a hallway, intrusive images of the stairwell that arrive without warning during the day, and a startle response so pronounced that a slammed door made her drop a full tray at work. She has refused to re-enter any building with an interior stairwell and now takes a 40-minute detour to avoid the block where the fire occurred. She has become convinced that she is 'the kind of person who lets people die,' has withdrawn from her closest friends, and no longer takes the photography classes she once organized her week around. She reports no hallucinations and no fixed false beliefs. She has no psychiatric history, does not drink alcohol, and urine toxicology screening is negative. Vital signs are within normal limits and physical examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This is the identical presentation with one variable moved — 3 weeks becomes 7 months — and that single change converts the diagnosis. PTSD requires Criterion A trauma exposure plus intrusion (B), avoidance (C), negative alterations in cognition and mood (D), and arousal (E), all persisting beyond 1 month (F) with impairment (G) and no substance or medical explanation (H). The persistent negative self-belief that she is the kind of person who lets people die, plus social withdrawal and loss of a valued activity, supplies Criterion D, which was not required at 3 weeks. Board pearl — most acute stress disorder resolves within the first 30 days; the patients still symptomatic past that mark are the ones whose diagnosis converts.  [Learning objectives: LO 060, 098]

wrongExplanations.0: Acute stress disorder is capped at 1 month post-trauma. At 7 months she is well outside that window, and the diagnosis converts rather than persisting under the same name.
wrongExplanations.1: Adjustment disorder applies when the presentation does not meet criteria for another specific disorder, and its own timing rule expects resolution within 6 months after the stressor ends. She meets full PTSD criteria at 7 months.
wrongExplanations.2: Brief psychotic disorder requires a core psychotic symptom lasting 1 day to less than 1 month. She has neither hallucinations nor delusions, and her belief about herself is a negative self-appraisal, not a fixed false belief held against evidence.
wrongExplanations.3: Generalized anxiety disorder requires excessive worry about multiple everyday domains rather than symptoms anchored to a single traumatic event.
wrongExplanations.5: Withdrawal and loss of interest could suggest depression, but they occur here within a trauma syndrome that also includes nightmares, intrusive images, trauma-specific avoidance, and exaggerated startle — none of which major depressive disorder accounts for. Her negative cognitions are Criterion D of PTSD.

questions.eli5: Same fire, same nightmares and jumpiness, but now it has been seven months instead of three weeks, and she has started believing she is a person who lets people die. Once these symptoms last longer than a month, the name changes to PTSD.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman is brought to the office by her sister 10 weeks after her husband of 5 years left her for a younger colleague. Since then she has been tearful most days, has quit her accounting job without notice, and has begun drinking four to five glasses of wine nightly, having previously drunk only socially. She has telephoned her former husband's new partner repeatedly at night, twice leaving messages that the sister describes as 'threatening,' and last week she keyed the partner's car. She denies suicidal ideation and denies any period of elevated mood or decreased need for sleep. She has no prior psychiatric or legal history, and reports no anhedonia, appetite change, or feelings of worthlessness. Vital signs are within normal limits. Aminotransferases and complete blood count are normal, and urine toxicology screening is negative. On mental status examination, affect is tearful and reactive, and thought process is linear. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
choices: A. Adjustment disorder with depressed mood
C. Adjustment disorder with mixed anxiety and depressed mood
D. Adjustment disorder with disturbance of conduct
E. Major depressive disorder, single episode
F. Adjustment disorder with mixed disturbance of emotions and conduct
questions.explanation: Adjustment disorder requires symptoms beginning within 3 months of an identifiable stressor, distress out of proportion to that stressor or clear functional impairment, and a presentation that does not meet criteria for another disorder. Her stressor was 10 weeks ago and did not have to be life-threatening — that is precisely what separates adjustment disorder from PTSD and acute stress disorder. The subtype is decided by counting what is present: she has emotional symptoms (tearfulness, low mood) AND conduct symptoms (quitting without notice, threatening calls, property destruction), which together define the mixed disturbance of emotions and conduct subtype. Board pearl — adjustment disorders are the most commonly encountered psychiatric disorders overall, and symptoms must resolve within 6 months after the stressor and its consequences end.  [Learning objectives: LO 060, 098]

wrongExplanations.0: The depressed mood subtype is used when emotional symptoms stand alone. It ignores the threatening calls and the keyed car, which are conduct symptoms that must be captured in the subtype.
wrongExplanations.1: The anxiety subtype requires nervousness, worry, or jitteriness as the predominant feature. Her presentation is tearful and behaviorally disinhibited rather than anxious.
wrongExplanations.2: This subtype combines two emotional presentations, anxiety and depressed mood. It still leaves her disturbance of conduct unaccounted for.
wrongExplanations.3: The disturbance of conduct subtype is used when behavior violating norms or the rights of others is the whole picture. She is also tearful most days, so an emotional component is present alongside the conduct.
wrongExplanations.4: Major depressive disorder requires 5 or more SIG E CAPS symptoms including depressed mood or anhedonia. She explicitly denies anhedonia, appetite change, and worthlessness, and her affect is reactive — these stated negatives keep her below the MDE threshold, which is what allows an adjustment disorder to be diagnosed at all.

questions.eli5: Ten weeks after her husband left, she is crying a lot and also doing things she never used to do, like quitting her job on the spot and scratching someone's car. Because she has both the feelings part and the behavior part, the diagnosis names both.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man who served two combat deployments is seen for follow-up of posttraumatic stress disorder. He has taken sertraline 150 mg PO daily for 5 months, with meaningful improvement in intrusive daytime memories and avoidance. He continues to have vivid combat nightmares four to five nights weekly that wake him in a panic, after which he patrols the house before he can lie back down; his wife has moved to the guest room. He denies hallucinations, denies suicidal ideation, and has no history of substance use. Pulse is 68/min and blood pressure is 118/70 mm Hg supine; physical examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate addition to his regimen?
questions.explanation: The PTSD pharmacotherapy algorithm branches first on the sleep complaint. Sleep disturbed by nightmares and nighttime hyperarousal gets prazosin, an alpha-1 adrenergic blocker; sleep-onset difficulty without nightmares gets trazodone. Only after that does the algorithm proceed to an SSRI trial, then a second SSRI, SNRI, or mirtazapine, with an antipsychotic added only if psychosis is present. His SSRI is already working on the daytime cluster, so the correct move targets the residual symptom specifically. Board pearl — prazosin for PTSD nightmares is a board favorite precisely because the drug is better known for benign prostatic hyperplasia and hypertension; check for orthostasis when starting it.  [Learning objectives: LO 076]

wrongExplanations.0: Clonidine is an alpha-2 agonist listed as an augmenting option for the hyperarousal cluster generally, but prazosin is the agent specifically indicated for nightmares and nighttime hyperarousal and is the first branch point in the algorithm.
wrongExplanations.1: Benzodiazepines are generally avoided in PTSD — they do not meaningfully improve core symptoms, carry dependence risk, and diazepam's long half-life and active metabolites make it a particularly poor choice for chronic nightly use.
wrongExplanations.2: Mirtazapine appears in the algorithm only after a second SSRI or SNRI trial, and it is a global antidepressant-plus-sedative strategy rather than a targeted treatment for nightmares. His SSRI is already producing meaningful benefit.
wrongExplanations.4: Quetiapine is an augmentation option for the hyperarousal cluster, but antipsychotics are reserved for later steps or for the presence of psychosis, which he explicitly denies. It also carries metabolic and sedation burden that prazosin does not.

questions.eli5: His main medicine is already helping during the day, but the combat nightmares are still waking him up every night. Prazosin, a blood-pressure pill, is the specific medicine known to quiet trauma nightmares.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman has been given a diagnosis of panic disorder after a negative cardiac and pulmonary evaluation. She is started on the medication class considered first-line for long-term control of this disorder and is scheduled for follow-up in 4 weeks. She asks what to expect. Which of the following is the most appropriate statement to make to this patient?
choices: A. "This works within 30 minutes, so take one only when you feel an attack beginning."
B. "You may have stomach upset and feel more anxious in the first week or two, before the benefit arrives at four to six weeks."
C. "You will need to avoid aged cheeses, cured meats, and draft beer for as long as you take this."
D. "We will draw a blood level in five days and adjust your dose based on the result."
E. "Stopping this abruptly can cause a withdrawal seizure, so it is critical never to miss a dose."
questions.explanation: Two inferential steps, with the middle one unstated: panic disorder's first-line long-term pharmacotherapy is an SSRI (short-acting benzodiazepines are reserved for the acute attack), and the counseling point that matters most for an SSRI is the mismatch in timing. The transporter is blocked the moment the first dose is taken, so serotonin floods the synapse immediately and hits gastrointestinal and other peripheral targets right away — but postsynaptic receptors need roughly 4 to 6 weeks to adapt before the patient feels better. Board pearl — this is why side effects appear in weeks 1 to 2 while benefit appears at weeks 4 to 6, and why 'I have taken it two weeks and feel no different' is an expected course rather than treatment failure. Warning the patient in advance is what keeps them from stopping during the worst window.  [Learning objectives: LO 048, 050, 073, 076]

wrongExplanations.0: This describes a short-acting benzodiazepine used as needed for an attack in progress. Benzodiazepines are not the first-line long-term treatment for panic disorder, and instructing a patient to take a daily SSRI only during attacks would make it ineffective.
wrongExplanations.2: Tyramine restriction applies to MAOIs, where dietary tyramine can precipitate a hypertensive crisis. MAOIs are fourth-line antidepressants and are not first-line for panic disorder.
wrongExplanations.3: Serum concentration monitoring applies to lithium, valproate, and carbamazepine. SSRIs have no established therapeutic drug-monitoring range and are titrated to clinical response and tolerability.
wrongExplanations.4: Abrupt discontinuation of an SSRI causes a discontinuation syndrome — flu-like symptoms, dizziness, brain zaps, irritability — not a withdrawal seizure. Withdrawal seizures are the danger with abrupt cessation of benzodiazepines, barbiturates, or alcohol.

questions.eli5: The pill starts changing her brain chemistry the very first day, which is why upset stomach and jitters show up right away. Feeling better takes about a month, so she needs to know the rough part comes first.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man has a 2-year history of intrusive thoughts that his hands are contaminated with fecal bacteria. He washes them until they crack and bleed, currently spending about 3 hours daily on washing rituals, and he is emphatic that the thoughts are 'stupid and irrational — I know they are not true, and I hate that I do this.' Twelve weeks ago he was started on fluoxetine 20 mg PO daily and has taken every dose. His washing has decreased from 5 hours to about 3 hours daily and he reports the obsessions are 'a little quieter,' but he is still late to class most days. He has had no nausea, insomnia, sexual dysfunction, or other adverse effects. He has no cardiac history, no seizure history, and does not use alcohol or illicit drugs. Vital signs are within normal limits. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in pharmacotherapy?
choices: E. Increase fluoxetine toward the maximum dose
questions.explanation: The trap is reading a partial response at 12 weeks as a failed trial. It is not a failed trial, because he was never at an OCD dose. Obsessive-compulsive disorder requires substantially higher SSRI doses than depression does, and 20 mg of fluoxetine is a standard depression starting dose. He is improving and has no adverse effects at all, which means the dose has room to move. Board pearl — the discriminator confirming OCD here is that the obsessions are ego-dystonic: he recognizes them as irrational and unwanted, which separates OCD from obsessive-compulsive personality disorder, where the traits are ego-syntonic and the patient sees nothing wrong with them.  [Learning objectives: LO 036, 081]

wrongExplanations.0: Benzodiazepines have limited benefit in OCD and do not treat obsessions or compulsions. Adding one exposes a 22-year-old to dependence risk while leaving an underdosed SSRI in place.
wrongExplanations.1: Adjunctive antipsychotics are reserved for OCD that remains resistant after multiple adequate trials of SSRIs or clomipramine. He has not yet completed even one adequate trial, since the dose has never reached the OCD range.
wrongExplanations.2: Clomipramine is the established alternative for OCD, but cross-tapering abandons an agent that is producing measurable improvement without adverse effects, and it trades a clean SSRI for a tricyclic with anticholinergic and cardiac liabilities.
wrongExplanations.3: Bupropion is not an effective treatment for OCD — it has no serotonergic activity at all — and its activating profile can worsen anxiety.

questions.eli5: He is getting better on his medicine and having no side effects, but he is on a depression-sized dose. Obsessive-compulsive disorder needs a much bigger dose of the same drug, so you climb the dose before you change anything.

questions.stem: Marcus is a 38-year-old estate attorney whose partners have asked him to seek an evaluation. He redrafts routine documents six or seven times to perfect the formatting and has missed three filing deadlines as a result. He keeps every draft of every file going back 12 years and will not let the office discard any of them. He has not taken a vacation in 9 years, describes weekends as 'wasted time,' and refuses to delegate because no associate will 'do it the correct way.' He lives well below his means and reuses envelopes. He denies any unwanted intrusive thoughts and denies performing any repetitive act to relieve anxiety. When his partners' concerns are described to him, he appears puzzled and states that his standards are 'simply the correct way to practice law' and that the firm's real problem is everyone else's carelessness. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This is a pervasive, lifelong pattern of perfectionism that interferes with task completion, excessive devotion to work at the expense of leisure, inability to delegate, miserliness, and inability to discard worn-out or worthless objects — the LOW MIRTH picture of obsessive-compulsive personality disorder. The decisive discriminator is in the last two sentences: he has no true obsessions or compulsions, and the traits are ego-syntonic. He sees no problem with himself and locates the problem in everyone else. Board pearl — OCD is ego-dystonic and the patient wants the thoughts gone; OCPD is ego-syntonic and the patient wants the world to meet his standard.
