wrongExplanations.0: Dexmethylphenidate ER is a member of the methylphenidate family he has already failed for tic exacerbation. Trying another formulation of the same family invites the same adverse effect.
wrongExplanations.1: Lisdexamfetamine belongs to the amphetamine family, and tics are called out as especially associated with amphetamines. He had his worst tic exacerbation on mixed amphetamine salts, and its appetite suppression is a further problem at the 10th weight percentile.
wrongExplanations.2: Guanfacine is a central alpha-2 agonist that reduces hyperactivity and impulsivity but does NOT meaningfully improve attention. His primary functional problem is attention, so it targets the wrong domain.
wrongExplanations.4: Bupropion is used off-label for ADHD but is not a standard second-line agent, and it lowers the seizure threshold without offering any specific advantage in a child with tics.
wrongExplanations.5: Clonidine is the other alpha-2 agonist and shares guanfacine's limitation — it calms the body without improving focus — and adds fatigue and blood pressure effects in a child whose blood pressure is already 104/64 mm Hg.

questions.eli5: Both stimulants he tried made his tics much worse, so he needs a non-stimulant. Atomoxetine actually helps attention, which is his biggest problem — the calming medicines would settle his body but not help him focus.

questions.stem: Compared with stimulant medications, central alpha-2 agonists such as guanfacine and clonidine used in the treatment of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder:
choices: A. produce a higher overall response rate, approaching 90 percent.
B. reduce hyperactivity and impulsivity but do not meaningfully improve attention.
C. carry a greater risk of tic exacerbation than amphetamine-family agents.
D. are the preferred first-line agents in children younger than 12 years of age.
E. act by blocking dopamine and norepinephrine reuptake at the presynaptic terminal.
questions.explanation: Guanfacine and clonidine are central alpha-2 adrenergic agonists borrowed from hypertension management. They decrease sympathetic tone, which quiets hyperactivity and impulsivity — but they do not improve attention itself, and that limitation determines when they are the right choice. The memory hook is that atomoxetine focuses while the alphas calm: atomoxetine genuinely helps attention, just less often at about 60% versus 80 to 90% for stimulants, whereas the alpha-2 agonists address the body rather than the focus. Board pearl — their expected adverse effects are fatigue and blood pressure lowering, consistent with their sympatholytic mechanism and antihypertensive origins.  [Learning objectives: LO 092]

wrongExplanations.0: The 80 to 90% response figure belongs to stimulants. Alpha-2 agonists are a negotiated compromise used when stimulants cannot be given, not a higher-yield alternative.
wrongExplanations.2: Tic exacerbation is associated especially with amphetamine-family stimulants. Alpha-2 agonists are in fact among the agents chosen when tics are a concern, so this reverses the relationship.
wrongExplanations.3: Long-acting stimulants are first-line in children unless contraindicated; alpha-2 agonists are used when stimulants are not preferred or not tolerated.
wrongExplanations.4: Blocking dopamine and norepinephrine reuptake, plus enhancing their release, is the stimulant mechanism. Alpha-2 agonists act at postsynaptic alpha-2 adrenergic receptors to reduce sympathetic outflow.

questions.eli5: These medicines come from blood-pressure treatment. They settle a child's body down so there is less squirming and blurting, but they do not actually make it easier to pay attention.

questions.stem: Which of the following instruments is most commonly used to gather the collateral information required for the evaluation of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder in a school-aged child?
choices: A. Modified Checklist for Autism in Toddlers, Revised with Follow-Up (M-CHAT-R/F)
E. Vanderbilt parent and teacher rating forms
questions.explanation: The Vanderbilt scales exist in matched parent and teacher versions for a structural reason: ADHD requires symptoms in at least 2 settings, so the instrument is built to collect home and school data separately and compare them. The Conners scale and the ADHD Rating Scale serve the same purpose. Board pearl — pair each scale with its disorder: Vanderbilt, Conners, and ADHD-RS for ADHD; M-CHAT-R/F and related tools for autism screening with ADOS as the gold-standard formal evaluation; GAD-7 for generalized anxiety with a threshold of 10 or greater; and PHQ-9 for depression.  [Learning objectives: LO 100, 101]

wrongExplanations.0: The M-CHAT-R/F is an autism screening tool for toddlers, applied at the 18-month and 24-month autism-specific screening visits rather than for ADHD in a school-aged child.
wrongExplanations.1: The ADOS is the gold-standard formal evaluation instrument for autism spectrum disorder — and even there it is not required, since ASD remains a clinical diagnosis. It has no role in ADHD assessment.
wrongExplanations.2: The GAD-7 screens for generalized anxiety disorder, with a score of 10 or greater suggesting a probable diagnosis. It does not assess attention or hyperactivity.
wrongExplanations.3: The PHQ-9 is the validated depression screener that allows primary care providers to reach a diagnosis quickly. It is not an ADHD instrument.

questions.eli5: ADHD only counts if the problems show up in more than one place, so the standard questionnaire comes in two versions — one for parents and one for teachers — and you compare them.

questions.stem: An 11-year-old boy is evaluated for restricted interests centered on subway maps, poor eye contact, limited back-and-forth conversation, and repetitive twisting of objects. His parents ask about diagnostic testing. Which of the following statements is most accurate?
choices: A. The ADOS must be completed before autism spectrum disorder can be diagnosed
B. The M-CHAT-R/F is the formal diagnostic instrument for patients of this age
C. The ADOS is a gold-standard formal evaluation, but the diagnosis remains clinical
D. Autism-specific screening is recommended at the 9-month and 30-month visits
E. Asperger disorder remains a distinct diagnosis separate from autism spectrum disorder
questions.explanation: Autism spectrum disorder is a clinical diagnosis resting on persistent deficits in social communication and reciprocity plus restricted and repetitive behaviors, with symptoms present in early development and causing functional impairment. The ADOS is the gold-standard formal evaluation instrument and is genuinely useful, particularly in trained and research settings, but it is a support to the clinical judgment rather than a gate in front of it. Board pearl — general developmental screening occurs at 9, 18, and 30 months, while autism-SPECIFIC screening occurs at 18 and 24 months; the two schedules overlap only at 18 months, and mixing them up is a favorite distractor.  [Learning objectives: LO 101]

wrongExplanations.0: Requiring the ADOS would make the diagnosis inaccessible wherever trained administrators are unavailable. The diagnosis is clinical, and this is the exact misconception the objective targets.
wrongExplanations.1: The M-CHAT-R/F is a screening tool for toddlers, not a diagnostic instrument, and it is not designed for an 11-year-old.
wrongExplanations.3: 9 and 30 months are two of the three general developmental screening visits. Autism-specific screening is recommended at 18 and 24 months.
wrongExplanations.4: Asperger disorder was folded into autism spectrum disorder in DSM-5 and is no longer a separate diagnosis; severity is now conveyed by support levels 1 through 3.

questions.eli5: There is a very good formal test for autism, but a doctor does not have to run it before making the diagnosis. Autism is diagnosed by carefully watching and asking, not by a single test result.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old girl is brought to the office by her father because of 3 months of irritability, frequent stomachaches with no identified medical cause, tearfulness, loss of interest in gymnastics, and declining grades. She has begun refusing to see friends and reports feeling 'bad about myself all the time.' She denies suicidal ideation and there are no psychotic symptoms. She has no history of elevated mood or decreased need for sleep. Physical examination, complete blood count, and thyroid-stimulating hormone are normal. She has been in weekly cognitive behavioral therapy for 3 months with insufficient improvement, and her parents wish to add medication. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
questions.explanation: Childhood depression often presents with irritability and somatic complaints rather than classic sadness, which is exactly this picture. For pharmacotherapy, only two SSRIs carry pediatric MDD approval and the age cutoffs are the tested point: fluoxetine from age 8 and escitalopram from age 12. At 9 years old, fluoxetine is the only approved option. Board pearl — fluoxetine is the drug of choice in children generally, and its very long half-life makes it forgiving of the missed doses that are common in this age group.  [Learning objectives: LO 103]

wrongExplanations.1: Escitalopram carries a pediatric MDD indication only from age 12. She is 9, and this single age difference is the buried clue the item turns on.
wrongExplanations.2: Sertraline is widely used and carries a pediatric indication for obsessive-compulsive disorder, but not for major depressive disorder in children.
wrongExplanations.3: Bupropion has no pediatric depression indication, lowers the seizure threshold, and is contraindicated in eating disorders — it is not an appropriate first choice in a 9-year-old.
wrongExplanations.4: Paroxetine has the shortest half-life and the worst discontinuation syndrome of the class, carries a pregnancy cardiac-defect signal, and has no pediatric depression approval; it is generally avoided in children.

questions.eli5: Kids with depression often look irritable and get stomachaches instead of looking sad. Only two of these medicines are approved for depression in children, and the other one cannot be used until age twelve — so fluoxetine it is.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old girl has been brought to the emergency department seven times in 5 months for unexplained episodes of vomiting and rectal bleeding. Every episode has begun while she was alone with her mother, and no episode has occurred during any of her three inpatient admissions once continuous nursing observation was in place. Extensive gastroenterologic and hematologic workups have been normal. Nursing staff note that the mother is unusually conversant with the child's central line care, requests specific laboratory tests by name, and has asked twice today when the child will be admitted. The mother has no medical training on record. She has stable finances, no pending litigation, and no custody dispute. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate action?
choices: A. Discharge the child home with close outpatient gastroenterology follow-up
B. Refer the mother for outpatient psychotherapy and reassess in 6 months
C. Confront the mother directly and ask her to stop inducing symptoms
D. Report the case to child protective services
E. Obtain a skeletal survey before making any report
F. Arrange a family meeting with both parents to discuss the pattern
questions.explanation: This is factitious disorder imposed on another, historically Munchausen syndrome by proxy: a caregiver induces or fabricates illness in a dependent to obtain the sick role by proxy. The pattern is diagnostic — symptoms occur only in the caregiver's presence and stop entirely under independent observation, workups are repeatedly normal, and the caregiver welcomes admission and displays unusual medical fluency without training. The absence of financial, legal, or custody incentives rules out malingering by proxy. This is child abuse and carries a mandatory reporting obligation. Board pearl — on examination stems, do not over-investigate at the expense of immediate safety and reporting duties.  [Learning objectives: LO 080]

wrongExplanations.0: Discharging the child returns her to the person inducing the illness. The stem establishes that episodes occur only in the mother's presence, which makes discharge the single most dangerous option.
wrongExplanations.1: Outpatient psychotherapy for the caregiver does not protect the child, and a 6-month reassessment interval leaves a 2-year-old in an actively harmful situation.
wrongExplanations.2: Direct confrontation typically produces denial and flight to a different hospital, breaking continuity of care and delaying protection. It is not the appropriate management step.
wrongExplanations.4: A skeletal survey may become part of a broader abuse evaluation, but reporting is not contingent on completing an investigation. Suspicion is the reporting threshold, and delaying the report to gather more evidence inverts the obligation.
wrongExplanations.5: A family meeting neither protects the child nor discharges the mandatory reporting duty, and it may alert the caregiver before protective services can act.

questions.eli5: The little girl only gets sick when she is alone with her mom, and never when nurses are watching. That means someone is making her sick, which is a form of child abuse, and it has to be reported right away.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old woman submits a written request for a complete copy of her medical record from the psychiatric clinic where she has been treated for 3 years. She has signed the clinic's authorization form and there is no pending litigation or court order. Under the HIPAA Privacy Rule, which of the following portions of her record may the clinic withhold from her?
choices: C. Discharge summaries from prior hospitalizations
questions.explanation: HIPAA grants patients a right of access to their protected health information, and that right explicitly EXCLUDES psychotherapy notes — the clinician's separately maintained process notes from a counseling session, kept apart from the rest of the chart. Everything else in the record is accessible to her. Board pearl — the Privacy Rule covers all PHI whether paper, electronic, or spoken, while the Security Rule covers electronic PHI only; no authorization is required for treatment, payment, or healthcare operations; and states are free to enact rules stricter than this federal floor.  [Learning objectives: LO 057]

wrongExplanations.0: Laboratory results are ordinary protected health information within the designated record set and are subject to the patient's right of access.
wrongExplanations.2: Discharge summaries document care delivered and are part of the accessible medical record; they are not the separately maintained process notes the exclusion covers.
wrongExplanations.3: The medication list is core clinical information and is among the portions patients most clearly have a right to obtain.
wrongExplanations.4: Radiology reports are diagnostic results within the designated record set and carry no special exclusion.

questions.eli5: Patients can ask for their own medical records, and the hospital has to hand almost all of it over. The one exception is the therapist's private session notes, which are kept separate and do not have to be shared.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man with a newly diagnosed operable colon cancer refuses surgery. When asked, he can state his diagnosis, describe the proposed operation and its risks and benefits, explain the likely consequences of declining it, and give a consistent reason for his choice grounded in his own values. He has a remote history of a single depressive episode, is not currently depressed, and has no delusions or hallucinations. His surgeon requests a psychiatric consultation to determine whether he is 'competent to refuse.' Which of the following statements is most accurate?
choices: A. Competence is determined at the bedside by the consulting psychiatrist
B. Capacity is a global attribute that applies across all of a patient's decisions
C. A prior psychiatric diagnosis by itself establishes that a patient lacks capacity
D. Involuntary hospitalization would render him automatically unable to refuse treatment
E. Capacity is a clinical, decision-specific judgment; competence is decided by a court
questions.explanation: Capacity and competence are routinely conflated but belong to different systems. Capacity is a clinical determination made by a physician about a specific decision at a specific time, assessed against four standards — often remembered as CARD: communicate a choice, appreciate the facts, reason through them, and demonstrate understanding. This patient satisfies all four, so he has capacity to refuse. Competence, by contrast, is a legal status decided by a court. Board pearl — involuntary hospitalization does NOT equal incompetence to refuse medication; overriding a refusal still requires proving incapacity and that treatment serves the patient's best interest, except in a genuine emergency.  [Learning objectives: LO 057, 079]

wrongExplanations.0: Physicians assess capacity, not competence. A psychiatrist can testify and offer an opinion, but the competence determination itself belongs to a judge.
wrongExplanations.1: Capacity is task-specific and time-specific. A patient may lack capacity for a complex surgical decision while retaining it for simpler ones, and capacity can fluctuate with delirium or illness.
wrongExplanations.2: A psychiatric history never by itself establishes incapacity. Capacity is judged on the patient's actual performance against the four standards, which he meets fully.
wrongExplanations.3: Involuntary hospitalization and incompetence to refuse medication are separate determinations. Medicating over objection in a non-emergency requires due process — a judicial petition — rather than following automatically from commitment.

questions.eli5: Doctors decide whether a patient can understand and make one particular decision — that is capacity. Only a judge can declare someone legally incompetent overall. This man understands everything, so his refusal stands.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman develops involuntary, non-rhythmic, flowing movements of the trunk and proximal limbs that she cannot suppress. She remains fully oriented, her mood is euthymic, and she reports no intrusive or unwanted thoughts. Disruption of which of the following re-entrant circuits best accounts for her presentation?
choices: A. Limbic loop: anterior cingulate cortex to ventral striatum to ventral pallidum to dorsomedial thalamus
B. Associative loop: parietal and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex to caudate to globus pallidus to ventral anterior thalamus
C. Motor loop: motor cortex to putamen to globus pallidus to ventrolateral thalamus
D. Mesolimbic pathway: ventral tegmental area to nucleus accumbens
E. Mesocortical pathway: ventral tegmental area to prefrontal cortex
F. Tuberoinfundibular pathway: hypothalamus to anterior pituitary
questions.explanation: The basal ganglia are organized as parallel re-entrant cortico-striato-pallido-thalamocortical loops (Heimer's macrosystems), and each loop maps onto a distinct clinical failure. The MOTOR loop runs motor cortex → putamen → globus pallidus → ventrolateral thalamus and back to cortex; when it overfunctions the result is hyperkinesis and dyskinesia. The two stated negatives — euthymic mood and no intrusive thoughts — deliberately exclude the other two loops. Board pearl — these loops normally regulate how much output leaves the cortex, so hyperfunction produces excess movement, excess thought, or excess emotional lability depending on which loop is involved.  [Learning objectives: LO 025]

wrongExplanations.0: The limbic loop runs through the ventral striatum and ventral pallidum to the anterior, ventral anterior, and dorsomedial thalamic nuclei; its disruption produces labile emotions and mood disorders. Her mood is explicitly euthymic.
wrongExplanations.1: The associative loop runs through the caudate to the ventral anterior thalamus; its disruption produces disordered and intrusive thoughts — what the lecture calls choreiform movements of the mind. She explicitly reports no intrusive thoughts.
wrongExplanations.3: The mesolimbic pathway is a dopaminergic projection whose hyperactivity produces the positive symptoms of psychosis and which antipsychotics target therapeutically. It is not a basal ganglia re-entrant loop and does not generate chorea.
wrongExplanations.4: The mesocortical pathway is the dopaminergic projection whose hypoactivity is linked to the negative symptoms of schizophrenia. It has no role in generating involuntary movements.
wrongExplanations.5: The tuberoinfundibular pathway carries dopamine from hypothalamus to pituitary, where blockade causes hyperprolactinemia with galactorrhea, amenorrhea, and gynecomastia. It has no motor function.

questions.eli5: The brain has three separate loops that each keep one thing in check: movement, thoughts, and emotions. Hers is stuck on the movement loop, so her body moves when she does not want it to — her mood and thinking are fine.
questions.topic: Limbic Neuroanatomy, ADHD, Pregnancy & Psychosexual Development

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man describes unwanted thoughts that, in his words, 'just dive through my mind at random' throughout the day. He has no involuntary movements, and his mood has been stable without periods of tearfulness, elation, or irritability. Neurologic examination shows normal tone, no chorea, and no tremor. Disruption of which of the following re-entrant circuits best accounts for his presentation?
choices: A. Motor loop: motor cortex to putamen to globus pallidus to ventrolateral thalamus
B. Limbic loop: anterior cingulate cortex to ventral striatum to ventral pallidum to dorsomedial thalamus
C. Mesolimbic pathway: ventral tegmental area to nucleus accumbens
D. Mesocortical pathway: ventral tegmental area to prefrontal cortex
E. Tuberoinfundibular pathway: hypothalamus to anterior pituitary
F. Associative loop: parietal and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex to caudate to globus pallidus to ventral anterior thalamus
questions.explanation: The ASSOCIATIVE loop carries sensory, parietal, and dorsolateral prefrontal cortical activity through the caudate and globus pallidus to the ventral anterior and ventrolateral thalamic nuclei and back to cortex. Its overfunction produces disordered and intrusive thoughts — the lecture's memorable phrase is choreiform movements of the mind, thoughts that dart through consciousness the way chorea darts through muscle. The parallel is the point: the same architecture, applied to cognition instead of movement. Board pearl — three loops, three failures. Motor loop breaks and you get dyskinesias; associative loop breaks and you get intrusive thoughts; limbic loop breaks and you get labile mood.  [Learning objectives: LO 025]

wrongExplanations.0: The motor loop passes through the putamen to the ventrolateral thalamus, and its disruption produces dyskinesias. His neurologic examination explicitly shows no chorea, no tremor, and normal tone.
wrongExplanations.1: The limbic loop passes through the ventral striatum and ventral pallidum, and its disruption produces labile emotions. His mood is explicitly stable with no elation, irritability, or tearfulness.
wrongExplanations.2: The mesolimbic pathway is a dopaminergic projection linked to positive psychotic symptoms and is the therapeutic target of antipsychotics. Intrusive thoughts recognized as one's own are not delusions or hallucinations.
wrongExplanations.3: The mesocortical pathway relates to negative symptoms such as avolition and flat affect, and it is notably untouched by typical antipsychotics. It does not generate intrusive thought content.
wrongExplanations.4: The tuberoinfundibular pathway governs prolactin release and has no cognitive function; blocking it causes galactorrhea, amenorrhea, and gynecomastia.

questions.eli5: The same kind of brain loop that can make muscles jerk on their own can also make thoughts jump into your head on their own. His movement and mood loops are fine — it is the thinking loop that is overactive.
questions.topic: Limbic Neuroanatomy, ADHD, Pregnancy & Psychosexual Development

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman is evaluated for rapid, unpredictable shifts in emotional state throughout the day. She has no involuntary movements and no intrusive or unwanted thoughts, and her neurologic examination shows normal tone and coordination. Disruption of which of the following re-entrant circuits best accounts for her presentation?
choices: A. Limbic loop: anterior cingulate and hippocampal cortex to ventral striatum to ventral pallidum to anterior, ventral anterior, and dorsomedial thalamic nuclei
B. Motor loop: motor cortex to putamen to globus pallidus to ventrolateral thalamus
C. Associative loop: parietal and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex to caudate to globus pallidus to ventral anterior thalamus
D. Nigrostriatal pathway: substantia nigra pars compacta to dorsal striatum
E. Mesocortical pathway: ventral tegmental area to prefrontal cortex
F. Tuberoinfundibular pathway: hypothalamus to anterior pituitary
questions.explanation: The LIMBIC loop originates in anterior cingulate, hippocampal, and orbital and medial prefrontal cortex, projects to the ventral striatum, then to the ventral pallidum, then to the anterior, ventral anterior, and dorsomedial thalamic nuclei, and returns to cortex. Its disruption produces labile emotions and mood disorders. This is the loop that contains the nucleus accumbens and amygdala, the two structures anchoring the opposing drives that underlie mood-disorder circuitry. Board pearl — this loop model sits on top of older frameworks worth recognizing by name: Papez's proposed circuit of emotion and MacLean's triune brain, in which a brainstem carrying base behavioral patterns is overlaid by an old-mammalian limbic brain and then by neocortex.  [Learning objectives: LO 025]

wrongExplanations.1: The motor loop's disruption produces dyskinesias. Her examination explicitly shows normal tone and coordination with no involuntary movements.
wrongExplanations.2: The associative loop's disruption produces disordered and intrusive thoughts, which she explicitly denies. Note that it passes through the caudate, whereas the limbic loop passes through the ventral striatum — the striatal territory is the anatomic discriminator.
wrongExplanations.3: The nigrostriatal pathway is a dopaminergic projection whose blockade produces extrapyramidal symptoms and whose degeneration produces parkinsonism. It is a motor pathway, not the limbic loop.
wrongExplanations.4: The mesocortical pathway relates to the negative symptoms of schizophrenia — avolition, alogia, flat affect — rather than to emotional lability.
wrongExplanations.5: The tuberoinfundibular pathway controls prolactin secretion and has no role in mood regulation.

questions.eli5: Her movement and thinking loops both check out fine, and what is left swinging is her mood. That is the emotion loop, which runs through the deep front part of the brain and contains the reward and fear centers.
questions.topic: Limbic Neuroanatomy, ADHD, Pregnancy & Psychosexual Development

questions.stem: Within the limbic loop, the nucleus accumbens and the amygdala anchor opposing functions that together form the basis of mood-disorder circuitry. Which of the following correctly pairs each structure with its principal neurotransmitter and behavioral output?
choices: A. Nucleus accumbens, norepinephrine, fear response; amygdala, dopamine, pleasure response
B. Nucleus accumbens, dopamine, behavioral restraint; amygdala, norepinephrine, behavioral augmentation
C. Nucleus accumbens, serotonin, pleasure response; amygdala, acetylcholine, fear response
D. Nucleus accumbens, dopamine, pleasure and behavioral augmentation; amygdala, norepinephrine, fear and behavioral restraint
E. Both structures use dopamine to mediate reward and differ only in their cortical projection target
questions.explanation: These two structures sit inside the limbic loop and pull in opposite directions. Dopamine release into the nucleus accumbens drives pleasure and behavioral augmentation — the push toward reward-seeking and, when accelerated, toward more manic behavior. The amygdala drives the fear response and behavioral restraint through norepinephrine. Mood-disorder circuitry is built on the balance between them. Board pearl — the accumbens is also the terminal field of the mesolimbic dopamine pathway and the shared final common pathway for every drug of abuse, which is why the same structure appears in the psychosis, mood, and addiction lectures.  [Learning objectives: LO 025]

wrongExplanations.0: This inverts both structures. The amygdala is the fear structure and the accumbens is the reward structure, and the neurotransmitters are swapped along with the functions.
wrongExplanations.1: The behavioral outputs are reversed. Dopamine in the accumbens augments behavior rather than restraining it, and the noradrenergic amygdala restrains rather than augments.
wrongExplanations.2: Neither neurotransmitter is correct. The accumbens is dopaminergic, not serotonergic, and the amygdala's role here is described in noradrenergic rather than cholinergic terms.
wrongExplanations.4: The two structures are functionally opposed, not parallel. Collapsing them into a single reward system erases the fear-versus-reward balance that the mood-disorder model rests on.

questions.eli5: Two little structures deep in the brain pull against each other. One uses dopamine and says go, this feels good; the other uses norepinephrine and says stop, this is scary. Mood problems come from that balance tipping.
questions.topic: Limbic Neuroanatomy, ADHD, Pregnancy & Psychosexual Development

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder has taken methylphenidate ER for 4 months. His teacher reports that he now completes and turns in nearly all assignments and that his reading has improved by a full grade level. However, both his teacher and his parents report that he still cannot remain seated through a meal or a class period, blurts out answers, and repeatedly interrupts conversations. His appetite and sleep are adequate and his weight is tracking along the 45th percentile. He has no tics and no cardiac history. Pulse is 84/min and blood pressure is 100/62 mm Hg. His parents are pleased with his academic gains and do not want to stop the current medication. Which of the following is the most appropriate addition to his regimen?
questions.explanation: Match the adjunct to the residual symptom domain. His stimulant has clearly succeeded on the inattention domain — assignments completed, reading up a grade level — and what remains is pure hyperactivity and impulsivity. Central alpha-2 agonists such as guanfacine and clonidine reduce hyperactivity and impulsivity but do not meaningfully improve attention, which makes them exactly right as an add-on here and wrong as monotherapy for an attention problem. Board pearl — ATOMs FOCUS, alphas CALM: atomoxetine actually improves attention (about 60% response versus 80 to 90% for stimulants), whereas the alpha-2 agonists quiet the body. Watch for fatigue and blood pressure lowering, consistent with their sympatholytic origin in hypertension management.  [Learning objectives: LO 042, 092]

wrongExplanations.0: Atomoxetine is a norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor that targets attention — the one domain already well controlled by his stimulant. Adding it addresses the wrong residual symptom and duplicates an effect he already has.
wrongExplanations.2: Bupropion is used off-label for ADHD but is not a standard adjunct, lowers the seizure threshold, and offers no specific advantage for residual hyperactivity in a child already responding well to a stimulant.
wrongExplanations.3: Adding a second stimulant from the amphetamine family on top of methylphenidate compounds appetite suppression, insomnia, and cardiovascular effects without addressing a domain stimulants have already maximized in him.
wrongExplanations.4: Viloxazine is a 5-HT2C partial agonist with norepinephrine reuptake inhibition — another norepinephrine-focused agent aimed at attention, so like atomoxetine it targets the domain that is already controlled.

questions.eli5: His medicine fixed his schoolwork but he still cannot sit still or stop interrupting. Guanfacine is good at calming the body down, which is exactly the part still causing trouble.
questions.topic: Limbic Neuroanatomy, ADHD, Pregnancy & Psychosexual Development

questions.stem: An 11-year-old boy weighing 40 kg (88 lb) was started on atomoxetine 18 mg PO daily 10 weeks ago after his family declined stimulant therapy. His mother reports that the medication 'never did anything at all' and asks to try something else. He has taken every dose, and she confirms no missed days. He has had no gastrointestinal upset, sedation, dizziness, irritability, or new mood symptoms. Aspartate aminotransferase is 24 U/L and alanine aminotransferase is 21 U/L. Pulse is 76/min and blood pressure is 102/64 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
choices: A. Cross-taper to viloxazine and reassess in 8 weeks
B. Add guanfacine to the current atomoxetine dose
C. Discontinue atomoxetine and begin methylphenidate ER
D. Obtain repeat liver function tests and a bilirubin level
E. Increase atomoxetine to a weight-based dose of 1 to 1.4 mg/kg
questions.explanation: This is not a failed trial — it is an underdosed one. Atomoxetine is dosed by weight at 1 to 1.4 mg/kg, which for a 40 kg child means roughly 40 to 56 mg daily. He has been taking 18 mg, about 0.45 mg/kg, well under a third of the top of the range. Underdosing is explicitly the reason clinicians conclude the drug 'never works.' The absence of any adverse effect is the buried clue that there is room to titrate. Board pearl — atomoxetine helps roughly 60% of patients versus 80 to 90% for stimulants, so it is a genuine compromise, but that comparison only applies once the drug has actually been given at a therapeutic dose.  [Learning objectives: LO 042, 092]

wrongExplanations.0: Switching to another norepinephrine-focused non-stimulant abandons an agent that has never been adequately tried, and it costs another 8 weeks to find out whether the new drug works.
wrongExplanations.1: Guanfacine reduces hyperactivity and impulsivity but does not improve attention, so it does not substitute for an adequate atomoxetine dose, and adding it papers over the dosing error.
wrongExplanations.2: His family declined stimulant therapy, and abandoning a non-stimulant that was never titrated is premature. Stimulants remain first-line in general, but the immediate problem here is a dosing failure rather than a drug failure.
wrongExplanations.3: Atomoxetine does carry a liver-injury concern worth knowing, but his aminotransferases are already normal and he has no jaundice, abdominal pain, or malaise. Repeating normal labs does not address why the medication is not working.

questions.eli5: The medicine was never given at a real dose — he was on less than a third of what a 40-kilogram child should get. Before deciding it does not work, you have to actually try enough of it.
questions.topic: Limbic Neuroanatomy, ADHD, Pregnancy & Psychosexual Development

questions.stem: A 13-year-old girl with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder is to be started on atomoxetine after her family declines stimulant therapy. She has no cardiac disease, no tics, and no history of a mood disorder, and her baseline aminotransferases are normal. Which of the following is most important to discuss with the patient and her family before beginning treatment?
choices: A. The risk of new or worsening motor and vocal tics
B. The potential for physical dependence and medication diversion
C. The possible emergence of suicidal thoughts or behavior
D. The need for weekly complete blood counts during the first 6 months
E. The risk of dose-dependent QT-interval prolongation
questions.explanation: Atomoxetine and viloxazine both carry warnings for suicidal thoughts and behavior, which is the counseling point that must be raised before starting either agent in a child or adolescent — families need to know what to watch for and when to call. Atomoxetine additionally carries a liver-injury concern, so new jaundice, dark urine, right upper quadrant pain, or unexplained malaise warrants prompt evaluation. Board pearl — the two norepinephrine-focused non-stimulants share this warning, which is a useful way to remember them as a pair distinct from both the stimulants and the alpha-2 agonists.  [Learning objectives: LO 042, 092]

wrongExplanations.0: Tic exacerbation is associated with stimulants and especially with the amphetamine family. Atomoxetine is in fact one of the agents chosen when tics are a concern, so this reverses the relationship.
wrongExplanations.1: Atomoxetine is not a controlled substance and carries no abuse or diversion potential — that is precisely one of its advantages in households where diversion is a risk. Stimulants are Schedule II.
wrongExplanations.3: Mandatory weekly blood count monitoring belongs to clozapine, because of its agranulocytosis risk. Atomoxetine requires no scheduled hematologic monitoring.
wrongExplanations.4: Dose-dependent QT prolongation is a warning attached to citalopram among the SSRIs and to ziprasidone among the antipsychotics, not to atomoxetine.

questions.eli5: This medicine can occasionally make young people start having thoughts of hurting themselves, so families are told upfront to watch for that and call right away. They should also report yellow eyes or belly pain, since it can rarely affect the liver.
questions.topic: Limbic Neuroanatomy, ADHD, Pregnancy & Psychosexual Development

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has been euthymic for 3 years on lithium, with levels consistently between 0.8 and 1.0 mEq/L. She presents for a routine visit and a urine pregnancy test is positive; dating by last menstrual period places her at 6 weeks' gestation. She wishes to continue the pregnancy and is highly motivated to avoid a relapse, noting that her last manic episode required hospitalization. Serum creatinine is 0.7 mg/dL and thyroid-stimulating hormone is 1.9 μU/mL. Which of the following is the most appropriate management of her lithium?
choices: A. Continue lithium unchanged at the current dose throughout the pregnancy
B. Substitute valproate for lithium for the remainder of the pregnancy
C. Substitute carbamazepine for lithium for the remainder of the pregnancy
D. Minimize or hold lithium now, then resume or increase it later in pregnancy
E. Discontinue all psychotropic medication until after delivery
questions.explanation: Lithium's teratogenic risk is trimester-specific rather than uniform. Ebstein anomaly — right atrial enlargement with a downwardly displaced tricuspid valve — arises from disrupted cardiac organogenesis, which occurs early, so the risk is concentrated in the first trimester. That is why many clinicians minimize or hold lithium during the first trimester and then resume or increase the dose later in pregnancy once cardiac formation is complete and the risk has dropped substantially. Board pearl — pregnancy is one of the four exceptions that override lithium as the default answer for bipolar disorder; the other three are significant renal impairment, cardiac conduction disease, and difficult-to-manage thyroid disease. A serum hCG is part of lithium prescreening in women for exactly this reason.  [Learning objectives: LO 074, 082]

wrongExplanations.0: Continuing unchanged through the window of cardiac organogenesis accepts the peak Ebstein anomaly risk when a time-limited modification can largely avoid it.
wrongExplanations.1: Valproate is not a safer substitute — it carries neural tube defect risk, and neural tube closure also occurs in the first trimester, so this trades one early teratogenic exposure for another.
wrongExplanations.2: Carbamazepine likewise carries neural tube defect risk, and it adds autoinduction of its own metabolism plus inactivation of oral contraceptives. It is not a first-trimester-safe alternative.
wrongExplanations.4: Stopping everything ignores that untreated bipolar disorder in pregnancy carries its own substantial fetal and maternal risk, and she has a documented history of mania requiring hospitalization. The goal is an informed risk-benefit adjustment, not blanket avoidance.

questions.eli5: The baby's heart is being built right now, and lithium can damage it during that specific window. So doctors pull back on the lithium early in pregnancy and then bring it back once the heart is finished forming.
questions.topic: Limbic Neuroanatomy, ADHD, Pregnancy & Psychosexual Development

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has been maintained on valproate for 2 years with good symptom control. She tells her psychiatrist that she and her partner intend to begin trying to conceive within the next year. She is currently taking a standard over-the-counter prenatal vitamin. Aspartate aminotransferase is 26 U/L, alanine aminotransferase is 23 U/L, and a urine pregnancy test today is negative. She has no renal disease, no cardiac conduction abnormality, and normal thyroid function. Which of the following is the most appropriate plan?
choices: A. Transition off valproate and supplement folic acid above standard prenatal dosing
B. Continue valproate and continue the standard prenatal vitamin alone
C. Continue valproate through conception and stop it once pregnancy is confirmed
D. Transition from valproate to carbamazepine before conception
E. Add lithium to valproate to permit a lower valproate dose
F. Continue valproate with monthly maternal alpha-fetoprotein monitoring
questions.explanation: Valproate carries neural tube defect risk, and the neural tube closes very early — often before a woman knows she is pregnant — so the planning has to happen preconception rather than at the first positive test. Folic acid supplementation at doses above what a standard prenatal vitamin provides helps mitigate the risk of neural tube defects. Because she has a year of lead time and no contraindication to alternatives, transitioning off valproate is the move. Board pearl — antipsychotics are often preferred for bipolar disorder in pregnancy, not because they are proven safe but because most simply lack pregnancy data, and that data gap is judged preferable to valproate's and carbamazepine's documented teratogenicity; clozapine is the notable antipsychotic that has accumulated real outcome data.  [Learning objectives: LO 082, 084]

wrongExplanations.1: A standard prenatal vitamin does not supply enough folic acid to mitigate anticonvulsant-associated neural tube defect risk, and continuing valproate leaves the underlying teratogenic exposure fully in place.
wrongExplanations.2: Waiting for a confirmed pregnancy is too late. Neural tube closure occurs in the first weeks of gestation, frequently before a missed period is noticed, so stopping at confirmation misses the window entirely.
wrongExplanations.3: Carbamazepine carries the same neural tube defect risk, so this is a lateral move. It also induces hepatic metabolism, making standard oral contraceptives unreliable — a serious problem in a woman whose conception timing matters.
wrongExplanations.4: Adding lithium introduces first-trimester Ebstein anomaly risk on top of valproate's neural tube risk, doubling rather than reducing the teratogenic exposure.
wrongExplanations.5: Alpha-fetoprotein screening can detect a neural tube defect after it has formed, but it is surveillance rather than prevention and does nothing to lower the risk.

questions.eli5: The part of the spine that valproate can damage closes in the first few weeks, often before someone even knows they are pregnant. So the medicine has to change before she starts trying, along with extra folic acid — not after a positive test.
questions.topic: Limbic Neuroanatomy, ADHD, Pregnancy & Psychosexual Development

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman at 5 weeks' gestation comes to the office because she is worried about medication she has taken. She has panic disorder and has been using alprazolam as needed, most recently three doses in the past 2 weeks. She wishes to understand the timing of fetal risk. Which of the following statements is most accurate?
choices: A. The greatest risk of malformation occurs during the third trimester
B. The greatest risk of malformation occurs between 2 and 8 weeks of gestation
C. Benzodiazepines are pregnancy category A, indicating reassuring human data
D. Risk from benzodiazepines is confined entirely to the neonatal period
E. Pregnancy category C indicates that harm has been documented in humans
questions.explanation: Benzodiazepines fall into pregnancy categories D and X, and the window of greatest risk for malformation, growth retardation, and functional deficits is between 2 and 8 weeks of gestation — the period of organogenesis. The lecture compares this risk profile to that of drinking alcohol during pregnancy. Board pearl — the category letters function like school grades and are a simplified stand-in for risk-benefit data: A and B are reassuring, C means there is insufficient information either way, and D means harm has been documented. Most psychiatric medications sit in category C simply because pregnant patients are rarely enrolled in trials, not because danger has been shown.  [Learning objectives: LO 082]

wrongExplanations.0: Third-trimester exposure raises concerns about neonatal effects such as sedation and withdrawal, but structural malformation risk is tied to organogenesis in the first trimester, not to late gestation.
wrongExplanations.2: Category A denotes reassuring controlled human data. Benzodiazepines are categories D and X, which sit at the opposite end of the scale.
wrongExplanations.3: Restricting the risk to the neonatal period ignores the malformation, growth-retardation, and functional-deficit risks concentrated at 2 to 8 weeks, which is the specific window being tested.
wrongExplanations.4: Category C means insufficient information, not documented harm. Documented human harm is category D — and conflating the two leads to both unnecessary alarm about category C drugs and false reassurance about category D ones.

questions.eli5: The baby's organs are being built between about two and eight weeks, which is when medicines can do the most damage. She is right at that window, which is why the timing matters so much.
questions.topic: Limbic Neuroanatomy, ADHD, Pregnancy & Psychosexual Development

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman is newly diagnosed with bipolar I disorder following a manic episode. Carbamazepine is being considered for maintenance treatment. She is sexually active with a male partner, uses a combined oral contraceptive pill as her only method of contraception, and states clearly that she does not wish to become pregnant in the foreseeable future. A urine pregnancy test today is negative. Complete blood count with differential and platelets, liver function tests, and serum sodium are within normal limits. Which of the following is the most appropriate additional step before starting this medication?
choices: A. No contraceptive change is needed, as carbamazepine does not affect hormonal contraception
B. Increase the estrogen component of her combined oral contraceptive pill
C. Add a barrier method for the first month of carbamazepine therapy only
D. Perform monthly urine pregnancy testing while she remains on carbamazepine
E. Recommend a non-hormonal contraceptive method such as an intrauterine device
questions.explanation: Carbamazepine is a potent inducer of hepatic metabolism — it even autoinduces its own clearance — and that induction makes standard oral contraceptives unreliable. In a young woman who is sexually active and does not want to become pregnant, this matters enormously, because carbamazepine also carries neural tube defect risk. The recommended approach is a method that does not depend on hepatically metabolized hormones, such as an intrauterine device. Board pearl — carbamazepine is described as a genuinely dirty drug with many interactions, and its other signature liabilities are agranulocytosis, hyponatremia from SIADH, and the autoinduction that causes levels to drift downward over the first weeks of therapy.  [Learning objectives: LO 082, 084]

wrongExplanations.0: Carbamazepine's enzyme induction accelerates clearance of contraceptive steroids, which is precisely why standard oral contraceptives become unreliable. Assuming no interaction is the error the item is built around.
wrongExplanations.1: Raising the estrogen dose is an unreliable workaround against ongoing induction, adds thromboembolic risk, and still leaves her contraception dependent on the pathway carbamazepine is accelerating.
wrongExplanations.2: Induction persists for as long as she takes carbamazepine, not just the first month, so time-limited barrier use leaves her unprotected thereafter.
wrongExplanations.3: Monthly pregnancy testing detects a pregnancy after it has occurred. Given the neural tube defect risk and that the neural tube closes very early, detection is no substitute for prevention.

questions.eli5: Carbamazepine speeds up the liver so much that it burns through birth control pills and makes them stop working. Since this drug can also harm a developing spine, she needs a method the liver cannot undo, like an IUD.
questions.topic: Limbic Neuroanatomy, ADHD, Pregnancy & Psychosexual Development

questions.stem: In Freud's model of psychosexual development, an adult who is described as obsessively organized, excessively neat, and rigidly controlling is classically said to have a fixation at which of the following stages?
questions.explanation: Freud's psychosexual stages tie each age band to an erogenous zone: oral from birth to 1 year, anal from 1 to 3 years, phallic from 3 to 6 years, latency from 6 years to puberty, and genital from puberty onward. Fixation at the anal stage splits two ways — retentive fixation yields the obsessively organized, excessively neat adult, while expulsive fixation yields the reckless, careless, defiant, and disorganized one. Board pearl — this framework has been largely superseded as a clinical model and the notes flag it as lower-yield than descriptive DSM-5 criteria, but it survives in vocabulary you will still encounter, including the phrase anal-retentive itself.  [Learning objectives: LO 104]

wrongExplanations.0: Oral fixation, from the birth-to-1-year stage, produces behaviors centered on the mouth — nail-biting and pencil-chewing in the aggressive form, and smoking or overeating in the passive form.
wrongExplanations.1: The phallic stage, from 3 to 6 years, is where Freud located the Oedipus and Electra complexes and theorized that the superego develops. It is not associated with compulsive orderliness.
wrongExplanations.3: Latency, from age 6 to puberty, is the stage Freud described as having dormant sexual feelings; fixation there was theorized to produce sexual unfulfillment.
wrongExplanations.4: The genital stage runs from puberty through the rest of life; difficulties there were framed as frigidity, impotence, or unsatisfactory relationships rather than compulsive neatness.

questions.eli5: Freud thought children pass through stages, and getting stuck at the toilet-training stage shows up later as being obsessively tidy and controlling. That is where the phrase anal-retentive comes from.
questions.topic: Limbic Neuroanatomy, ADHD, Pregnancy & Psychosexual Development

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man is brought to the office by his wife 6 weeks after an ischemic stroke. She describes him as previously reserved, deeply private, and frugal. Since the stroke he has told sexually explicit jokes to the office staff, has purchased two motorcycles he cannot ride, and insists he has been selected to run the hospital system. He sleeps about 3 hours nightly and describes his mood as 'the best it has ever been.' He has no personal or family history of psychiatric illness, and urine toxicology screening is negative. Neurologic examination shows preserved fluent speech with intact comprehension and repetition, no visual field cut, and no hemiparesis. Which of the following regions is most likely involved by the infarct?
questions.explanation: Frontal-lobe stroke produces psychiatric syndromes that lateralize. A RIGHT frontal infarct produces the disinhibited/psychotic picture: impulsivity, socially inappropriate behavior, euphoria, mania, and delusions — exactly this man's presentation, and a sharp break from a premorbidly reserved and frugal personality. Board pearl — the three-way scheme is worth memorizing as a set: right frontal gives mania and disinhibition, left frontal gives depression and a catastrophic reaction, and central or medial frontal gives apathy. The preserved fluent speech with intact comprehension and repetition is the negative that keeps you out of the left hemisphere language areas.  [Learning objectives: LO 065]

wrongExplanations.0: A left frontal infarct produces the depressive or catastrophic syndrome — severe dysphoria, profound anxiety, low mood, and acute tearfulness. His mood is euphoric and elevated, which is the opposite pole.
wrongExplanations.2: Medial frontal involvement produces the apathetic or akinetic syndrome: abulia, emotional blunting, and reduced speech output. He is hyperactive, expansive, and talking freely.
wrongExplanations.3: A left temporal infarct would be expected to disturb language comprehension. His comprehension and repetition are explicitly intact, which closes this option.
wrongExplanations.4: A right parietal infarct classically produces hemineglect, constructional difficulty, and anosognosia rather than a sustained manic syndrome with grandiose delusions.
wrongExplanations.5: An occipital infarct produces visual field deficits and, with bilateral involvement, cortical blindness. He has no visual field cut and no visual complaints.

questions.eli5: A stroke in the right front part of the brain takes the brakes off — people become giddy, spend wildly, say things they never would have, and think they are far more important than they are. His whole personality flipped after the stroke.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman sustains an anterior cerebral artery territory infarct involving the medial frontal lobes bilaterally. Six weeks later she is medically stable and her hemiparesis has largely resolved. Which of the following presentations is most likely?
choices: A. Severe dysphoria with profound anxiety and frequent tearfulness
B. Euphoria, impulsivity, and grandiose delusions
C. Fluent speech output with markedly impaired comprehension
D. Loss of motivation with emotional blunting and reduced speech output
E. Vivid visual hallucinations with fully preserved insight
questions.explanation: Central or medial frontal involvement produces the apathetic/akinetic syndrome — complete loss of motivation (abulia), emotional blunting, and selective mutism. These patients are often mistaken for depressed, but the defining feature is absence of drive rather than presence of sadness: they typically do not report dysphoria, guilt, or hopelessness, and they may answer when pressed while initiating nothing on their own. Board pearl — the three frontal syndromes divide by location, not by severity: left frontal is the depressive/catastrophic one, right frontal is the disinhibited/manic one, and central or medial is this apathetic one.  [Learning objectives: LO 065]

wrongExplanations.0: Severe dysphoria with anxiety and tearfulness is the LEFT frontal depressive or catastrophic syndrome. That presentation has too much emotion, not too little, and the medial location predicts the opposite.
wrongExplanations.1: Euphoria with impulsivity and grandiose delusions is the RIGHT frontal disinhibited syndrome — again a state of excess output rather than absent output.
wrongExplanations.2: Fluent speech with impaired comprehension describes a receptive aphasia from posterior left hemisphere involvement, which is outside the anterior cerebral artery territory.
wrongExplanations.4: Visual hallucinations with preserved insight raise concern for an occipital lesion, a Lewy body process, or Charles Bonnet syndrome. They are not a feature of medial frontal injury.

questions.eli5: The middle-front part of the brain is what makes you want to do things. Damage there does not make people sad — it makes them stop starting anything at all, barely speaking unless spoken to.

questions.stem: A toddler screams loudly in the supermarket checkout line. To end the screaming, her father hands her a candy bar, and she immediately stops. Over the following weeks the father begins handing over candy faster and faster each time she starts to scream. With respect to the FATHER's behavior of handing over the candy, this pattern best illustrates which of the following?
questions.explanation: Work Skinner's quadrants in two steps. First, is the behavior increasing or decreasing? The father hands over candy faster and faster, so his behavior is INCREASING — that makes it reinforcement, not punishment. Second, was a stimulus added or removed? The screaming was removed, so it is NEGATIVE. Negative reinforcement. The trap is reading 'negative' as bad and 'giving candy' as adding something; the plus and minus signs describe addition or removal of a stimulus, not whether the outcome is desirable. Board pearl — always name whose behavior you are analyzing. From the CHILD's side, receiving candy after screaming is positive reinforcement of the screaming, which is why this loop is so hard to break: both parties are being reinforced simultaneously.  [Learning objectives: LO 002, 012]

wrongExplanations.1: Positive reinforcement adds a pleasant stimulus to increase a behavior. That correctly describes what is happening to the CHILD, who receives candy — but the question asks about the father, for whom something aversive was taken away.
wrongExplanations.2: Negative punishment removes a pleasant stimulus to DECREASE a behavior. The father's behavior is increasing, so this fails the first step of the analysis.
wrongExplanations.3: Positive punishment adds an aversive stimulus to decrease a behavior. Again the father's behavior is increasing, and nothing aversive was added to him.
wrongExplanations.4: Extinction is the fading of a behavior once reinforcement stops. Reinforcement here is being delivered more reliably over time, which is the opposite of extinction.
wrongExplanations.5: Shaping is rewarding successive approximations toward a target behavior. No graded progression toward a goal is described; a single behavior is being reinforced whole.

questions.eli5: Dad gives candy because it makes the screaming stop, and taking away something annoying makes him do it more. Negative here does not mean bad — it just means something was removed.

questions.stem: In a laboratory experiment, a rat presses a lever and receives a food pellet. Over successive sessions the rat presses the lever with increasing frequency. This experiment best demonstrates which of the following?
questions.explanation: Operant conditioning, associated with Skinner, shapes a VOLUNTARY behavior through reward or punishment — the rat chooses to press the lever, and the consequence changes how often it does so. Classical conditioning, associated with Pavlov and the Little Albert experiment, transfers an INVOLUNTARY innate response onto a previously neutral stimulus. Board pearl — this specific example is flagged in the lecture as a classic exam trap: the rat pressing a button for food is the textbook illustration of what classical conditioning is NOT. The fastest test is to ask whether the response is voluntary (operant) or reflexive (classical).  [Learning objectives: LO 002, 012]

wrongExplanations.0: Classical conditioning pairs a neutral stimulus with one that already produces an innate, involuntary response — salivation to a bell, fear to a white rat. Lever-pressing is a deliberate action performed to obtain an outcome, not a reflex.
wrongExplanations.1: Extinction is the fading of a behavior when reinforcement is withdrawn. Reinforcement is being delivered consistently and the behavior is increasing.
wrongExplanations.3: Systematic desensitization is a clinical behavioral technique pairing graded exposure to a feared stimulus with relaxation training. There is no feared stimulus and no relaxation component here.
wrongExplanations.4: Modeling is learning by observing another organism perform a behavior. The rat is learning from its own consequences, not from watching another rat.

questions.eli5: The rat decides to press the lever because food shows up when it does. Learning that your own choices have consequences is operant conditioning — different from learning to drool at a bell, which happens to you automatically.

questions.stem: During her fourth psychotherapy session, a 38-year-old woman becomes abruptly angry and tells her psychiatrist, "You are just sitting there judging me, exactly like my father did — you have already decided I am a failure." The psychiatrist has been silent and non-evaluative throughout the session and notes no basis for her interpretation in anything he has said. He observes his own reaction, notices no unusual feeling toward her, and remains curious rather than defensive. Which of the following best describes the patient's response?
questions.explanation: Transference is the patient projecting feelings from a past relationship onto the provider — here, her experience of a judgmental father is transferred wholesale onto a psychiatrist who has done nothing to invite it. Countertransference is the mirror image: the provider projecting their own past feelings onto the patient, which the stem explicitly rules out by noting he observes no unusual reaction in himself. Board pearl — the direction is the whole distinction. Transference runs patient to doctor; countertransference runs doctor to patient, and recognizing your own is part of competent practice rather than a failure.  [Learning objectives: LO 011, 061]

wrongExplanations.0: Countertransference would require the PSYCHIATRIST to be projecting his own past feelings onto her. The stem states he notices no unusual feeling toward her and remains curious rather than defensive.
wrongExplanations.1: Projection attributes one's own unacceptable impulse to another person — a person who cheated becoming convinced everyone else cheats. She is not disowning a judgmental impulse of her own; she is reliving a specific past relationship.
wrongExplanations.2: Displacement redirects an emotion from its true target onto a safer one, such as snapping at a spouse after a bad day with a boss. Transference is the more specific term when the redirection lands on the treating clinician and reproduces a past relationship pattern.
wrongExplanations.3: Identification is unconsciously patterning one's own behavior after someone more powerful. She is not becoming like her father; she is perceiving her psychiatrist as him.

questions.eli5: She is reacting to her doctor as if he were her critical father, even though he has done nothing critical. Feelings from an old relationship getting aimed at the therapist is called transference.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old surgical resident is passed over for a fellowship position in favor of a co-resident whom he privately considers less capable. Over the following months he becomes conspicuously effusive in praising that co-resident at conferences, volunteers repeatedly to cover his call shifts, and organizes a celebration in his honor. He tells his own mentor that he feels 'nothing but genuine happiness' about the outcome and appears puzzled when asked whether any part of him is disappointed. Which of the following defense mechanisms does this behavior best illustrate?
questions.explanation: Reaction formation transforms an unacceptable feeling into its exact opposite, keeping the original impulse out of awareness. Resentment and envy become conspicuous, effortful praise and generosity — and the giveaway is the intensity and the patient's genuine puzzlement at the suggestion of any negative feeling. Board pearl — this defense is recognizable by disproportion: the behavior is not merely gracious, it is over-the-top, because it takes energy to hold a strong feeling at bay. The textbook illustration is the child who unconsciously resents a new sibling and becomes their most devoted caretaker.  [Learning objectives: LO 058]

wrongExplanations.0: Passive aggression expresses hostility indirectly through inaction or subtle resistance — arriving late, 'forgetting' assigned tasks. He is doing the opposite: acting with exaggerated helpfulness rather than covert obstruction.
wrongExplanations.2: Sublimation, a mature defense, channels an unacceptable impulse into a socially productive outlet, such as aggressive drives expressed through competitive sport. He is not redirecting the impulse into productive work; he is converting it into its opposite.
wrongExplanations.3: Identification is unconsciously modeling oneself after someone perceived as powerful. He is praising his colleague, not becoming like him.
wrongExplanations.4: Rationalization constructs a logical-sounding explanation for a distressing outcome — 'they never valued hard work here anyway.' He offers no justifying explanation; he denies any negative feeling exists at all.

questions.eli5: He is furious about losing the spot, so instead he throws his rival a party and says he is thrilled. Turning a feeling into its exact opposite, extra loudly, is reaction formation.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old physician is diagnosed with metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma. Over the following weeks he spends every evening reading primary literature on molecular subtypes and survival curves, maintains a spreadsheet comparing trial regimens, and corrects his oncologist's terminology. When his wife asks how he is feeling about the diagnosis, he redirects the conversation to hazard ratios and states that emotional discussion is 'not a productive use of the time I have.' He acknowledges the diagnosis fully and accurately, is not tearful, and has no memory gaps. Which of the following defense mechanisms is he most likely using?
questions.explanation: Intellectualization converts an emotionally overwhelming event into a purely cognitive, academic problem — the textbook example is a physician diagnosed with a serious illness who becomes consumed with reading every available clinical research report. The engagement is active and effortful: he is not merely flat, he is building an intellectual structure that leaves no room for feeling. Board pearl — the nearest neighbor is isolation of affect, and the distinction is subtle but real: isolation of affect strips the feeling from a fact that is simply being reported, whereas intellectualization substitutes sustained analytic activity for the feeling.  [Learning objectives: LO 058]

wrongExplanations.0: Denial refuses to accept an unbearable piece of external reality — insisting nothing is wrong and skipping the workup. He acknowledges the diagnosis fully and accurately, which is stated explicitly.
wrongExplanations.1: Rationalization constructs a more comfortable logical explanation for a distressing outcome. He is not explaining away the cancer; he is studying it.
wrongExplanations.2: Isolation of affect separates a distressing fact from its emotional charge — describing a traumatic event in graphic detail with a flat, unaffected tone. It is the closest competitor, but it describes emotionally blank reporting rather than the sustained intellectual project he has undertaken.
wrongExplanations.4: Sublimation channels an unacceptable impulse into a productive outlet and is classed as a mature defense. There is no impulse being redirected here, only an emotion being avoided.
wrongExplanations.5: Dissociation is detachment from one's self or memory under stress, with gaps in recall. He explicitly has no memory gaps and is fully oriented to his situation.

questions.eli5: He turned his own cancer into a research project so he never has to feel anything about it. Burying an emotion under facts and data is intellectualization.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman has been unable to fly for 9 years because of intense fear of air travel, which has cost her two job promotions. She has no other anxiety symptoms and no obsessions or compulsions. Her therapist begins by teaching her progressive muscle relaxation, then has her view photographs of aircraft while relaxed, then visit an airport terminal, then sit in a parked aircraft, and finally take a 45-minute flight, advancing only when her anxiety at each step has substantially decreased. Which of the following best describes this technique?
choices: E. Eye movement desensitization and reprocessing
questions.explanation: Systematic desensitization pairs GRADED exposure to the feared stimulus with relaxation training, advancing stepwise as anxiety habituates at each level — the lecture's illustration runs picture of a spider, then plastic spider, then dead spider, then live spider. Exposure-based therapy has the largest evidence base for specific phobia, outperforming medication. Board pearl — the contrast to hold is ladder versus cannonball: systematic desensitization climbs the ladder with relaxation, whereas flooding drops the patient straight into massive exposure until the anxiety extinguishes.  [Learning objectives: LO 081]

wrongExplanations.1: Flooding uses massive, immediate exposure to the feared stimulus rather than a graded hierarchy — the lecture's example is placing a spider-phobic patient directly into a tank of live spiders. Her treatment advanced through five progressive steps.
wrongExplanations.2: Exposure and response prevention is the gold-standard behavioral treatment for OCD, pairing exposure with blockade of the compulsive ritual. She has no compulsions to prevent.
wrongExplanations.3: Aversive conditioning pairs an unwanted behavior with a noxious stimulus, as with disulfiram and alcohol. Nothing unpleasant is being paired with flying here.
wrongExplanations.4: EMDR is trauma-focused, using bilateral stimulation while the patient processes traumatic material. Her phobia is not described as arising from a traumatic event, and no bilateral stimulus is used.

questions.eli5: She works up to flying one small step at a time — first pictures, then the airport, then a parked plane — staying relaxed at each stage. Climbing the ladder slowly is systematic desensitization; jumping straight into the deep end would be flooding.

questions.stem: A 39-year-old man comes to the office because he has been unable to work for 4 months. He avoids buses and subways, will not use elevators, cannot tolerate standing in a checkout line, and becomes intensely anxious in crowds or when alone far from home. When asked what specifically frightens him about these situations, he answers, "It is always the same thing — if something happened to me there, I could not get out, and no one could help me." He now leaves his apartment only when his sister accompanies him. He denies fear of being judged or embarrassed by others, denies obsessions and compulsions, and states that he has never had an attack in a situation outside this list. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Agoraphobia is fear across MULTIPLE situations unified by a single theme — that escape might be difficult or help unavailable if something went wrong. His quoted sentence supplies the theme verbatim, and the situations span public transport, enclosed spaces, lines and crowds, and being alone outside the home. Board pearl — DSM-5 unlinked agoraphobia from panic disorder, so they are now separate diagnoses that may co-occur rather than agoraphobia being a specifier of panic disorder. Note also that a patient with agoraphobia can often tolerate a crowd perfectly well as long as they know they can get out; the fear is about escape, not about the crowd itself.  [Learning objectives: LO 036]

wrongExplanations.0: Generalized anxiety disorder requires excessive worry about multiple everyday life domains for more than 6 months. His anxiety is confined to a defined set of situations sharing one theme, not spread across finances, health, and family.
wrongExplanations.1: Panic disorder requires recurrent attacks that are at least partly unexpected, plus a month of worry or behavior change. He states he has never had an attack outside this specific list of situations, which makes his attacks entirely cued.
wrongExplanations.2: Social anxiety disorder centers on fear of scrutiny and negative evaluation by others. He explicitly denies fear of being judged or embarrassed, which is the stated negative that closes this option.
wrongExplanations.3: A specific phobia is fear of ONE discrete object or situation. His fear spans at least five different situations, and it is the shared escape theme rather than any single trigger that unites them.
wrongExplanations.4: Separation anxiety disorder is fear of separation from an attachment figure and worry that harm will befall them. His sister's presence helps because she could summon help, not because he fears losing her.

questions.eli5: Buses, elevators, lines, crowds, being far from home — all different places, but he is scared of the same one thing in each: not being able to get out or get help. That single thread is what makes it agoraphobia.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her daughter because of 4 days of increasing confusion, unsteadiness, and nausea. She was started on sertraline 6 weeks ago for major depressive disorder and takes no other medications; she is on no diuretic, no lithium, and no carbamazepine. Temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F), pulse is 76/min, and blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg with no orthostatic change. Examination shows moist mucous membranes, no edema, and no jugular venous distention. Serum sodium is 118 mEq/L, serum osmolality is 248 mOsm/kg, and urine osmolality is 480 mOsm/kg with a urine sodium of 52 mEq/L. Thyroid-stimulating hormone and a morning cortisol are within normal limits. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her presentation?
choices: C. Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion due to sertraline
D. Hypovolemic hyponatremia from poor oral intake
questions.explanation: SIADH is one of the four SSRI adverse effects worth memorizing alongside gastrointestinal distress, sexual dysfunction, and serotonin syndrome, and it is most common in older adults within the first weeks of therapy. Her laboratory pattern is textbook: hyponatremia with LOW serum osmolality but INAPPROPRIATELY concentrated urine (480 mOsm/kg) and a urine sodium above 40 mEq/L, in a clinically euvolemic patient with normal thyroid and adrenal function. The 6-week timeline and the absence of every alternative culprit — no diuretic, no lithium, no carbamazepine — make the SSRI the answer. Board pearl — this is a genuine reason an elderly patient started on an SSRI can present as delirious, so check a sodium before assuming the depression itself is worsening.  [Learning objectives: LO 073, 097]

wrongExplanations.0: Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus produces polyuria with inappropriately DILUTE urine and a rising serum sodium. Her urine is concentrated at 480 mOsm/kg and her sodium is low — the opposite pattern on both counts. It is also lithium's complication, and she is not on lithium.
wrongExplanations.1: Primary polydipsia produces hyponatremia with maximally dilute urine, typically under 100 mOsm/kg, as the kidney appropriately excretes the water load. Her urine is concentrated, which means antidiuretic hormone is acting when it should not be.
wrongExplanations.3: Hypovolemic hyponatremia would show dry mucous membranes, orthostatic hypotension, and a LOW urine sodium as the kidney avidly retains sodium. She has moist membranes, no orthostatic change, and a urine sodium of 52 mEq/L.
wrongExplanations.4: Thiazide diuretics are a classic cause of hyponatremia in older adults, but the stem explicitly states she takes no diuretic — a negative planted specifically to eliminate this option.

questions.eli5: Her antidepressant made her body hold on to water it should have peed out, so her blood salt dropped very low and made her confused. Her urine was concentrated when it should have been dilute, which is the giveaway.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man comes to the office because of 3 days of symptoms that began after he ran out of his medication and was unable to reach the pharmacy. He describes generalized muscle aches, chills without fever, dizziness on standing, nausea, insomnia, irritability, and brief sensations he calls 'electric shocks going through my head.' He has taken paroxetine 40 mg PO daily for major depressive disorder for 2 years with good response and no adverse effects. Temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), pulse is 84/min, and blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg with no orthostatic drop. Examination shows normal muscle tone, deep tendon reflexes of 2+ throughout with no clonus, moist skin, and normal bowel sounds. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
choices: C. Observe without intervention, as symptoms are self-limited
D. Substitute fluoxetine at an equivalent dose
E. Restart paroxetine and then taper it gradually
questions.explanation: This is antidepressant discontinuation syndrome, captured by FINISH: Flu-like symptoms, Insomnia, Nausea, Imbalance, Sensory disturbance (the electric shocks patients call brain zaps), and Hyperarousal. It follows abrupt cessation or missed doses of any antidepressant class, not just SSRIs. Management is to restart the antidepressant and taper slowly. Board pearl — risk tracks inversely with half-life, so paroxetine, the shortest-acting SSRI, is the worst offender, while fluoxetine's 2 to 4 day half-life makes it the most forgiving. The normal reflexes with no clonus are the negative that separates this from serotonin syndrome, which would show hyperreflexia and clonus.  [Learning objectives: LO 056, 097]

wrongExplanations.0: Cyproheptadine treats serotonin syndrome, which requires hyperreflexia, clonus, hyperthermia, and autonomic instability after a serotonergic ADDITION. He is afebrile with 2+ reflexes and no clonus, and his problem is drug removal rather than excess.
wrongExplanations.1: A benzodiazepine might blunt the irritability and insomnia but leaves the underlying cause untreated, adds dependence risk, and does nothing for the sensory disturbances or flu-like symptoms.
wrongExplanations.2: Discontinuation syndrome does eventually resolve, but it can be severe and prolonged with paroxetine specifically, and simply waiting abandons a medication that has controlled his depression for 2 years with no adverse effects.
wrongExplanations.3: Cross-tapering to fluoxetine is a recognized strategy for managing difficult paroxetine discontinuation, but the correct immediate step in a patient who wants to remain treated and was doing well is to restart the effective agent and taper deliberately if stopping is the goal.
