questions.eli5: He ran out of his pills and his body reacted with aches, dizziness, and little zaps in his head. The fix is to get back on the medicine and then come off it slowly instead of all at once.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old man with major depressive disorder has been treated with venlafaxine, titrated from 75 mg PO daily to 300 mg PO daily over 10 weeks. His mood, sleep, and concentration have improved substantially. At his baseline visit his blood pressure was 118/74 mm Hg; today, on three separate readings 5 minutes apart, it is 158/98, 156/96, and 160/100 mm Hg. He has gained no weight, takes no decongestants or stimulants, does not use alcohol or illicit drugs, and urine toxicology screening is negative. Serum creatinine, electrolytes, and thyroid-stimulating hormone are within normal limits. Which of the following best explains this finding?
choices: A. At higher doses venlafaxine increasingly inhibits norepinephrine reuptake
B. Venlafaxine's active metabolite is a potent alpha-1 adrenergic agonist
C. Venlafaxine inhibits CYP2D6, raising circulating catecholamine concentrations
D. Venlafaxine causes syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone with volume expansion
E. Venlafaxine is a direct beta-1 adrenergic receptor agonist
questions.explanation: Venlafaxine is the SNRI with a genuinely dose-dependent mechanism: at low doses it behaves essentially like an SSRI, blocking serotonin reuptake, and as the dose climbs it recruits progressively more norepinephrine reuptake inhibition (at the highest doses some dopaminergic effect as well). That accumulating noradrenergic tone is what raises blood pressure, which is why blood pressure monitoring is a specific requirement with this drug and why uncontrolled hypertension is a relative contraindication to it. Board pearl — the dose ladder is the testable point: a patient stable at 75 mg who develops hypertension after titration to 300 mg is demonstrating pharmacology, not a new comorbidity.  [Learning objectives: LO 019, 097]

wrongExplanations.1: Desvenlafaxine is venlafaxine's norepinephrine-specific active metabolite and acts as a reuptake inhibitor, not as a direct alpha-1 agonist. Direct receptor agonism is not the mechanism of any antidepressant in this class.
wrongExplanations.2: Venlafaxine is not a notable CYP2D6 inhibitor — that description fits fluoxetine, paroxetine, and bupropion — and enzyme inhibition affects drug levels rather than generating catecholamines.
wrongExplanations.3: SIADH does occur with serotonergic antidepressants, but it produces hyponatremia with euvolemia rather than hypertension; the water retention in SIADH is not clinically volume-expanding enough to raise blood pressure this way.
wrongExplanations.4: No antidepressant acts as a direct beta-1 agonist. All the monoamine antidepressants work by altering transporter function or receptor modulation, not by directly stimulating adrenergic receptors.

questions.eli5: At small doses this drug mostly works on serotonin, but as the dose goes up it starts working on adrenaline too. More adrenaline signaling means higher blood pressure, which is why his went up as the dose climbed.

questions.stem: A 56-year-old woman with major depressive disorder and painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy is being started on an antidepressant that could address both conditions. Her history includes alcohol-related cirrhosis, and she has been abstinent for 2 years. Aspartate aminotransferase is 148 U/L, alanine aminotransferase is 176 U/L, total bilirubin is 2.4 mg/dL, and INR is 1.5. She has no history of myocardial infarction, no arrhythmia, and a normal electrocardiogram with a QTc of 418 ms. Blood pressure is 122/78 mm Hg and she has no history of narrow-angle glaucoma. Which of the following medications should be avoided in this patient?
questions.explanation: Duloxetine is the obvious pick for depression plus neuropathic pain — it carries indications for both, along with fibromyalgia — and that is precisely the trap. Hepatic impairment is a listed contraindication because duloxetine has been associated with fatal hepatotoxicity, and her transaminases in the 150s, bilirubin of 2.4 mg/dL, and INR of 1.5 indicate genuine synthetic dysfunction rather than incidental enzyme elevation. Board pearl — the mnemonic is DULL-oxetine: it dulls pain but punishes the liver and the eye, the second half referring to uncontrolled narrow-angle glaucoma, which the stem clears explicitly so that the liver is the only clue that matters.  [Learning objectives: LO 019, 097]

wrongExplanations.0: Amitriptyline is a reasonable option for depression with chronic pain, and the contraindications that would block it — recent myocardial infarction and arrhythmia — are explicitly negated. Its real limitation is lethality in overdose, not hepatic impairment.
wrongExplanations.2: Nortriptyline is a secondary tricyclic with fewer off-target effects than the tertiary agents and is indicated for pain and migraine. Her cardiac history and ECG are clean, so no contraindication applies.
wrongExplanations.3: Venlafaxine's cautions are uncontrolled hypertension and a difficult discontinuation syndrome. Her blood pressure is 122/78 mm Hg, which clears the relevant concern.
wrongExplanations.4: Mirtazapine's liabilities are sedation, increased appetite, and weight gain. It has no hepatic contraindication and would be a safe if imperfect choice, since it does not address her neuropathic pain.

questions.eli5: The perfect-looking drug here treats both her depression and her nerve pain — but it can badly damage the liver, and her liver is already scarred. That one detail takes the obvious answer off the table.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has taken lithium for 6 years. She comes to the office because of 4 months of urinating large volumes throughout the day and night and drinking constantly to keep up; she estimates her output at about 5 liters daily. She denies polyphagia and has lost no weight. Serum glucose is 92 mg/dL and hemoglobin A1c is 5.2%. Serum sodium is 147 mEq/L, serum osmolality is 300 mOsm/kg, and urine osmolality is 120 mOsm/kg. Serum calcium is 10.1 mg/dL and serum lithium concentration is 0.9 mEq/L. She has a fine bilateral hand tremor unchanged from prior visits, with no ataxia, no slurred speech, and no confusion. Which of the following best explains her symptoms?
questions.explanation: Lithium antagonizes antidiuretic hormone at the collecting duct, producing a nephrogenic diabetes insipidus — the I in the LiTHIUM mnemonic (Low thyroid, Heart/Ebstein anomaly, Insipidus, Unwanted movements). The laboratory signature is a HIGH-normal or elevated serum sodium with high serum osmolality alongside inappropriately DILUTE urine at 120 mOsm/kg, meaning the kidney cannot concentrate despite a clear stimulus to do so. Board pearl — the condition is generally reversible, and the two quiet negatives that steer you are the therapeutic lithium level of 0.9 mEq/L and the unchanged FINE tremor, both of which exclude toxicity.  [Learning objectives: LO 074, 085]

wrongExplanations.0: Diabetes mellitus causes an osmotic diuresis, but her glucose is 92 mg/dL and hemoglobin A1c is 5.2%, and she has no polyphagia or weight loss.
wrongExplanations.1: Primary polydipsia drives water intake first, so the serum sodium and osmolality would be LOW as the excess water dilutes the blood. Hers are elevated at 147 mEq/L and 300 mOsm/kg, meaning water is being lost rather than over-consumed.
wrongExplanations.2: Central diabetes insipidus produces an identical urine picture but arises from deficient antidiuretic hormone release from the posterior pituitary. In a patient on 6 years of lithium the lesion is renal resistance to the hormone, not failure to secrete it — the distinction a desmopressin challenge would settle.
wrongExplanations.4: Lithium toxicity occurs above roughly 1.2 mEq/L and presents with COARSE tremor, ataxia, slurred speech, confusion, nausea, and diarrhea. Her level is 0.9 mEq/L and her tremor remains fine and unchanged, with none of those findings.
wrongExplanations.5: Lithium can cause mild hypercalcemia, and marked hypercalcemia can impair urinary concentration — a genuinely tempting distractor. But her calcium is 10.1 mg/dL, essentially normal, and far too low to explain 5 liters of daily output.

questions.eli5: Lithium makes the kidney stop listening to the hormone that tells it to hold on to water. So she pours out huge amounts of very watery urine and has to keep drinking to keep up.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man is started on carbamazepine for bipolar I disorder after intolerance to lithium. At week 2 his serum carbamazepine concentration is within the therapeutic range and he reports good symptom control. At week 6, on an unchanged dose, he reports the return of irritability and decreased need for sleep, and a repeat concentration has fallen well below the therapeutic range. His mother, who administers each dose and keeps a log, confirms he has not missed a dose, and a pharmacy refill history is consistent. He has started no new medications, has not changed his diet, and does not smoke. Serum creatinine and aminotransferases are within normal limits. Which of the following best explains the fall in his drug concentration?
choices: A. Covert nonadherence not captured by the medication log
B. Reduced gastrointestinal absorption when taken with food
C. Displacement of carbamazepine from plasma protein binding sites
D. A progressive increase in renal clearance of the parent drug
E. Carbamazepine induces the hepatic enzymes that metabolize it
questions.explanation: Carbamazepine autoinduction is the classic answer to a level that drifts downward on an unchanged dose over the first weeks of therapy: the drug induces the very hepatic enzymes responsible for its own metabolism, so clearance rises and concentrations fall, typically requiring upward dose adjustment over the first month. The stem forecloses nonadherence twice, with a witnessed dosing log and a consistent refill history. Board pearl — carbamazepine's other signature liabilities are agranulocytosis, hyponatremia from SIADH, and induction of the metabolism of other drugs including oral contraceptives, which is why a non-hormonal contraceptive method is recommended in patients who could become pregnant.  [Learning objectives: LO 028, 043]

wrongExplanations.0: Nonadherence is the reflexive explanation for any falling level, and the stem closes it deliberately with witnessed administration, a written log, and a matching pharmacy refill record — the same construction used for the smoking and clozapine interaction.
wrongExplanations.1: Food effects on carbamazepine absorption are minor and would not produce a progressive decline over 4 weeks, and the stem states his diet has not changed.
wrongExplanations.2: Protein-binding displacement transiently raises FREE drug concentration and is quickly redistributed and cleared; it does not cause a sustained fall in measured total concentration, and no displacing agent has been added.
wrongExplanations.3: Carbamazepine is cleared hepatically rather than renally, and his creatinine is normal. Renal handling is what governs lithium levels, not carbamazepine.

questions.eli5: Carbamazepine teaches the liver to break down carbamazepine faster. So after a few weeks the same dose produces a smaller amount in the blood, and the dose usually has to go up.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia was started on clozapine 18 days ago after two failed antipsychotic trials, with titration proceeding on schedule. He comes to the clinic because of 3 days of fatigue, chest discomfort, and shortness of breath climbing stairs. Temperature is 38.2°C (100.8°F), pulse is 118/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 104/66 mm Hg. Examination shows bibasilar crackles and mild bilateral ankle edema. Troponin I is elevated, C-reactive protein is elevated, and the complete blood count shows eosinophilia with a normal absolute neutrophil count of 3,400/mm3. Echocardiography shows a left ventricular ejection fraction of 38% with global hypokinesis. Coronary angiography shows no obstructive disease. Which of the following is the most appropriate management of his clozapine?
choices: A. Discontinue clozapine permanently and do not rechallenge
B. Reduce the clozapine dose by half and continue with weekly echocardiography
C. Continue clozapine at the current dose and add a beta-blocker
D. Hold clozapine for 1 week, then rechallenge at a lower starting dose
E. Continue clozapine and increase absolute neutrophil count monitoring to twice weekly
F. Discontinue clozapine now and restart it once cardiac function has recovered
questions.explanation: Clozapine-induced myocarditis is a rare but potentially fatal adverse effect that characteristically appears within the first several weeks of treatment — day 18 sits squarely in that window. The picture here is complete: fever, tachycardia, chest discomfort, heart failure signs, elevated troponin and C-reactive protein, eosinophilia, and a new global reduction in ejection fraction with clean coronaries. It warrants immediate and PERMANENT discontinuation, because rechallenge carries a substantial risk of recurrence that can be more severe or fatal. Board pearl — the normal absolute neutrophil count is the deliberate misdirection: agranulocytosis is clozapine's most famous risk, but myocarditis is the one that ends the drug forever.  [Learning objectives: LO 086, 087, 095]

wrongExplanations.1: Dose reduction does not remove the offending exposure, and myocarditis is not a dose-dependent phenomenon that can be titrated around. Continuing any clozapine in confirmed myocarditis risks progression to fulminant heart failure.
wrongExplanations.2: A beta-blocker is appropriate management for the resulting cardiomyopathy but does nothing about the ongoing drug exposure driving the inflammation. Treating the consequence while continuing the cause is the wrong order.
wrongExplanations.3: This is the central trap. Rechallenge after clozapine-induced myocarditis carries substantial recurrence risk with higher associated mortality, which is exactly why the teaching point is permanent discontinuation without rechallenge.
wrongExplanations.4: Intensified neutrophil monitoring addresses agranulocytosis, a different clozapine complication. His absolute neutrophil count is normal at 3,400/mm3, and no amount of blood count monitoring detects or treats myocarditis.
wrongExplanations.5: Restarting after cardiac recovery is still a rechallenge, and recovery of ejection fraction does not reduce the risk of a more severe recurrence on re-exposure.

questions.eli5: Clozapine can inflame the heart muscle in the first few weeks, and this is exactly that. It has to be stopped for good, because starting it again can bring the heart problem back worse.

questions.stem: Which of the following medications is specifically indicated for the treatment of tardive dyskinesia?
questions.explanation: Valbenazine is a vesicular monoamine transporter type 2 inhibitor developed specifically for tardive dyskinesia; management otherwise consists of withdrawing or switching the offending antipsychotic. Board pearl — two things make tardive dyskinesia behave unlike the other extrapyramidal syndromes. First, anticholinergics do not help and can worsen it, which inverts the reflex you build treating dystonia and parkinsonism. Second, the movements characteristically WORSEN transiently when the causative drug is withdrawn before they improve, so a patient getting worse after the antipsychotic is stopped is following the expected course rather than failing treatment.  [Learning objectives: LO 049, 095]

wrongExplanations.0: Benztropine is the standard anticholinergic for acute dystonia and drug-induced parkinsonism. In tardive dyskinesia it is ineffective and may worsen the movements — the single most important negative in this topic.
wrongExplanations.1: Propranolol is the first-line treatment for akathisia, the subacute restlessness that appears around 4 months into therapy, not for the choreoathetoid movements of tardive dyskinesia appearing around 4 years.
wrongExplanations.3: Diphenhydramine is an antihistamine with anticholinergic activity used for acute dystonic reactions, including as the Benadryl component of the B-52 intramuscular combination. It shares benztropine's problem here.
wrongExplanations.4: Amantadine is used for drug-induced parkinsonism, where it is an alternative to an anticholinergic. It is not the agent developed for or indicated in tardive dyskinesia.

questions.eli5: Most movement side effects from antipsychotics get better with anticholinergic medicines, but this late one does not — it needs valbenazine. It also usually looks worse for a while right after the antipsychotic is stopped.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old girl comes to a walk-in clinic alone requesting evaluation for vaginal discharge and possible sexually transmitted infection. She states that she is sexually active, that she does not want her parents informed, and that she will leave without care rather than have them contacted. She is alert, articulate, and demonstrates a clear understanding of testing and treatment. She is not pregnant, is not seeking an abortion, is medically stable with normal vital signs, and shows no evidence of abuse or coercion. Which of the following is the most appropriate action?
choices: A. Require parental consent before performing any testing
B. Evaluate and treat her without parental consent
C. Perform testing but withhold treatment until a parent can be reached
D. Refer her to the emergency department to obtain a court order
E. Proceed only after a judicial bypass has been granted
questions.explanation: Minors may consent to their own care in a defined set of domains, remembered as sex, drugs, and rock and roll — sexually transmitted infection and reproductive care, substance use treatment, and mental health care — plus legal emancipation and psychiatric emergencies. Sexually transmitted infection evaluation and treatment sits squarely in the first category, and requiring parental involvement here would predictably drive her out untreated, which is exactly the public health outcome these statutes exist to prevent. Board pearl — abortion is the exception to the exceptions, the domain where many jurisdictions do require parental involvement or judicial bypass, and the stem clears that explicitly by stating she is not pregnant.  [Learning objectives: LO 057]

wrongExplanations.0: Requiring parental consent for sexually transmitted infection care in a minor defeats the purpose of the statutory exception and, on her stated intention to leave, results in an untreated infection.
wrongExplanations.2: Splitting testing from treatment is internally inconsistent: the same consent authority covers both, and diagnosing an infection you then refuse to treat leaves her worse off than not testing at all.
wrongExplanations.3: No court order is needed. Emergency department referral adds delay and cost for care this clinic is already authorized to provide.
wrongExplanations.4: Judicial bypass is the mechanism associated with abortion consent requirements in jurisdictions that impose them. She is explicitly not pregnant and not seeking that care.

questions.eli5: Teenagers are allowed to get tested and treated for sexually transmitted infections on their own, without a parent signing off. The rule exists so that fear of parents does not stop them from getting care.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man with schizophrenia is charged with assault. At the time of the offense, according to multiple witnesses and his own subsequent account, he believed the victim was a demon sent to destroy his family and that stopping the victim was a righteous and necessary act. He has now been treated with an antipsychotic for 4 months in a forensic hospital, his delusions have resolved, and on examination he accurately describes the charges against him, the roles of the judge, prosecutor, and his own attorney, and the potential penalties, and he is able to discuss trial strategy with his attorney. Which of the following statements is most accurate?
choices: A. He is incompetent to stand trial, because he was psychotic at the time of the offense
B. He is competent to stand trial, which also establishes criminal responsibility
C. Both competence and criminal responsibility are judged by his current mental state
D. He is competent to stand trial; the insanity standard addresses his state at the time of the act
E. Criminal responsibility is determined by the treating psychiatrist rather than the court
F. Competence to stand trial requires the absence of any active psychiatric diagnosis
questions.explanation: These are two separate determinations at two different points in time. Competence to stand trial, under the Dusky standard, asks about the defendant NOW: can he understand the charges and assist his attorney? He plainly can, so he is competent. Criminal responsibility asks about him THEN: under the M'Naughton rule, a defendant may be found not guilty by reason of insanity if mental illness prevented him from understanding the nature and quality of the act or that it was wrong. His delusion that the act was righteous speaks directly to that second determination. Board pearl — treatment can restore competence to stand trial without changing criminal responsibility one bit, because responsibility was fixed at the moment of the offense.  [Learning objectives: LO 052, 079]

wrongExplanations.0: Competence is assessed at the time of trial, not at the time of the offense. His psychosis months ago has no bearing on whether he can participate in proceedings today, and he demonstrably can.
wrongExplanations.1: Competence and criminal responsibility are independent. A defendant can be fully competent to stand trial and still be found not guilty by reason of insanity, which is in fact the common configuration after treatment restores competence.
wrongExplanations.2: Only competence is judged by current mental state. Criminal responsibility is judged retrospectively, by the defendant's mental state at the moment of the act.
wrongExplanations.4: Psychiatrists evaluate and testify, but the determination itself belongs to the court — the same division that separates clinical capacity, decided by a physician, from legal competence, decided by a judge.
wrongExplanations.5: The Dusky standard requires the ability to understand the charges and assist counsel, not the absence of a diagnosis. Many defendants with active psychiatric illness are competent to stand trial.

questions.eli5: Two different questions get asked at two different times. Can he follow his trial and help his lawyer right now? Yes. Did his illness stop him from knowing his act was wrong back when it happened? That is the separate insanity question.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy adopted at 30 months of age from an overseas institution is brought to the office by his adoptive parents. Records document severe neglect, with high infant-to-caregiver ratios and no consistent caregiver. His parents report that when he falls and hurts himself he does not come to them, and that when they attempt to comfort him he stiffens and turns away. He watches adults warily from across the room and rarely shows positive emotion. He does not approach or wander off with unfamiliar adults and shows no unusual familiarity with strangers. His language is at age level, he engages in imaginative pretend play with peers at preschool, and he has no restricted interests, stereotyped movements, or sensory hyperreactivity. Hearing screening is normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Reactive attachment disorder is the INHIBITED, withdrawn pattern that follows severe early neglect: the child does not seek comfort from caregivers, does not respond to comfort when offered, shows minimal positive affect and limited social and emotional reciprocity, and appears watchful and hypervigilant. Both trauma-related attachment disorders require a documented history of insufficient care, which his institutional records supply. Board pearl — the pair splits by direction of behavior toward adults: reactive attachment disorder pulls AWAY from caregivers, while disinhibited social engagement disorder pushes indiscriminately TOWARD strangers, and the stem negates the latter explicitly.  [Learning objectives: LO 035, 080]

wrongExplanations.0: Autism spectrum disorder requires restricted, repetitive behaviors alongside social communication deficits, and it is not caused by neglect. The stem negates every element on that side — age-level language, imaginative pretend play with peers, and no restricted interests, stereotypies, or sensory hyperreactivity.
wrongExplanations.1: Disinhibited social engagement disorder arises from the same neglect history but produces the opposite behavior: overly familiar approach to unfamiliar adults and willingness to wander off with them. He explicitly does neither.
wrongExplanations.2: Selective mutism is a consistent failure to speak in one specific setting despite normal speech elsewhere, lasting at least 1 month. His language is at age level and no setting-specific mutism is described.
wrongExplanations.3: Separation anxiety disorder is excessive distress at separation from an attachment figure. He shows too little attachment behavior rather than too much, and he does not seek his parents even when hurt.

questions.eli5: After years with no one to care for him, this little boy stopped going to grown-ups for comfort at all — he pulls away even when his parents try. That withdrawn pattern after neglect is reactive attachment disorder; the opposite version runs up to strangers instead.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old woman recovering from hip arthroplasty is in a dimly lit hospital room at night. She calls the nurse and reports, with visible alarm, that a man is standing motionless in the far corner watching her. When the nurse turns on the overhead light, the patient looks again and says, "Oh — it is just the coat rack with my robe on it." She is fully oriented, her attention does not fluctuate, and she has no other perceptual complaints. Which of the following best describes this experience?
questions.explanation: An illusion is a MISPERCEIVED real external stimulus — there genuinely is a coat rack there, and her brain assembled it into a person under poor lighting. A hallucination has no external stimulus at all. The distinction matters clinically because illusions are common, often benign, and frequently improve simply by correcting the sensory conditions, whereas hallucinations carry a much heavier diagnostic weight. Board pearl — psychosis is a symptom, not a diagnosis, and its presence dramatically narrows a differential; that is exactly why you should not inflate an illusion into a hallucination, and why her preserved orientation and non-fluctuating attention are stated to keep you out of delirium.  [Learning objectives: LO 063]

wrongExplanations.0: An auditory hallucination is a perception of sound with no external source. Her experience is visual, and it resolved when the actual object was properly illuminated.
wrongExplanations.1: A delusion is a fixed false BELIEF held despite contrary evidence. She revised her interpretation immediately when the light was turned on, which is the opposite of fixity.
wrongExplanations.3: A visual hallucination requires the absence of any external stimulus. Here there was a real object — the coat rack — that generated the percept, which makes it an illusion by definition.
wrongExplanations.4: An idea of reference is the belief that neutral external events carry special personal meaning, such as a television broadcast speaking directly to the patient. She misidentified an object rather than assigning it personal significance.

questions.eli5: Something really was in the corner — a coat rack — and in the dark her brain made it into a person. Misreading a real object is an illusion; seeing something that is not there at all would be a hallucination.

questions.stem: A 43-year-old woman with no psychiatric history is referred after being arrested for repeatedly appearing at a television station. For the past 11 months she has been convinced that a local news anchor is secretly in love with her and communicates through coded phrasing and gestures during his broadcasts. She interprets his public statement that he does not know her as something his contract requires him to say. She has continued to work full-time as an accountant, maintains her apartment and her friendships, and her family reports no change in her self-care. She has no hallucinations, no disorganized speech or behavior, and no negative symptoms. Urine toxicology screening and thyroid-stimulating hormone are normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Delusional disorder requires a fixed, plausible (non-bizarre) delusion of at least 1 month with preserved functioning and no other prominent psychotic symptoms — and the subtype is assigned by the content of the belief. The EROTOMANIC subtype is the belief in a secret, often sexual, relationship with another person, characteristically someone of higher status. Board pearl — the test for non-bizarre is whether the belief could in principle be true, and a news anchor secretly loving a viewer could in principle be true even though the evidence says otherwise. These patients often go years or decades before coming to clinical attention, because they appear entirely normal until the delusion surfaces.  [Learning objectives: LO 059, 063]

wrongExplanations.0: The grandiose subtype involves belief in a special ability to make something happen that is not realistically plausible, such as clairvoyance or wishing an outcome into reality. Her belief concerns a relationship, not her own powers.
wrongExplanations.1: The jealous subtype is the fixed belief that a spouse or partner is being unfaithful, maintained against ample contrary evidence. She has no partner in the belief system; she believes she is loved rather than betrayed.
wrongExplanations.2: The persecutory subtype is the belief that one is being unfairly harmed or targeted, and it is the single most common subtype — which is exactly why it is the reflexive wrong answer here. Nothing in her belief involves being harmed.
wrongExplanations.3: The somatic subtype involves a fixed belief about having a serious or unusual illness, such as insides rotting or a body part being made of something impossible. She has no physical complaint.
wrongExplanations.5: Schizophrenia requires at least 6 months of disturbance with two or more active-phase symptoms and characteristic functional decline. She has an isolated delusion with fully preserved work, housing, self-care, and relationships, and explicitly no hallucinations, disorganization, or negative symptoms.

questions.eli5: She is certain a TV anchor loves her and is signaling her through his broadcasts, and nothing else about her life has fallen apart. A single believable-sounding false belief about someone loving you is the erotomanic type of delusional disorder.

questions.stem: Antipsychotic therapeutic effect and extrapyramidal side effects are both related to the degree of striatal dopamine D2 receptor occupancy achieved. Which of the following pairs of approximate occupancy thresholds is correct?
choices: A. Therapeutic effect at 40%; extrapyramidal symptoms at 50%
B. Therapeutic effect at 50%; extrapyramidal symptoms at 60%
C. Therapeutic effect at 60%; extrapyramidal symptoms at 90%
D. Therapeutic effect at 70%; extrapyramidal symptoms at 80%
E. Therapeutic effect and extrapyramidal symptoms share an identical threshold
questions.explanation: Therapeutic antipsychotic effect emerges around 70% D2 occupancy, while extrapyramidal symptoms begin around 78 to 80%. That narrow ten-point window is the entire practical basis for antipsychotic dosing: there is a real but slim band in which psychosis improves without movement side effects, and pushing the dose past it buys extrapyramidal symptoms rather than additional efficacy. Board pearl — this is why escalating the dose is the wrong answer for akathisia. The side effect is occupancy-dependent, so raising the dose drives occupancy further above the EPS threshold and predictably makes the restlessness worse.  [Learning objectives: LO 083, 086]

wrongExplanations.0: These thresholds are far too low. Occupancy in the 40 to 50% range is generally subtherapeutic, and setting the EPS threshold there would make movement side effects nearly universal at any effective dose.
wrongExplanations.1: Also too low on both counts, and a 10-point gap starting at 50% would misrepresent the dose at which clinical benefit actually appears.
wrongExplanations.2: The therapeutic figure is too low and the EPS figure too high. A 30-point safety margin would make extrapyramidal symptoms far rarer than they actually are in practice.
wrongExplanations.4: Identical thresholds would make every effective dose produce extrapyramidal symptoms, which is not what is observed — there is a genuine, if narrow, therapeutic window between the two.

questions.eli5: You need to block about seventy percent of a certain dopamine receptor for the medicine to work, and movement side effects start at about eighty. That thin gap is the whole target you are aiming for.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man is hospitalized for a first episode of schizophrenia. He has never taken an antipsychotic, has no cardiac or metabolic disease, does not smoke, and has no history of substance use. His body mass index is 23 kg/m2, fasting glucose and lipid panel are within normal limits, and electrocardiography shows a QTc of 418 ms. He and his family are willing to accept any recommended treatment. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial pharmacologic approach?
choices: D. Clozapine augmented with a second antipsychotic
E. A first-generation and a second-generation antipsychotic in combination
questions.explanation: The first-line consensus is a second-generation antipsychotic, and all five major guideline bodies agree on that point. The full ladder runs SGA first, then SGA or FGA second, then clozapine third, then clozapine augmentation fourth. Board pearl — hold this alongside the trial data, which complicates it usefully: CATIE and CUtLASS found that first-generation agents (perphenazine in particular) perform roughly as well as second-generation agents for routine use and are more cost-effective, while clozapine is genuinely superior for treatment-resistant disease. Guideline position and comparative-efficacy data are not the same question, and an exam can ask either one.  [Learning objectives: LO 045, 066]

wrongExplanations.0: A first-generation antipsychotic sits at the second rung of the consensus ladder, not the first, despite CATIE showing perphenazine to be roughly equivalent and more cost-effective for routine use. Guideline-based first-line is still an SGA.
wrongExplanations.1: Clozapine is third-line and is reserved for treatment-resistant disease, conventionally defined as failure of two adequate antipsychotic trials. Using it first exposes an untreated patient to agranulocytosis, myocarditis, and seizure risk with mandatory monitoring, none of which is justified yet.
wrongExplanations.3: Clozapine augmentation is the fourth and final rung, reached only after clozapine monotherapy has failed. It is three steps ahead of where this patient is.
wrongExplanations.4: Antipsychotic polypharmacy is not a recommended starting strategy and compounds side-effect burden without established added benefit in a treatment-naive first episode.

questions.eli5: For someone's first episode of schizophrenia, every major guideline says start with a newer antipsychotic. Clozapine is powerful but is saved for after two other medicines have failed.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man with schizophrenia was started on olanzapine 4 weeks ago and reports substantial improvement in auditory hallucinations. Before starting the medication, his personal and family history were documented and his weight, body mass index, waist circumference, blood pressure, fasting glucose, and fasting lipid panel were all recorded and within normal limits. He has no symptoms today and reports good adherence. He asks what monitoring he needs at this visit. Which of the following is the most appropriate?
choices: A. Recheck weight and obtain a fasting glucose
B. Recheck weight only, deferring all laboratory studies to 12 weeks
C. Obtain a fasting lipid panel only
D. Measure waist circumference and blood pressure only
E. No monitoring is indicated until the 6-month visit
questions.explanation: The metabolic monitoring schedule for second-generation antipsychotics is staggered rather than uniform, and the 4-week visit is a specific checkpoint: weight is rechecked at 4 and 8 weeks and then quarterly, and fasting GLUCOSE is repeated at 4 weeks, whereas the lipid panel is not due again until the quarterly or annual interval. Waist circumference and blood pressure are followed annually to quarterly. Board pearl — this schedule exists because olanzapine and clozapine carry the heaviest weight and type 2 diabetes burden of the class, and psychiatric patients on antipsychotics already carry a 2- to 4-fold baseline diabetes risk.  [Learning objectives: LO 086, 087]

wrongExplanations.1: Weight is correctly due at 4 weeks, but deferring the glucose misses the specific laboratory checkpoint the schedule places here — the one designed to catch early dysglycemia on a high-risk agent.
wrongExplanations.2: Lipids are obtained at baseline and then on a quarterly to annual cadence, not at 4 weeks. Choosing lipids alone also omits the weight, which is the most sensitive early signal.
wrongExplanations.3: Waist circumference and blood pressure are followed on an annual to quarterly basis. Neither is the 4-week priority, and taking them instead of weight and glucose inverts the schedule.
wrongExplanations.4: Deferring everything for 6 months forfeits the early window in which metabolic change is most detectable and most reversible, on the antipsychotic with the highest metabolic burden.

questions.eli5: Four weeks in, the checklist says weigh him and check a fasting blood sugar. Cholesterol can wait until the three-month check, but weight and sugar move early on this medicine.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man with schizophrenia requires a change in antipsychotic because of inadequate symptom control. Height is 173 cm (5 ft 8 in) and weight is 102 kg (225 lb); body mass index is 34 kg/m2. Hemoglobin A1c is 6.2%, fasting triglycerides are 310 mg/dL, and both of his parents have type 2 diabetes mellitus. Blood pressure is 138/86 mm Hg. Electrocardiography shows a QTc of 412 ms with normal potassium and magnesium, and his absolute neutrophil count is normal. He has had no extrapyramidal symptoms and no galactorrhea on prior therapy. Which of the following antipsychotics carries the lowest metabolic risk for this patient?
questions.explanation: His prediabetes, hypertriglyceridemia, obesity, and family history make metabolic burden the deciding variable. Aripiprazole sits in the lowest-metabolic-risk group alongside ziprasidone, lurasidone, and cariprazine, while olanzapine and clozapine sit at the opposite extreme for both weight gain and type 2 diabetes risk. The stem clears every competing constraint deliberately — normal QTc with normal electrolytes, normal neutrophil count, no prior EPS, no galactorrhea — so that metabolic risk is the only axis left. Board pearl — aripiprazole is a D2 partial agonist, which also makes it the agent that lowers rather than raises prolactin; its own trade-off is a comparatively high rate of akathisia.  [Learning objectives: LO 045, 086]

wrongExplanations.0: Chlorpromazine is a low-potency first-generation agent whose burden is anticholinergic effects, sedation, and alpha-1 blockade with orthostatic hypotension. It also carries the highest extrapyramidal risk group alongside haloperidol and offers no metabolic advantage.
wrongExplanations.1: Clozapine is in the highest metabolic risk tier for both weight gain and type 2 diabetes, and it additionally requires mandatory neutrophil monitoring. It is also third-line, reserved for treatment-resistant disease.
wrongExplanations.2: Olanzapine carries the worst weight gain of the class and shares the highest diabetes risk with clozapine — the single worst choice for a man with a hemoglobin A1c of 6.2% and triglycerides of 310 mg/dL.
wrongExplanations.4: Quetiapine carries substantial metabolic burden along with the highest sedation and orthostatic hypotension risk. Its distinct niche is psychosis in Parkinson disease and Lewy body dementia, which does not apply here.
wrongExplanations.5: Risperidone has intermediate metabolic risk but the highest prolactin elevation of the second-generation agents along with paliperidone, and dose-dependent extrapyramidal symptoms. It is not the lowest-risk option on the axis that matters here.

questions.eli5: He is already heavy, prediabetic, and has high triglycerides, so the medicine must not make any of that worse. Aripiprazole is in the group least likely to cause weight gain and diabetes; olanzapine and clozapine are the worst.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old woman has taken a prescription hypnotic nightly for 3 months for insomnia. Her husband reports that on two occasions he found her in the kitchen at 3 AM eating cereal directly from the box and unresponsive to conversation, and that last week she drove 4 miles to a convenience store and was found asleep in the parked car by police. She has no recollection of any of these events. She drinks no alcohol, takes no other sedating medication, and urine toxicology screening is negative. Neurologic examination, electroencephalography, and MRI of the brain are normal. Which of the following medications is she most likely taking?
questions.explanation: The Z-drugs — zolpidem, eszopiclone, and zaleplon — act selectively at the BZ1 subtype of the GABA-A receptor and are indicated for sleep only. Their signature adverse effects are complex sleep-related behaviors, or parasomnias: sleep-eating, sleep-sex, and most notoriously sleep-driving, which has produced real crashes and is most strongly associated with zolpidem specifically. Anterograde amnesia for the episodes is characteristic and is why the patient herself cannot report them. Board pearl — because Z-drugs act at the benzodiazepine site, flumazenil reverses them in overdose, which is a favorite pairing to test.  [Learning objectives: LO 013, 026]

wrongExplanations.0: Ramelteon is a melatonin receptor agonist with no action at the GABA-A receptor. It has no abuse potential and is not associated with complex sleep behaviors.
wrongExplanations.2: Suvorexant is an orexin receptor antagonist. Its typical adverse effects are next-day somnolence and abnormal dreams rather than the complex motor parasomnias described here.
wrongExplanations.3: Hydroxyzine is an antihistamine used as a non-addictive as-needed anxiolytic and sleep aid. It causes sedation and anticholinergic effects and warrants QTc attention, but not sleep-driving.
wrongExplanations.4: Trazodone is widely used off-label for insomnia through 5-HT2, alpha-1, and H1 blockade. Its signature adverse effects are sedation, orthostatic hypotension, and priapism — not complex sleep behaviors.

questions.eli5: This sleep medicine can make people get up and do complicated things — eat, or even drive — while still asleep, with no memory of it afterward. Zolpidem is the one famous for sleep-driving.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man with generalized anxiety disorder has taken sertraline for 5 months with substantial improvement in his baseline worry. He continues to have occasional discrete surges of anxiety two or three times monthly, usually before client presentations, and asks for something he can take in the moment when one occurs. He has opioid use disorder in sustained remission and is maintained on buprenorphine, and he discloses a prior period of alprazolam misuse. He has no cardiac disease; electrocardiography shows a QTc of 410 ms with normal potassium and magnesium. He has no history of glaucoma or urinary retention. Which of the following is the most appropriate as-needed medication?
questions.explanation: Two constraints narrow this to one answer. His opioid use disorder in remission and documented prior alprazolam misuse make any benzodiazepine a poor choice, and the request is specifically for AS-NEEDED relief in the moment. Hydroxyzine is an H1 inverse agonist that works acutely, carries no abuse potential, and is explicitly the as-needed option for exactly this situation. Board pearl — the reason buspirone fails here is timing, not safety: it is a 5-HT1A partial agonist that requires 4 to 6 weeks to work and is useless acutely, which is why patients switched from a benzodiazepine to it describe it as being like taking water. Do check the QTc with hydroxyzine, which the stem has already documented as normal.  [Learning objectives: LO 048, 081]

wrongExplanations.0: Alprazolam has the shortest half-life and highest abuse potential of the benzodiazepines, and he has a documented history of misusing this exact drug. Combining a benzodiazepine with buprenorphine also adds respiratory depression risk.
wrongExplanations.1: Clonazepam is less abuse-prone than alprazolam but is still a benzodiazepine with cross-dependence liability in a patient with a substance use history, and it carries the same interaction concern with buprenorphine.
wrongExplanations.2: Diazepam is long-acting with active metabolites that accumulate, which makes it a poor as-needed agent regardless, and it shares the full dependence and respiratory-depression problem.
wrongExplanations.3: Buspirone is an excellent non-addictive choice for GENERALIZED anxiety and would be right if the question asked about ongoing augmentation — but it takes 4 to 6 weeks to work and does nothing at all taken in the moment, which is what he is asking for.

questions.eli5: He needs something he can take right when anxiety hits, and he cannot safely have anything addictive. Hydroxyzine is an antihistamine that calms anxiety quickly and cannot be abused.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman comes to the office because she has been unable to complete required immunizations for her nursing program. Since about age 14 she has fainted during every attempted blood draw; on the last two attempts she became pale and diaphoretic, her pulse fell to 44/min, and she lost consciousness for several seconds before recovering fully. She now avoids all medical appointments and dental care and has missed two required vaccinations. She has no fear of other situations, no attacks occurring outside medical settings, and no fear of being watched or judged. She has no cardiac history, and echocardiography and Holter monitoring performed after the last episode were normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Specific phobia is fear of one discrete object or situation, and the blood-injection-injury subtype is physiologically unique among the phobias: instead of the sympathetic tachycardia seen with every other phobic stimulus, it produces a vasovagal response with BRADYCARDIA, hypotension, and syncope — her pulse of 44/min is the buried clue. Board pearl — the subtypes have characteristic ages of onset worth holding: animal type begins in childhood, blood-injury type in adolescence (hers began at 14), and situational or other types around the twenties. Specific phobia has a roughly 9% prevalence, and the treatment with by far the strongest evidence is in vivo exposure.  [Learning objectives: LO 036, 081]

wrongExplanations.0: Panic disorder requires recurrent attacks that are at least partly UNEXPECTED. Her episodes occur exclusively and reliably with needles, and she explicitly has no attacks outside medical settings.
wrongExplanations.1: Social anxiety disorder centers on fear of scrutiny and negative evaluation by others. She explicitly denies any fear of being watched or judged, and her response is a physiologic faint rather than an evaluative fear.
wrongExplanations.3: Agoraphobia requires fear across multiple situations united by the theme that escape or help may be unavailable. Her fear is tied to one specific stimulus, not to being trapped.
wrongExplanations.4: Generalized anxiety disorder requires excessive worry across multiple everyday domains for more than 6 months. Her anxiety is entirely circumscribed to needles and blood.
wrongExplanations.5: Illness anxiety disorder is preoccupation with HAVING a serious illness despite reassurance. She has no such preoccupation; she is avoiding a procedure, not fearing a diagnosis.

questions.eli5: Most fears make your heart race, but the fear of needles and blood does the opposite — your heart slows down and you faint. That is its own subtype of specific phobia, and it usually starts in the teenage years.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man comes to the office at his sister's urging. For the past 3 years he has been preoccupied with the belief that his nose is 'grotesquely crooked and deformed'; on examination his nose is entirely within normal limits and the deviation he describes is not apparent to the examiner. He spends 3 to 4 hours daily checking his profile in mirrors and reflective surfaces, comparing photographs of himself, and arranging his hair and hats to conceal his face. He has consulted five plastic surgeons, two of whom declined to operate. He has stopped dating and withdrew from a course requiring oral presentations. His weight is normal, he eats regularly without binges or compensatory behavior, and he expresses no concern about his body weight or shape. He acknowledges that others tell him his nose looks fine but says he cannot make himself believe it. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Body dysmorphic disorder is preoccupation with an imagined or minor defect in physical APPEARANCE, occupying an hour or more daily and driving repetitive behaviors such as mirror checking, comparing, camouflaging, and seeking cosmetic procedures. It sits in the obsessive-compulsive and related disorders chapter alongside hoarding, trichotillomania, and excoriation disorder. Board pearl — BDD is explicitly excluded if the preoccupation is better explained by an eating disorder, which is why the stem states his weight is normal, his eating is unremarkable, and he has no concern about body weight or shape. Treatment across the OCD-spectrum entries is serotonergic medication plus CBT.  [Learning objectives: LO 036]

wrongExplanations.0: Anorexia nervosa requires restriction of intake, fear of weight gain, and body image distortion centered on WEIGHT and SHAPE. He eats normally at a normal weight and explicitly has no weight or shape concern — the specific exclusion that separates these two diagnoses.
wrongExplanations.1: Illness anxiety disorder is preoccupation with having a serious DISEASE despite reassurance. His preoccupation is about how a body part looks, not about being ill.
wrongExplanations.2: Social anxiety disorder centers on fear of negative evaluation in social situations generally. His avoidance of dating and presentations is downstream of a specific appearance preoccupation rather than a primary fear of scrutiny.
wrongExplanations.3: OCD involves obsessions and compulsions across varied content domains. When the preoccupation is exclusively about a perceived appearance defect, the more specific diagnosis within the same DSM-5 chapter is body dysmorphic disorder.
wrongExplanations.4: Delusional disorder, somatic type involves a fixed belief about having a serious or unusual illness — insides rotting, a body part made of something impossible — rather than a perceived cosmetic flaw. He also retains some insight, acknowledging that others see his nose as normal.

questions.eli5: He is convinced his nose is deformed even though it looks completely normal, and he spends hours a day checking mirrors and hiding his face. Being consumed by a flaw that is minor or not really there is body dysmorphic disorder.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old girl is brought to the office by her mother, who noticed thinning at the crown of her scalp. For the past 2 years the patient has pulled out her own scalp hair, describing a mounting sense of tension beforehand and relief immediately afterward. She has tried repeatedly to stop and has been unable to, and she now wears a wide headband to conceal the area and has stopped swimming with friends. Examination shows patchy hair loss with broken hairs of varying lengths within the affected area and no scaling, erythema, or scarring; potassium hydroxide preparation is negative. She has no contamination fears, no checking or washing rituals, no preoccupation with her appearance beyond the hair loss itself, and no delusions. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Trichotillomania is recurrent hair pulling resulting in hair loss, with repeated unsuccessful attempts to stop and resulting distress or impairment. The tension-then-relief cycle she describes is characteristic, and the examination finding that clinches it is broken hairs of VARYING lengths within the patch — evidence of ongoing mechanical pulling rather than a disease process. It sits in the obsessive-compulsive and related disorders chapter and is treated with serotonergic medication plus CBT. Board pearl — the same tension-and-relief logic underlies the self-harm seen in borderline personality disorder, where physical sensation is used to displace unbearable emotional distress.  [Learning objectives: LO 036, 081]

wrongExplanations.1: Alopecia areata produces smooth, well-demarcated patches of COMPLETE hair loss without broken hairs of varying lengths. It is an autoimmune process with no associated urge, tension, or relief cycle.
wrongExplanations.2: OCD requires obsessions the patient experiences as intrusive and unwanted, typically paired with neutralizing compulsions. She explicitly has no contamination fears, checking, or washing rituals, and her pulling relieves tension rather than neutralizing a specific feared outcome.
wrongExplanations.3: Excoriation disorder is the skin-picking analogue in the same chapter, producing skin lesions rather than hair loss. Her behavior is directed at hair, not skin.
wrongExplanations.4: Body dysmorphic disorder is preoccupation with a perceived appearance defect. Her distress about her appearance is a consequence of the hair loss she has caused, not the driver of the behavior.

questions.eli5: She pulls out her own hair because the tension builds until she does, and then it feels better for a moment. Hairs broken off at different lengths in the bald patch is the clue that they were pulled rather than fell out.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old veteran with posttraumatic stress disorder reports persistent negative beliefs that she is 'permanently damaged and cannot be trusted with anything,' an inability to experience happiness or affection toward her children, and persistent guilt that she could have prevented a comrade's death. These particular symptoms fall under which of the following DSM-5 criteria for posttraumatic stress disorder?
choices: A. Criterion A — exposure to the traumatic stressor
D. Criterion D — negative alterations in cognition and mood
E. Criterion E — alterations in arousal and reactivity
F. Criterion F — duration greater than 1 month
questions.explanation: PTSD's criteria run A through H: A is the stressor, B is intrusion, C is avoidance, D is negative alterations in cognition and mood, E is alterations in arousal and reactivity, F is duration greater than 1 month, G is functional impairment, and H is exclusion of substance or medical causes. Persistent exaggerated negative beliefs about oneself, persistent inability to experience positive emotions, and persistent distorted guilt all belong to Criterion D. Board pearl — Criterion D is the cluster most often mistaken for a comorbid major depressive episode; the distinction is that these cognitions are anchored to the trauma and coexist with intrusion, avoidance, and hyperarousal, and Criterion D is also what distinguishes PTSD from acute stress disorder in the first month.  [Learning objectives: LO 060]

wrongExplanations.0: Criterion A is the exposure itself — actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence, whether experienced, witnessed, or learned of. Her comrade's death satisfies Criterion A, but her guilt ABOUT it is a Criterion D cognition.
wrongExplanations.1: Criterion B is intrusion: recurrent involuntary memories, nightmares, flashbacks, and psychological or physiologic reactivity to reminders. None of the three symptoms described is an intrusive re-experiencing phenomenon.
wrongExplanations.2: Criterion C is avoidance of trauma-related internal reminders such as thoughts and feelings, or external reminders such as people, places, and activities. She is describing beliefs and emotional numbing rather than avoidance behavior.
wrongExplanations.4: Criterion E is arousal and reactivity: irritability, recklessness, hypervigilance, exaggerated startle, concentration difficulty, and sleep disturbance. Her symptoms are cognitive and affective rather than hyperaroused.
wrongExplanations.5: Criterion F is a duration rule requiring more than 1 month, not a symptom cluster at all — it is what converts acute stress disorder into PTSD.

questions.eli5: PTSD symptoms are sorted into lettered groups. Thinking you are permanently ruined, not being able to feel good things, and blaming yourself all belong to group D, the one about negative thoughts and mood.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man comes to a family medicine clinic for an annual examination. He reports drinking three to four beers most evenings. His physician administers a brief validated four-item screening instrument that asks whether he has ever felt he should cut down on his drinking, whether he has been annoyed by others criticizing his drinking, whether he has felt guilty about his drinking, and whether he has ever had a drink first thing in the morning to steady his nerves. He answers yes to two of the four items. Physical examination is unremarkable and aminotransferases are within normal limits. Which of the following is the most appropriate interpretation?
choices: A. A negative screen requiring no further assessment
B. A negative screen warranting repeat screening in 1 year
C. An indeterminate result requiring a fifth question
D. A positive result only if all four items had been endorsed
E. A positive screen warranting further assessment for alcohol use disorder
questions.explanation: This is the CAGE questionnaire — Cut down, Annoyed, Guilty, Eye-opener — and two or more affirmative answers constitutes a POSITIVE screen warranting a fuller assessment for alcohol use disorder. A screening instrument does not make the diagnosis; it identifies who needs the full DSM-5 criteria applied. Board pearl — the other instrument to know by name is AUDIT-C, scored 0 to 12. Normal aminotransferases are deliberately unhelpful here: liver enzymes are neither sensitive nor specific for alcohol use disorder, and a normal panel never negates a positive screen.  [Learning objectives: LO 010, 015]

wrongExplanations.0: Two affirmative answers meets the positive threshold, and treating it as negative misses the entire purpose of screening — CAGE is designed to be sensitive at a low bar precisely so that at-risk drinkers are identified.
wrongExplanations.1: Deferring for a year applies to patients who screen negative. He has crossed the threshold now, and his reported intake of three to four beers nightly independently warrants assessment.
wrongExplanations.2: CAGE has exactly four items and a defined cutoff of two. There is no fifth question and no indeterminate band.
wrongExplanations.3: Requiring all four items would set the threshold far too high and defeat the instrument's purpose. The validated cutoff is two or more.

questions.eli5: This four-question quiz about drinking counts as positive at two yes answers, and he said yes to two. It does not diagnose anything by itself — it means the doctor now needs to ask a lot more.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of varenicline?
choices: A. Inhibition of norepinephrine and dopamine reuptake
B. Competitive antagonism at the mu-opioid receptor
C. Partial agonism at the alpha-4-beta-2 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor
E. Agonism at the alpha-2 adrenergic receptor
questions.explanation: Varenicline is a partial agonist at the alpha-4-beta-2 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor. Partial agonism does double duty: it provides enough receptor stimulation to blunt craving and withdrawal, while simultaneously occupying the receptor so that smoked nicotine produces less reward. Nausea is its most common adverse effect. Board pearl — the two pharmacologic options for smoking cessation are varenicline and bupropion, and bupropion's limitation is that it lowers the seizure threshold; nicotine replacement is the third, stepdown approach.  [Learning objectives: LO 001, 005, 026]

wrongExplanations.0: Norepinephrine and dopamine reuptake inhibition describes bupropion, the other agent used for smoking cessation. Bupropion works on monoamine transporters rather than at the nicotinic receptor.
wrongExplanations.1: Competitive mu-opioid antagonism describes naloxone and naltrexone. Naltrexone is used for alcohol and opioid use disorder, not for nicotine.
wrongExplanations.3: Aldehyde dehydrogenase inhibition describes disulfiram, which causes acetaldehyde to accumulate and produces an aversive reaction when alcohol is consumed.
wrongExplanations.4: Alpha-2 adrenergic agonism describes clonidine, which blunts the sympathetic surge common to most withdrawal syndromes and eases nicotine withdrawal symptomatically — but that is not varenicline's mechanism.

questions.eli5: Varenicline sits on the same brain receptor nicotine uses, pressing it just a little. That takes the edge off cravings and also blocks cigarettes from giving their usual reward.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old woman with severe treatment-resistant major depressive disorder is undergoing electroconvulsive therapy. Before the neuromuscular blocking agent is administered, a blood pressure cuff is inflated around one ankle to a pressure above her systolic blood pressure and left inflated through the induced seizure. Which of the following best explains the purpose of this maneuver?
choices: A. To reduce the risk of deep venous thrombosis during the procedure
B. To isolate one foot from the paralytic so that seizure duration can be observed
C. To permit continuous non-invasive blood pressure monitoring
D. To lower the seizure threshold and reduce the required stimulus intensity
E. To prevent musculoskeletal injury to the ankle during the convulsion
questions.explanation: The anesthetic recipe is thiopental plus succinylcholine, and the cuff is inflated before the succinylcholine circulates so that the paralytic never reaches that foot. The isolated foot therefore still convulses visibly, letting the team time the motor seizure directly — which matters because therapeutic effect is proportional to seizure duration. Board pearl — the rest of the ECT profile is worth holding together: roughly 8 treatments in a typical course, about 80% respond, there are no absolute contraindications, and it is safe in pregnancy and in older adults. Expected adverse effects are transient disorientation, headache, and partial anterograde and retrograde amnesia that usually resolves within 6 months.  [Learning objectives: LO 066, 072]

wrongExplanations.0: Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis has nothing to do with this maneuver, and a brief tourniquet during a several-minute procedure would not serve that purpose.
wrongExplanations.2: Blood pressure is monitored on the arm as in any anesthetized patient. A cuff held above systolic pressure for the duration of the seizure is a tourniquet, not a measuring device.
wrongExplanations.3: Seizure threshold is influenced by the anesthetic agent, hyperventilation, and stimulus parameters. An ankle tourniquet has no effect on threshold.
wrongExplanations.4: The purpose of the paralytic is precisely to prevent musculoskeletal injury by suppressing the convulsion — so deliberately excluding one foot from that protection is the opposite of an injury-prevention strategy, and it is accepted specifically because seeing the seizure is worth more.

questions.eli5: The paralyzing drug stops the body from shaking, which is safer but means you cannot see the seizure. Cuffing off one foot keeps the drug out of it, so that foot still twitches and the team can time how long the seizure lasts.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman has major depressive disorder that has failed three adequate antidepressant trials and one augmentation trial with an atypical antipsychotic. She reports passive suicidal ideation without a plan. She has no psychotic features and no history of substance use, and urine toxicology screening is negative. Blood pressure is 126/78 mm Hg on repeated readings. Her medical history is notable for an incidentally discovered unruptured 7-mm anterior communicating artery aneurysm currently followed with serial imaging by neurosurgery. Intranasal esketamine is being considered. Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action?
choices: A. Proceed with intranasal esketamine at the standard dose
B. Proceed with intranasal esketamine at a reduced starting dose
C. Proceed with esketamine after initiating an antihypertensive agent
D. Esketamine is contraindicated; consider electroconvulsive therapy
E. Proceed with esketamine and observe blood pressure for 2 hours after dosing
questions.explanation: Esketamine's contraindications are aneurysmal vascular disease, arteriovenous malformation, prior intracerebral hemorrhage, and uncontrolled hypertension — because it produces a transient blood pressure surge that could rupture a vulnerable vessel. Her documented unruptured anterior communicating artery aneurysm falls squarely within the first of those, and no dose adjustment or monitoring protocol makes a contraindicated drug appropriate. ECT, by contrast, has NO absolute contraindications and is the gold standard for affective disorders, including refractory depression with suicidality. Board pearl — both esketamine and ECT appear on the short list of four treatments with direct evidence for reducing death by suicide, alongside lithium and clozapine, so switching between them does not sacrifice that property.  [Learning objectives: LO 066, 072]

wrongExplanations.0: Proceeding at standard dose ignores a listed contraindication in a patient with a vessel that is already being watched for growth and rupture risk.
wrongExplanations.1: Dose reduction does not convert a vascular contraindication into a safe exposure; even a smaller transient pressure surge is an unacceptable risk against an intracranial aneurysm.
wrongExplanations.2: Her blood pressure is already normal at 126/78 mm Hg, so there is no hypertension to treat. The contraindication here is the aneurysm itself, not her baseline pressure.
wrongExplanations.4: Post-dose blood pressure monitoring is standard practice for every esketamine administration and does nothing to address the underlying contraindication — it would detect a surge after it had already occurred.

questions.eli5: Esketamine briefly spikes blood pressure, and she has a weak spot on a brain artery that is already being watched. That rules the drug out entirely, and shock therapy is the option with no absolute reasons to avoid it.

questions.stem: A developmental theorist described a sequence of psychosocial stages characterized by the successive achievement of trust, autonomy, initiative, industry, and identity. Which of the following theorists proposed this framework?
questions.explanation: Erikson's psychosocial stages are keyed to a developmental task at each age, moving through trust, autonomy, initiative, industry, and identity. Board pearl — pair each theorist with their signature concept, because exams work backward from the concept to the name: Piaget with cognitive milestones (object permanence, egocentrism, conservation, abstraction), Vygotsky with scaffolding, Ainsworth and Bowlby with attachment and the Strange Situation, Winnicott with the holding environment, the good-enough mother, and play, and Freud with the psychosexual stages.  [Learning objectives: LO 103, 104]

wrongExplanations.1: Piaget described COGNITIVE development, with milestones including object permanence, egocentrism, conservation, and the emergence of abstract thought — not psychosocial tasks such as trust and industry.
wrongExplanations.2: Vygotsky is associated with scaffolding and the role of social interaction and guided support in learning, not with a staged sequence of psychosocial achievements.
wrongExplanations.3: Winnicott, a pediatrician and psychoanalyst, contributed the holding environment, the good-enough mother, and the developmental role of play.
wrongExplanations.4: Ainsworth, working with Bowlby, developed the Strange Situation paradigm and the classification of attachment styles — a framework about the caregiver relationship rather than a stage sequence.

questions.eli5: Erikson's idea is that at each age a child has one big life lesson to master — first trusting people, then doing things independently, then working hard, then figuring out who they are.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy is brought to the office by his parents. Since about age 10 he has had episodes of rapid eye blinking and shoulder shrugging, and for roughly the same period he has repeatedly cleared his throat and sniffed; his parents initially attributed the throat clearing and sniffing to seasonal allergies, but an allergy evaluation was negative and the symptoms persist year-round. The movements and sounds wax and wane in frequency, worsen when he is stressed or tired, and he can suppress them briefly at school before they return in a burst at home. He has attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder and takes no medication. Neurologic examination is otherwise normal, and he takes no stimulants or other medications. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Tourette disorder requires BOTH multiple motor tics AND at least one vocal tic, present for more than 1 year, with onset before age 18. He has motor tics (eye blinking, shoulder shrugging) and vocal tics (throat clearing, sniffing) running roughly 2 years since age 10 — all three requirements met. Waxing and waning, worsening with stress, and brief suppressibility followed by rebound are characteristic. Board pearl — remember the terrible triad: Tourette disorder clusters with OCD and ADHD, and he already carries the ADHD diagnosis. That matters practically, because stimulants can exacerbate tics, which is why atomoxetine is often chosen when both conditions coexist.  [Learning objectives: LO 035, 105]

wrongExplanations.0: Provisional tic disorder requires tics present for LESS than 1 year since first onset. His have persisted roughly 2 years.
wrongExplanations.1: Persistent motor tic disorder requires motor tics only, with vocal tics explicitly absent. His throat clearing and sniffing are vocal tics — the allergy workup was negative and they persist year-round, which is the negative that forces you to count them as tics.
wrongExplanations.2: Persistent vocal tic disorder requires vocal tics only. He also has clear motor tics, so this diagnosis is excluded for the mirror-image reason.
wrongExplanations.3: Stereotypic movement disorder involves repetitive, rhythmic, seemingly purposeful movements such as hand flapping or body rocking, typically beginning in early childhood and often in the context of a neurodevelopmental disorder. Tics are sudden, non-rhythmic, and preceded by an urge with brief suppressibility.
wrongExplanations.5: OCD involves obsessions and compulsions performed to neutralize anxiety. His movements and sounds are preceded by an urge and relieved by expression, not performed to prevent a feared outcome — though OCD, ADHD, and Tourette do co-occur as a recognized cluster.

questions.eli5: He has both movements (blinking, shrugging) and sounds (throat clearing, sniffing), and they have been going on for about two years starting at age ten. Needing both kinds for over a year is what makes it Tourette.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man admitted to a general medical floor repeatedly gets out of bed during the night and wanders into other patients' rooms, waking them. He is redirectable when staff escort him back, has not struck or threatened anyone, and has not attempted to pull out lines or leave the unit. The night nurse telephones the on-call physician to request an order for four-point restraints or an intramuscular sedating medication, explaining that the unit is short-staffed and the team needs time to complete documentation. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?
choices: A. Order four-point restraints for the remainder of the night shift
B. Decline; restraint is permitted only to protect immediate physical safety
C. Order intramuscular olanzapine to sedate him until morning
D. Order seclusion in a locked room until the morning team arrives
E. Order restraints with a documented review every 24 hours
questions.explanation: Seclusion and restraint may be used ONLY to protect the immediate physical safety of the patient or others — never for coercion, discipline, staff convenience, or as a substitute for adequate staffing. This patient is redirectable, non-aggressive, and has not endangered himself, so the safety threshold is not met, and the stated reason (short staffing and documentation time) is explicitly an impermissible one. Board pearl — medication given to subdue a patient rather than to treat a condition is a CHEMICAL restraint and is governed by the same rules, which is why the intramuscular option is not a workaround. When restraint is genuinely indicated it requires a written physician order, regular review, a time limit, and discontinuation as soon as possible.  [Learning objectives: LO 057, 079]

wrongExplanations.0: Restraining a redirectable, non-aggressive patient for an entire shift fails the immediate-safety requirement and additionally carries real risk in an older adult, including delirium worsening, injury, and deconditioning.
wrongExplanations.2: Sedating medication given to subdue rather than to treat is a chemical restraint by definition and is held to the identical standard. Calling it a medication order does not exempt it from the rule.
wrongExplanations.3: Seclusion is subject to the same immediate-safety requirement as restraint, and the least restrictive alternative principle applies: if a patient can be managed with redirection, they should be.
wrongExplanations.4: A 24-hour review interval is far too long, and no review schedule legitimizes a restraint that was never indicated. Orders must be time-limited and reviewed regularly, and the intervention stopped as soon as the safety justification ends.

questions.eli5: Tying someone down or knocking them out with a shot is only allowed when they are about to hurt themselves or someone else — never because the unit is busy. He is just wandering and comes back when asked.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man with advanced metastatic disease becomes encephalopathic and is determined by the treating team to lack decision-making capacity. A decision is required about whether to proceed with a palliative procedure. He completed no living will and designated no healthcare proxy. Present at the bedside and available to participate are his wife of 40 years, an adult daughter with whom he speaks weekly, and a younger brother who lives locally. There is no evidence of estrangement, no court-appointed guardian, and no dispute among the family members. Which of the following is the most appropriate surrogate decision-maker?
choices: E. A court-appointed guardian obtained through an emergency petition
questions.explanation: When a patient lacks capacity and has executed no advance directive, decision-making authority follows a defined surrogate hierarchy: spouse, then adult children, then parents, then siblings. His wife sits at the top of that order, and there is no estrangement, dispute, or guardianship to displace her. Board pearl — advance directives come in two forms, a living will stating the patient's wishes and a healthcare proxy naming a decision-maker, and both activate only ONCE capacity is lost. The standard the surrogate applies is substituted judgment: deciding based on what the patient would have wanted, not on what the surrogate would choose.  [Learning objectives: LO 057]

wrongExplanations.0: Adult children are the second tier of the hierarchy and are reached only when there is no spouse, or when the spouse is unavailable, estranged, or otherwise unable to serve. His wife is present and able.
wrongExplanations.1: Siblings sit at the bottom of the hierarchy, below spouse, adult children, and parents. A brother would be reached only if none of those higher tiers were available.
wrongExplanations.3: A physician may act in the patient's best interest when there is no capacity AND no available surrogate — that is the fallback, not the first option. A capable spouse is standing at the bedside.
wrongExplanations.4: Emergency guardianship is reserved for situations where no appropriate surrogate exists or where there is genuine, unresolvable dispute. The stem explicitly negates both, and pursuing a petition would introduce needless delay in a palliative decision.

questions.eli5: He never wrote down who should decide for him, so there is a set order: husband or wife first, then adult children, then parents, then brothers and sisters. His wife is there, so she decides.

questions.stem: A resident is taught a shorthand for predicting second-generation antipsychotic side-effect burden from the drug's name ending. Which of the following correctly pairs a suffix group with the adverse-effect profile it predicts?
choices: A. The -pines predict extrapyramidal symptoms and hyperprolactinemia
B. The -dones predict weight gain, metabolic burden, and sedation
D. The -dones predict akathisia and are the most kid-friendly group
E. The -pines predict weight gain, metabolic burden, and sedation
questions.explanation: The suffix shorthand runs: PINEs (olanzapine, quetiapine, asenapine) are sedating with high metabolic and weight burden; DONEs (risperidone, ziprasidone, paliperidone, iloperidone) behave like watered-down typicals, carrying more extrapyramidal symptoms, prolactin elevation, and NMS risk; PIPs (the aripiprazole partial-agonist family) are associated with akathisia and are the comparatively kid-friendly group; and RIP refers to clozapine as the last-resort agent. Board pearl — the shorthand is a starting point, not a substitute for the actual ranking tables: aripiprazole and ziprasidone sit in the lowest metabolic-risk tier, and olanzapine and clozapine sit at the top for both weight gain and type 2 diabetes.  [Learning objectives: LO 083, 086]
