wrongExplanations.0: This assigns the DONE profile to the PINEs. Extrapyramidal symptoms and hyperprolactinemia belong to risperidone and paliperidone, not to olanzapine and quetiapine.
wrongExplanations.1: This is the reverse error, assigning the PINE profile to the DONEs. Risperidone and ziprasidone are not the heavy metabolic offenders; olanzapine is.
wrongExplanations.2: Agranulocytosis is unique to clozapine, occurring in roughly 1 to 2% of patients and requiring mandatory neutrophil monitoring. It is not a class effect of the partial agonists.
wrongExplanations.3: Akathisia and pediatric use describe the PIPs — aripiprazole and its relatives — not the DONEs, which are the higher-EPS, higher-prolactin group.

questions.eli5: Drug endings give you a hint. The -pines make you heavy and sleepy, the -dones cause more stiffness and raise prolactin, and the aripiprazole family causes restlessness but is used most in kids.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old man with a 9-year history of Parkinson disease treated with carbidopa-levodopa is brought to the office by his wife because for the past 3 months he has seen small children and animals in the house that are not there, and has become convinced that his neighbor enters the home while he sleeps. The hallucinations and delusions now frighten him and disrupt the household. His levodopa dose has already been reduced as far as his motor symptoms permit, and further reduction produced disabling rigidity and freezing. Complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, thyroid-stimulating hormone, and urinalysis are normal, and noncontrast CT of the head shows no acute abnormality. Which of the following is the most appropriate antipsychotic?
questions.explanation: Quetiapine is the antipsychotic of choice for psychosis in Parkinson disease and dementia with Lewy bodies, because its D2 blockade is comparatively weak and loosely bound, so it controls hallucinations and delusions with the least worsening of parkinsonian motor symptoms. Every other option carries meaningful nigrostriatal D2 blockade and would trade psychosis for immobility in a man whose motor reserve is already exhausted. Board pearl — the memory hook is Suzie Q for quetiapine in Parkinson and Lewy body psychosis. Note also that the workup here is deliberately clean: normal metabolic panel, thyroid, urinalysis, and head CT exclude a secondary or delirious cause before an antipsychotic is reached for at all.  [Learning objectives: LO 045, 095]

wrongExplanations.0: Haloperidol is a high-potency first-generation agent with the highest extrapyramidal burden of the commonly used antipsychotics. Giving it to a patient with Parkinson disease would precipitate severe motor deterioration.
wrongExplanations.2: Risperidone behaves like a high-potency typical at usual doses, with dose-dependent extrapyramidal symptoms and the highest prolactin elevation among the second-generation agents. It is a poor choice in established parkinsonism.
wrongExplanations.3: Fluphenazine is another high-potency first-generation antipsychotic with substantial extrapyramidal risk, including drug-induced parkinsonism — the exact problem this patient already has from his disease.
wrongExplanations.4: Paliperidone is risperidone's active metabolite and shares its extrapyramidal and prolactin liabilities, making it equally unsuitable.

questions.eli5: His Parkinson medicine helps him move but is also causing hallucinations, and he cannot lower it further. Quetiapine is the one antipsychotic gentle enough on movement to treat the hallucinations without freezing him up.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man with schizophrenia was started on ziprasidone 3 weeks ago and titrated to a standard therapeutic dose. He reports that his auditory hallucinations are unchanged. His mother, who dispenses each dose and keeps a log, confirms he has taken every capsule, and pharmacy records are consistent. On further questioning, he states that he takes the medication first thing in the morning with black coffee and does not eat until midday, because the capsule 'makes me queasy if there is food in there.' He does not smoke. Serum creatinine and liver function tests are normal, and a serum ziprasidone concentration is below the expected range. Which of the following best explains his lack of response?
choices: A. Ziprasidone absorption is substantially reduced when taken without food
B. Caffeine induces the hepatic enzyme that metabolizes ziprasidone
C. Ziprasidone requires an acidic gastric pH that morning dosing does not provide
D. Ziprasidone undergoes extensive first-pass metabolism that food would bypass
E. Ziprasidone is a prodrug requiring pancreatic enzymes released with meals
questions.explanation: Ziprasidone is the food-dependent antipsychotic: its oral bioavailability roughly doubles when taken with a substantial meal of about 500 calories, and taking it on an empty stomach can leave serum concentrations subtherapeutic despite perfect adherence. His witnessed dosing log and consistent refill history close the nonadherence explanation, and the measured low level confirms a pharmacokinetic rather than pharmacodynamic failure. Board pearl — ziprasidone's other two signature facts are the highest QT-prolongation risk among the atypicals and a contraindication in bulimia; it does sit in the lowest metabolic-risk tier, which is why it gets used despite these quirks.  [Learning objectives: LO 027, 083]

wrongExplanations.1: Caffeine is not a meaningful inducer of ziprasidone metabolism. The 1A2 induction story belongs to cigarette smoke acting on clozapine and olanzapine, and the stem explicitly states he does not smoke.
wrongExplanations.2: Gastric pH dependence describes lisdexamfetamine, a prodrug cleaved only at a pH below 5 — which is why snorting or injecting it does nothing. Ziprasidone's limitation is caloric, not acidic.
wrongExplanations.3: Food does not bypass first-pass hepatic metabolism. The mechanism here is incomplete absorption from the gut, not altered hepatic extraction.
wrongExplanations.4: Ziprasidone is an active drug, not a prodrug, and no pancreatic enzyme activation step is involved.

questions.eli5: This particular antipsychotic needs a real meal alongside it to get absorbed. He was taking it on an empty stomach with coffee, so most of the dose never made it into his bloodstream.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with schizophrenia is started on chlorpromazine. Ten days later he reports a persistently dry mouth, difficulty reading small print, and constipation, and he presents to the emergency department unable to urinate for 12 hours. Bladder scan shows 620 mL of retained urine. Temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), pulse is 96/min, and blood pressure is 128/78 mm Hg. He is fully alert and oriented with no confusion, no hallucinations, and no rigidity or tremor. Blockade of which of the following receptors best accounts for this constellation of findings?
choices: C. Dopamine D2 receptors in the nigrostriatal pathway
E. Dopamine D2 receptors in the tuberoinfundibular pathway
questions.explanation: Muscarinic M1 blockade produces the peripheral anticholinergic cluster: dry mouth, blurred vision from impaired accommodation, constipation, and urinary retention. Chlorpromazine is a LOW-potency first-generation antipsychotic, and the potency see-saw predicts exactly this — low potency means low extrapyramidal risk but high anticholinergic and sedating burden, while high-potency agents such as haloperidol run the opposite way with high EPS and low anticholinergic effect. Board pearl — map each receptor to its side effect and most antipsychotic adverse effects become predictable: H1 gives sedation, alpha-1 gives orthostatic hypotension, M1 gives this anticholinergic picture, nigrostriatal D2 gives EPS, and tuberoinfundibular D2 gives galactorrhea, amenorrhea, and gynecomastia.  [Learning objectives: LO 083, 086]

wrongExplanations.0: H1 blockade causes sedation and contributes to weight gain. It does not produce urinary retention, dry mouth, or impaired accommodation.
wrongExplanations.1: Alpha-1 blockade causes orthostatic hypotension and dizziness on standing, and is the mechanism behind trazodone-associated priapism. His blood pressure is 128/78 mm Hg with no orthostatic complaint.
wrongExplanations.2: Nigrostriatal D2 blockade produces extrapyramidal symptoms — dystonia, akathisia, parkinsonism, and eventually tardive dyskinesia. The stem explicitly notes no rigidity and no tremor.
wrongExplanations.4: Tuberoinfundibular D2 blockade raises prolactin, producing galactorrhea, amenorrhea, and gynecomastia. None of those is described, and prolactin has no effect on bladder emptying.

questions.eli5: This older antipsychotic blocks the same nerve signal that keeps your mouth wet, your eyes focused, your bowels moving, and your bladder emptying. Block it and all four go wrong at once.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old man who has consumed approximately one liter of vodka daily for 8 years is admitted after his supply is abruptly interrupted. Over the next 40 hours he develops tremor, diaphoresis, tachycardia, and a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure. Which of the following best explains the neurochemical basis of his withdrawal syndrome?
choices: A. Acute alcohol inhibits GABA-A receptors, and chronic use upregulates them
B. Acute alcohol activates NMDA receptors, and chronic use downregulates them
C. Chronic alcohol use downregulates dopamine receptors in the nigrostriatal pathway
D. Chronic alcohol use depletes presynaptic serotonin stores in the raphe nuclei
E. Chronic use downregulates GABA-A receptors and upregulates NMDA receptors
F. Chronic alcohol use irreversibly destroys GABAergic interneurons in the cortex
questions.explanation: Acutely, alcohol ENHANCES inhibitory GABA-A signaling and INHIBITS excitatory NMDA glutamate signaling — the sedating, anxiolytic, ataxic picture of intoxication. With chronic exposure the brain adapts in the opposite direction, downregulating GABA-A receptors and upregulating NMDA receptors (particularly the NR2B subunit). Remove the alcohol and those adaptations stand unopposed: too little inhibition and too much excitation, producing tremor, autonomic hyperactivity, seizures, and delirium tremens. Board pearl — this is why cross-tolerant long-acting benzodiazepines work, since they restore GABA-A tone directly, and why clonidine alone is inadequate: it blunts the sympathetic surge without addressing the GABA deficit, so it does not prevent withdrawal seizures.  [Learning objectives: LO 010, 026]

wrongExplanations.0: This reverses the acute effect. Alcohol enhances rather than inhibits GABA-A signaling acutely, which is why intoxication is sedating rather than activating.
wrongExplanations.1: This also reverses the acute effect. Alcohol inhibits NMDA receptors acutely; the upregulation of NMDA receptors is the chronic compensatory adaptation, not an acute action.
wrongExplanations.2: Nigrostriatal dopamine receptor changes relate to antipsychotic-induced extrapyramidal symptoms, not to alcohol withdrawal. Alcohol's reward effect operates through the mesolimbic pathway.
wrongExplanations.3: Serotonin depletion is not the mechanism of alcohol withdrawal. Desipramine and fluoxetine are mentioned in relation to reducing stimulant craving, which is a separate matter entirely.
wrongExplanations.5: Withdrawal reflects reversible receptor-level adaptation, not structural destruction of interneurons — which is why the syndrome resolves over days and why a benzodiazepine taper works.

questions.eli5: Alcohol turns up the brain's brakes and turns down its gas pedal. After years, the brain compensates by weakening the brakes and strengthening the gas. Take the alcohol away and the brain races — tremor, sweating, and seizures.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man with treatment-resistant major depressive disorder has taken phenelzine for 4 months with good response. He undergoes an uncomplicated laparoscopic cholecystectomy, and the surgical team requests recommendations for postoperative analgesia. He has no renal or hepatic impairment, no history of substance use, and takes no other medications. Which of the following analgesics is most important to avoid in this patient?
choices: E. Local anesthetic infiltration of the port sites
questions.explanation: Meperidine combined with a monoamine oxidase inhibitor carries a boxed warning and can precipitate a severe, potentially fatal serotonergic reaction — the interaction that killed Libby Zion and reshaped American residency training. MAOIs block monoamine breakdown, so any additional serotonergic agent risks serotonin syndrome, and the risk climbs sharply when different serotonergic MECHANISMS are combined rather than when more drugs of the same class are stacked. Board pearl — the other agents on the MAOI avoid-list are sympathomimetics and decongestants, other antidepressants, tramadol, fentanyl, dextromethorphan, and triptans, plus tyramine-rich foods for the separate hypertensive-crisis risk. A 2-week washout is required when switching to or from an MAOI.  [Learning objectives: LO 056, 102]

wrongExplanations.0: Acetaminophen has no serotonergic activity and no interaction with monoamine oxidase inhibitors. It is a safe component of a multimodal postoperative regimen here.
wrongExplanations.1: Ketorolac is a parenteral NSAID with no serotonergic mechanism. Its concerns are gastrointestinal, renal, and bleeding-related, none of which applies given his normal renal function.
wrongExplanations.3: Ibuprofen likewise carries no MAOI interaction. Note that NSAIDs matter enormously with LITHIUM, where they raise levels toward toxicity, but that is a different drug and a different mechanism.
wrongExplanations.4: Local anesthetic infiltration acts on sodium channels at the surgical site and has no interaction with monoamine oxidase inhibition; it is in fact an ideal opioid-sparing choice here.

questions.eli5: His antidepressant stops the body from clearing certain brain chemicals. One particular pain medicine raises those same chemicals, and together they can be deadly — that combination has a famous history behind it.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has been stable on lithium for 4 years. She now presents with a 6-week depressive episode. Her psychiatrist mentions a combination product containing an antidepressant and a second-generation antipsychotic that carries an FDA indication in bipolar disorder. Which of the following statements about this combination is most accurate?
choices: A. It is fluoxetine plus olanzapine, indicated for maintenance rather than acute mania
B. It is sertraline plus quetiapine, indicated for acute manic episodes
C. It is fluoxetine plus olanzapine, indicated as first-line treatment for acute mania
D. It is bupropion plus aripiprazole, indicated for bipolar maintenance
E. It is venlafaxine plus risperidone, indicated for rapid-cycling bipolar disorder
questions.explanation: Fluoxetine combined with olanzapine is the ONLY FDA-approved antidepressant-containing combination in bipolar disorder, and the indication is maintenance-phase, specifically not acute mania. The distinction matters because antidepressants in bipolar disorder can worsen depression or precipitate a manic switch and are therefore used cautiously and never as unopposed monotherapy — which is exactly why the approved product pairs the antidepressant with an antipsychotic. Board pearl — you would not start an acutely manic patient on fluoxetine under any circumstances, and fluoxetine's own bipolar-context labeling flags worsening depression, manic episodes, and increased suicidality in children.  [Learning objectives: LO 084, 096]

wrongExplanations.1: No sertraline-quetiapine combination product carries this indication, and an antidepressant would be an inappropriate component of acute mania treatment regardless. Quetiapine alone does carry approvals across bipolar mania, depression, and maintenance.
wrongExplanations.2: The drugs are right but the indication is wrong, and this is the intended trap. The combination is a maintenance-phase treatment; giving it during acute mania adds a serotonergic antidepressant at precisely the wrong moment.
wrongExplanations.3: No such approved combination exists. Bupropion carries a seizure-threshold warning and is not paired with aripiprazole as a bipolar product.
wrongExplanations.4: No venlafaxine-risperidone combination product exists, and SNRIs are not a mainstay of bipolar treatment; rapid cycling is a course specifier rather than a separate approved indication for such a product.

questions.eli5: There is exactly one approved pill that combines an antidepressant with an antipsychotic for bipolar disorder — fluoxetine plus olanzapine — and it is for keeping someone stable, not for calming a manic episode.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman is seen 3 weeks after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery because of severe depressed mood, anhedonia, insomnia even when the infant sleeps, pervasive guilt about her adequacy as a mother, and intrusive thoughts that her family would be better off without her. She denies any intent or plan and denies thoughts of harming the infant. She has no hallucinations or delusions and no prior psychiatric history. Thyroid-stimulating hormone, complete blood count, and comprehensive metabolic panel are within normal limits, and she is not breastfeeding. She and her partner wish to pursue the treatment with the most rapid onset. Which of the following medications is specifically indicated for this condition?
questions.explanation: Brexanolone and zuranolone are neurosteroid GABA-A receptor modulators developed specifically for postpartum depression and are the agents with a dedicated indication for it. Brexanolone requires a 60-hour intravenous infusion with monitoring, while zuranolone is an oral course — which is why zuranolone is the practical answer when rapid onset is the stated priority. Board pearl — these sit alongside esketamine in the newer, faster-acting category, in contrast to conventional antidepressants that need 4 to 6 weeks; the stem's normal thyroid studies matter because postpartum thyroiditis is a genuine mimic that must be excluded first.  [Learning objectives: LO 066, 082]

wrongExplanations.0: Sertraline is a reasonable and commonly used first-line antidepressant in the postpartum period, but it takes 4 to 6 weeks to produce benefit and carries no postpartum-specific indication. The stem explicitly prioritizes rapid onset.
wrongExplanations.2: Lithium is a mood stabilizer for bipolar disorder with antisuicidal properties, but she has no history of mania or hypomania, and lithium is not a treatment for unipolar postpartum depression.
wrongExplanations.3: Aripiprazole is used as an adjunct in treatment-resistant depression and across bipolar indications, but it has no postpartum-specific indication and is not a rapid-onset monotherapy.
wrongExplanations.4: Prazosin is the alpha-1 blocker used for PTSD-related nightmares and nighttime hyperarousal. Her insomnia is a neurovegetative symptom of depression, not trauma-related nightmares.

questions.eli5: There are now medicines made specifically for depression after childbirth that work within days instead of weeks. Zuranolone is the pill version; the older one has to be given by IV for two and a half days straight.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man has fully remitted from his third lifetime major depressive episode after 5 months of combined psychotherapy and antidepressant treatment. He asks how long he should expect to remain on medication. Based on the relationship between episode number and recurrence risk, which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation?
choices: A. Continue for 3 months after remission, then discontinue
B. Continue for at least 1 year, then discontinue
C. Continue for 2 to 3 years, then reassess for discontinuation
D. Continue for 5 years, then discontinue regardless of course
E. Continue indefinitely, as maintenance is generally lifelong after a third episode
questions.explanation: Recurrence risk climbs with every episode, and treatment duration is scaled to it: after a FIRST episode, continue at least 1 year; after a SECOND, 2 to 3 years; after a THIRD, maintenance is generally lifelong. He has had three episodes, which places him in the indefinite-maintenance group. Board pearl — this ladder is a favorite because it converts a vague clinical question into three memorizable numbers, and it explains why stopping medication after symptomatic recovery is such a common route back into illness.  [Learning objectives: LO 072]

wrongExplanations.0: Three months is shorter than the continuation phase for even a first episode and would stop treatment while relapse risk is still at its highest.
wrongExplanations.1: One year is the recommendation after a FIRST episode. Applying it to a third episode substantially underestimates his recurrence risk.
wrongExplanations.2: Two to three years is the recommendation after a SECOND episode — one rung below where he sits.
wrongExplanations.3: Five years is not one of the taught thresholds, and a fixed stopping point ignores that the recommendation after a third episode is open-ended rather than time-limited.

questions.eli5: Every depression episode makes the next one more likely. After the first you stay on medicine about a year, after the second two or three years, and after the third you usually stay on it for good.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman comes to the office with a 7-week history of low mood, reduced interest in activities, and mild difficulty concentrating. She continues to work full-time and maintain her household, though she describes both as requiring more effort than usual. Her PHQ-9 score is 12. She denies suicidal ideation, has no psychotic symptoms, no history of mania or hypomania, and no substance use. Physical examination, thyroid-stimulating hormone, and complete blood count are unremarkable. She asks what treatment approach is recommended for her level of severity. Which of the following is most appropriate?
choices: A. Lifestyle modification and monitoring alone, without therapy or medication
B. Immediate referral for electroconvulsive therapy
C. Augmentation with a second-generation antipsychotic from the outset
D. Psychotherapy or an antidepressant, either of which may be sufficient
E. Brief inpatient hospitalization to permit rapid medication titration
questions.explanation: Depression treatment is severity-stratified. MILD depression is managed with lifestyle change, monitoring, and possibly app-based therapy; MODERATE depression — her PHQ-9 of 12 with preserved but effortful functioning — is treated with therapy OR an antidepressant, since response to therapy alone is common at this level; SEVERE depression warrants therapy AND an antidepressant together, with augmentation entering the picture; and treatment-resistant illness moves to augmentation or interventional approaches. Board pearl — the gold standard for depression overall is therapy plus medication combined, which is why the moderate tier is the one place where either alone is genuinely acceptable.  [Learning objectives: LO 024, 072]

wrongExplanations.0: Lifestyle change and monitoring alone is the MILD tier. Her PHQ-9 of 12 and 7 weeks of functional strain place her above that threshold, and withholding active treatment risks progression.
wrongExplanations.1: ECT is the gold standard for severe or refractory affective illness, and is reserved for psychotic features, catatonia, acute suicidality, or failed trials. She has none of those and has not tried anything yet.
wrongExplanations.2: Antipsychotic augmentation is a treatment-resistance strategy applied after multiple adequate trials have failed. She is treatment-naive.
wrongExplanations.4: Brief hospitalization is sometimes used in SEVERE depression to allow faster titration than a 4-to-6-week outpatient cadence permits. She is working, running her household, and denies suicidal ideation.

questions.eli5: How depression is treated depends on how bad it is. Hers is in the middle range, where either talk therapy or a medication on its own is usually enough — you do not need both yet.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old man is evaluated at his wife's insistence. For the past 4 years he has had recurring stretches lasting several days to 2 weeks during which he sleeps 4 hours, takes on multiple new projects, talks rapidly, and is unusually confident and productive; these alternate with stretches of low mood, fatigue, and reduced interest that also last days to weeks. His wife confirms he has never gone more than about 6 weeks without one pattern or the other. He has never been hospitalized psychiatrically, has never had hallucinations or delusions, has never missed work, and has never had a period meeting full criteria for either a manic episode or a major depressive episode. Urine toxicology screening and thyroid-stimulating hormone are normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
choices: C. Major depressive disorder with mixed features
questions.explanation: Cyclothymic disorder requires at least 2 years of numerous periods of hypomanic-level symptoms and numerous periods of depressive-level symptoms, with NEITHER ever meeting full episode criteria, and with symptom-free gaps never exceeding 2 months. All three conditions are met: 4 years of duration, subsyndromal highs and lows, and never more than about 6 weeks of euthymia. Board pearl — the whole family is built from episodes, so read for what is ABSENT: no full manic episode rules out Bipolar I, no full major depressive episode rules out Bipolar II, and the presence of hypomanic-level periods rules out persistent depressive disorder.  [Learning objectives: LO 017, 037]

wrongExplanations.0: Bipolar I requires at least one full manic episode — 7 or more days, or any duration with hospitalization or psychosis, plus significant impairment. He has never been hospitalized, never psychotic, and has never missed work.
wrongExplanations.1: Bipolar II requires at least one hypomanic episode PLUS at least one full major depressive episode. His depressive periods have never met full criteria, which is the specific element that fails.
wrongExplanations.2: Mixed features require a full major depressive episode with 3 or more concurrent manic symptoms. He has never had a full depressive episode.
wrongExplanations.3: Persistent depressive disorder is chronic low-grade depression for 2 or more years with no hypomanic-level periods at all. His recurring high periods with reduced sleep need and increased productivity are incompatible with it.
wrongExplanations.4: Borderline personality disorder produces mood shifts lasting hours to a day, reactive to interpersonal triggers, within a pattern of unstable relationships and identity. His shifts last days to weeks, are not described as trigger-linked, and involve reduced need for sleep, which is a mood-episode feature.

questions.eli5: For four years he swings between a little too up and a little too down, but neither side ever gets severe enough to count as a real episode, and he is almost never in between. That in-between-forever pattern is cyclothymic disorder.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl is referred by her second-grade teacher, who reports that in 4 months of school the child has never spoken a single word in the classroom, will not answer when called on directly, and communicates only by nodding or pointing. Her parents are puzzled, describing her at home as talkative, funny, and a fluent storyteller who converses easily with her siblings, grandparents, and neighborhood friends. Her speech and language development were normal and on schedule. Hearing screening is normal. She makes appropriate eye contact, engages in reciprocal imaginative play, and has no restricted interests or repetitive behaviors. She separates from her parents without distress and shows no fear that harm will befall them. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Selective mutism is consistent failure to speak in ONE specific setting despite normal speech elsewhere, lasting at least 1 month, and it sits in the DSM-5 anxiety disorders chapter. The defining contrast is right in the stem: silent for 4 months at school, fluent and talkative at home with multiple different people. Board pearl — the negatives do the diagnostic work here. Normal eye contact, reciprocal imaginative play, and absent restricted or repetitive behaviors exclude autism; normal speech development and fluency at home exclude a language disorder; and easy separation excludes separation anxiety disorder.  [Learning objectives: LO 035, 036]

wrongExplanations.0: Autism spectrum disorder requires persistent social communication deficits ACROSS contexts plus restricted, repetitive behaviors. She converses fluently at home, makes eye contact, plays reciprocally, and has no repetitive behaviors — every element is negated.
wrongExplanations.1: Social anxiety disorder involves fear of scrutiny and negative evaluation across social and performance situations, typically with distress the child can describe. Selective mutism is the more specific diagnosis when the presentation is a categorical failure to speak confined to one venue, and the two are separate entries in the same chapter.
wrongExplanations.3: Separation anxiety disorder is excessive fear of separation from attachment figures with worry that harm will befall them. She separates without distress, which the stem states explicitly.
wrongExplanations.4: A language disorder would impair speech and language across all settings. Her development was normal and she is described as a fluent storyteller at home.
wrongExplanations.5: Intellectual disability requires deficits in both intellectual and adaptive functioning with developmental onset. She is functioning normally at home and in play, with no cognitive concerns described.

questions.eli5: She talks all the time at home and never says a word at school. Being able to speak perfectly well but going silent in one particular place is called selective mutism.

questions.stem: Eleven days after a factory explosion in which two coworkers died, a 41-year-old survivor reports intrusive memories, nightmares, avoidance of the plant, and an exaggerated startle response. He meets criteria for acute stress disorder. The company has offered to fly in a consultant to conduct a mandatory one-time group session in which all survivors will be required to describe their experience of the event in detail. The occupational health physician asks for a recommendation. Which of the following is the most appropriate advice?
choices: A. Recommend against the single-session debriefing and arrange individual counseling
B. Endorse the mandatory single session as the standard of care after mass trauma
C. Recommend the single session but make attendance voluntary for survivors
D. Defer all psychological intervention until the 1-month mark clarifies the diagnosis
E. Recommend prophylactic benzodiazepines for all survivors before the session
questions.explanation: Acute stress disorder is treated with immediate therapy and counseling — but specifically NOT single-session debriefing, which is the point the lecture flags. Mandatory one-time group debriefing has not been shown to prevent PTSD and may worsen outcomes by compelling re-exposure to traumatic material without follow-up support. Ongoing individual therapeutic contact is what is indicated. Board pearl — remember the clock alongside the treatment: acute stress disorder runs 3 days to 1 month, and symptoms persisting past 1 month convert the diagnosis to PTSD, at which point SSRIs are first-line with prazosin added specifically for nightmares.  [Learning objectives: LO 060, 081]

wrongExplanations.1: Single-session psychological debriefing is precisely the intervention the lecture singles out as NOT the right approach, and calling it the standard of care inverts the teaching point.
wrongExplanations.2: Making it voluntary removes the coercion but leaves the intervention itself unsupported by evidence, and it still substitutes a one-time session for the ongoing counseling that is indicated.
wrongExplanations.3: Waiting a month withholds treatment during the window when acute stress disorder is actively treatable, and most patients who receive support in that period recover before the PTSD threshold is reached.
wrongExplanations.4: Benzodiazepines are generally avoided in trauma-related disorders — they do not improve core symptoms, may worsen outcomes, and carry dependence risk. Prophylactic dosing of an entire exposed workforce compounds every one of those problems.

questions.eli5: Making everyone sit in one big meeting and relive the disaster does not prevent PTSD and can make it worse. What helps is real, ongoing counseling for the people who need it.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old man is referred for evaluation of longstanding difficulty at work. Since his twenties he has turned down four promotions that would have required leading meetings, explaining each time that he was certain he would be exposed as inadequate and ridiculed. He eats lunch alone in his car daily. He has had one romantic relationship, which ended when he stopped returning calls after his partner made a mild joke about his shirt. He describes himself as inferior to his coworkers and says he thinks about their potential criticism constantly. He states plainly that he wishes he had friends and a partner, and that he does not understand why connection seems available to everyone but him. He reports no odd beliefs, no perceptual disturbances, no ideas of reference, and no distrust of others' motives. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Avoidant personality disorder is the Cluster C pattern captured by RIDICULE: restraint in relationships, inhibition in new situations, expectation of disapproval and criticism, a self-view of inadequacy, unwillingness to get involved without certainty of being liked, and preoccupation with embarrassment — all present since early adulthood. The single most decisive line is that he WANTS friends and a partner and does not understand why he cannot have them. Board pearl — that desire is the entire discriminator against schizoid personality disorder, where the solitude is genuinely preferred rather than painfully imposed by fear.  [Learning objectives: LO 041]

wrongExplanations.0: Schizoid personality disorder involves genuine indifference to relationships and a real preference for solitude with restricted affect. He explicitly longs for connection and is distressed by its absence, which is the opposite motivation for the same surface behavior.
wrongExplanations.1: Schizotypal personality disorder requires odd beliefs, magical thinking, perceptual disturbances, ideas of reference, or eccentric speech and appearance alongside social anxiety. The stem explicitly negates all of those.
wrongExplanations.2: Paranoid personality disorder centers on pervasive distrust and the assumption of malicious motive. He fears being judged inadequate, not being deliberately harmed, and the stem states he has no distrust of others' motives.
wrongExplanations.3: Dependent personality disorder centers on a need to be taken care of, difficulty making decisions without reassurance, and urgent replacement of ended relationships. He withdraws from relationships rather than clinging to them.
wrongExplanations.5: Narcissistic personality disorder involves grandiosity, entitlement, and a need for admiration. His self-view is one of inferiority, which is the opposite pole.

questions.eli5: He turns down promotions and eats lunch alone because he is sure people will find him inadequate — but he desperately wants friends and does not understand why he cannot have them. Wanting connection while being too afraid to reach for it is avoidant personality disorder.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman is referred after her fourth primary care physician in 2 years declined to continue seeing her. She arrives in dramatic makeup and a low-cut dress for a routine appointment, greets the physician as though they are old friends, and within minutes describes her previous doctor as "absolutely the most wonderful man alive." When asked what her abdominal pain feels like, she answers, "Oh, it is just awful, simply devastating," and cannot characterize it further despite repeated prompting. She becomes visibly tearful when the physician turns to the computer, then laughs brightly moments later. She describes several acquaintances as her closest friends, though she has met two of them once. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Histrionic personality disorder follows I CRAVE SIN: inappropriate seductiveness, need to be the center of attention, overestimation of relationship intimacy, appearance-focused presentation, suggestibility, exaggerated emotional expression, shifting and shallow emotions, impressionistic speech lacking detail, and novelty seeking. Two features here are especially diagnostic — impressionistic speech (she can say the pain is devastating but cannot describe it) and overestimated intimacy (calling near-strangers her closest friends). Board pearl — the histrionic versus narcissistic split is drama and attention versus grandiosity and superiority; both need the room's focus, but for different reasons.  [Learning objectives: LO 041]

wrongExplanations.0: Borderline personality disorder centers on frantic efforts to avoid abandonment, identity disturbance, chronic emptiness, self-harm, and idealization alternating with DEVALUATION. Her emotions are shallow and shifting rather than intensely unstable, and no self-harm or abandonment fear is described.
wrongExplanations.2: Narcissistic personality disorder involves grandiosity, entitlement, envy, and a need for admiration of one's superiority. She seeks attention and warmth, not acknowledgment of being better than others.
wrongExplanations.3: Dependent personality disorder centers on needing others to assume responsibility and difficulty making decisions alone. She is theatrical and engaging rather than submissive and indecisive.
wrongExplanations.4: Somatic symptom disorder requires excessive thoughts, feelings, and behaviors about somatic symptoms for 6 or more months. Her abdominal pain is the occasion for the visit, but the clinical picture is a pervasive interpersonal style present across every domain described.
wrongExplanations.5: Bipolar II requires discrete hypomanic and major depressive episodes lasting days to weeks. Her mood shifts occur within a single conversation, which is far too rapid to represent mood episodes.

questions.eli5: She dresses to be noticed, calls people she barely knows her best friends, and describes her pain as devastating without being able to say what it actually feels like. Big feelings with no detail underneath is histrionic personality disorder.

questions.stem: A 39-year-old man is admitted from the emergency department for intractable low back pain following a workplace fall 6 weeks ago. He has a pending disability claim and an active lawsuit against his employer. He reports pain of 10 out of 10 continuously, yet is observed by nursing staff laughing and moving freely in bed when unaware he is being watched. MRI of the lumbar spine, plain films, and inflammatory markers are all normal, and straight-leg raise is negative when performed as a distracted maneuver but strongly positive on formal testing. He declines an offered electromyography study and a diagnostic nerve block, stating they are unnecessary, and he requests a letter documenting permanent disability at every encounter. He specifically requests intravenous hydromorphone by name. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
choices: C. Factitious disorder imposed on self
F. Chronic pain disorder due to a general medical condition
questions.explanation: Run the decision tree. Is production of the symptom conscious? Yes — his behavior differs entirely when he believes he is unobserved, and his examination findings are internally inconsistent. Then ask what the goal is: an EXTERNAL incentive means malingering, whereas the sick role itself, an internal or primary gain, means factitious disorder. He has a pending disability claim, an active lawsuit, a request for a disability letter at every encounter, and a by-name opioid request. Board pearl — the sharpest behavioral discriminator is his refusal of the EMG and nerve block: malingerers avoid invasive procedures because the goal is the payoff, whereas factitious patients welcome them because the procedures are the point.  [Learning objectives: LO 014, 031]

wrongExplanations.0: Somatic symptom disorder involves UNCONSCIOUS production, with genuine distress and excessive thoughts and behaviors about symptoms over 6 or more months. His symptoms vanish when he thinks no one is watching, which establishes conscious production.
wrongExplanations.1: Conversion disorder produces neurologic deficits through unconscious mechanisms, with the patient genuinely believing in the deficit and often showing la belle indifférence. He is deliberately performing pain behavior and pursuing a specific external goal.
wrongExplanations.2: Factitious disorder requires that the goal be the sick role itself, with no external incentive — and such patients WELCOME procedures and hospitalization. He declined both offered diagnostic procedures and has substantial financial and legal incentives.
wrongExplanations.4: Illness anxiety disorder is preoccupation with HAVING a serious disease with minimal somatic symptoms. He is not worried about what his back pain means; he is using it.
wrongExplanations.5: A medical pain disorder is excluded by normal MRI, plain films, and inflammatory markers together with a negative distracted straight-leg raise, which demonstrates that the positive formal test is not physiologically driven.

questions.eli5: He says his pain is a ten out of ten but moves around fine when he thinks nobody is looking, and he turns down every test while asking for a disability letter and a specific strong painkiller. Faking symptoms for money or drugs is malingering.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man comes to the office because of a 14-month history of inability to achieve an erection sufficient for intercourse with his wife. He reports that he consistently awakens with a firm erection several mornings each week and has full erections during masturbation. The difficulty began shortly after he was passed over for a partnership at his firm, and he describes intense anticipatory worry before intimacy and a preoccupation during intercourse with whether he will lose the erection. He has no diabetes mellitus, no vascular disease, and takes no medications. Hemoglobin A1c is 5.3%, morning testosterone is normal, and thyroid-stimulating hormone is normal. Peripheral pulses are intact and genitourinary examination is unremarkable. Which of the following findings most strongly supports a psychogenic rather than a physiologic cause?
choices: A. Preserved nocturnal and morning erections
B. The 14-month duration of the complaint
C. The absence of diabetes mellitus and vascular disease
D. His normal morning serum testosterone concentration
E. The identifiable occupational stressor preceding onset
questions.explanation: The single most useful discriminator in erectile dysfunction is whether nocturnal and morning erections are PRESERVED. If they are, the vascular, neurologic, and hormonal machinery is demonstrably intact and the problem is psychogenic; if they are ABSENT as well, a physiologic cause is far more likely. His firm morning erections several times weekly and full erections during masturbation prove the apparatus works. Board pearl — normal hemoglobin A1c, testosterone, and thyroid studies are supportive but only exclude specific causes; the nocturnal erection history is the finding that positively establishes the mechanism.  [Learning objectives: LO 020, 031]

wrongExplanations.1: Duration does not distinguish the two. Psychogenic and physiologic erectile dysfunction can both persist for many months or years, and 14 months is compatible with either.
wrongExplanations.2: Absence of diabetes and vascular disease removes two common physiologic contributors, but many other physiologic causes exist. Excluding some causes is weaker evidence than positively demonstrating intact function.
wrongExplanations.3: A normal testosterone excludes hypogonadism specifically, one physiologic cause among several, and does not establish that the erectile mechanism is intact.
wrongExplanations.4: An identifiable stressor is suggestive and fits the history, but stressors are common and coincidental in a man of this age. Performance anxiety can also be secondary to an organic problem, so the stressor alone does not settle the mechanism.

questions.eli5: If he wakes up with erections and has no trouble alone, then all the plumbing and nerves work fine. That means the problem is happening in his head during intimacy, not in his body.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man with Parkinson disease is brought to the office by his wife because of a marked change in behavior over the past 5 months. He has begun propositioning female staff at his day program, has been spending several hours daily on paid pornography sites, and has twice been asked to leave a community center. His wife reports he was never like this in 38 years of marriage. His neurologist increased his pramipexole dose 6 months ago to control worsening tremor. He is fully oriented, his attention does not fluctuate, and he has no hallucinations or delusions. There is no history of head trauma or seizures, and MRI of the brain shows only age-expected changes without temporal lobe abnormality. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for his behavior?
choices: D. A newly emergent paraphilic disorder
questions.explanation: New-onset hypersexuality is a red-flag symptom that should trigger a search for an underlying cause rather than a primary psychiatric or paraphilic diagnosis. The recognized culprits are brain injury, Klüver-Bucy syndrome, Kleine-Levin syndrome, and DOPAMINE AGONISTS. His pramipexole dose was increased 6 months ago and the behavior began 5 months ago — a temporal link that is the whole item. Board pearl — this belongs to the same impulse-control family the FDA has warned about with dopaminergic drugs, which includes compulsive gambling, compulsive shopping, and hypersexuality, and it is seen with dopamine partial agonists such as aripiprazole as well.  [Learning objectives: LO 033, 034]

wrongExplanations.0: Klüver-Bucy syndrome follows bilateral temporal lobe damage and produces hypersexuality alongside hyperorality, placidity, visual agnosia, and hypermetamorphosis. His MRI shows no temporal lobe abnormality and none of the other components is present.
wrongExplanations.1: Kleine-Levin syndrome is a rare disorder of recurrent episodes of hypersomnia with hyperphagia and hypersexuality, typically in adolescent males, with normal function between episodes. His behavior is continuous and he is 63.
wrongExplanations.3: Paraphilic disorders reflect longstanding patterns of atypical sexual interest, generally traceable to adolescence or early adulthood. His wife reports nothing like this across 38 years of marriage, and a new-onset presentation at 63 demands a medical explanation.
wrongExplanations.4: Frontotemporal neurodegeneration can produce disinhibition, but it develops insidiously with progressive language or executive decline and characteristic imaging changes. His MRI shows only age-expected findings, and a reversible medication cause is present and temporally linked.

questions.eli5: His Parkinson medicine boosts dopamine, and too much dopamine can unleash impulsive behavior — gambling, shopping, or sexual behavior. The timing lines up exactly with his dose increase.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with a gunshot wound to the thigh. He is hemodynamically stable and the wound is superficial. He tells the treating physician that he was shot during an argument outside a bar, and he asks that the police not be contacted, stating that he does not wish to press charges and that involving law enforcement would put him in danger. He has decision-making capacity and no psychiatric history. Which of the following is the most appropriate action regarding notification?
choices: A. Honor his request and document that he declined police involvement
B. Notify law enforcement, as gunshot wounds are subject to mandatory reporting
C. Notify law enforcement only if he later loses decision-making capacity
D. Obtain a court order before any disclosure to law enforcement
E. Notify law enforcement only if he identifies a specific assailant
questions.explanation: Mandatory reporting is one of the six recognized exceptions to confidentiality, alongside Tarasoff, involuntary hospitalization, supervision, emergencies, and incompetence with a court-appointed guardian. Malicious wounding — a gunshot or stab wound — must be reported to law enforcement, and the obligation does not depend on the patient's consent, because the statute exists to protect the public rather than to serve the individual patient's preference. Board pearl — the same category covers danger to the public, such as driving while impaired or a seizure disorder affecting safe driving, which is reported to law enforcement or the licensing authority; many states grant immunity from liability for a good-faith report made under a mandatory reporting statute.  [Learning objectives: LO 057]

wrongExplanations.0: Patient preference does not override a mandatory reporting statute. Confidentiality is the default rule, but this is one of the defined exceptions where it yields.
wrongExplanations.2: Capacity governs whether a patient may make decisions about his own CARE. It has no bearing on a reporting obligation that exists independently of consent.
wrongExplanations.3: A court order is required to compel disclosure in situations where no exception applies. Mandatory reporting is itself the legal authority, so no additional order is needed.
wrongExplanations.4: The reporting duty attaches to the injury, not to whether an assailant can be named. Requiring identification would defeat the purpose of the statute in exactly the cases where it matters most.

questions.eli5: Doctors normally keep everything private, but gunshot and stab wounds are one of the few things the law requires them to report. The patient cannot waive that.

questions.stem: During a mental status examination, a physician asks a patient to begin at 100 and subtract 7 repeatedly, continuing until told to stop. Which of the following components of the mental status examination is being assessed by this task?
questions.explanation: Serial sevens require the patient to hold a running result in mind while performing an operation on it, which is the bedside test of arousal, attention, and concentration. Spelling a word backward tests the same domain. Board pearl — do not confuse the domains that sound similar: registration is immediate repetition of newly given information such as three objects, delayed recall is retrieval of that same information after several minutes, and concentration is holding and MANIPULATING information. Remember too that the MSE is the full narrative examination, while the MMSE and MoCA are scored 0-to-30 cognitive screens that form one component of it.  [Learning objectives: LO 016, 059]

wrongExplanations.0: Thought content covers the ideas, preoccupations, delusions, and suicidal or homicidal ideation the patient reports. It is assessed by asking what the patient is thinking about, not by a calculation task.
wrongExplanations.1: Delayed recall is tested by naming several objects and asking the patient to repeat them after a few minutes of distraction. Serial sevens involve no delay interval and nothing to retrieve.
wrongExplanations.2: Abstraction is assessed with proverb interpretation or similarities and differences — asking how an apple and an orange are alike. Serial subtraction is a concrete arithmetic operation.
wrongExplanations.3: Thought process describes how ideas are connected and organized — linear, tangential, circumstantial, or loose — and is assessed by listening to spontaneous speech rather than by administering a specific task.

questions.eli5: Counting backward by sevens forces you to hold a number in your head while doing math on it. That is a test of paying attention and concentrating, not of memory.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman is admitted for intractable nausea and vomiting from hyperemesis and has received scheduled metoclopramide for 3 days. On hospital day 4 the nurse reports she is confused and rigid. Temperature is 39.6°C (103.3°F), pulse is 128/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure fluctuates between 158/94 and 96/60 mm Hg over 2 hours. Examination shows profuse diaphoresis and generalized lead-pipe rigidity of all four limbs; deep tendon reflexes are 1+ throughout with no clonus, and the pupils are 3 mm. She takes no antidepressants, no antipsychotics, and no serotonergic agents, and urine toxicology screening is negative. Creatine kinase is 8,400 U/L and white blood cell count is 14,200/mm3. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The trap is that no antipsychotic appears anywhere in the chart. NMS follows exposure to any DOPAMINE-BLOCKING agent, and metoclopramide is a D2 antagonist used as an antiemetic — a common real-world cause. Everything else fits: onset over days rather than hours, lead-pipe rigidity, DIMINISHED reflexes, hyperthermia, autonomic instability, rhabdomyolysis with a creatine kinase of 8,400 U/L, and leukocytosis. Board pearl — the reflex findings and time course are the bedside discriminator: NMS gives lead-pipe rigidity with hyporeflexia over days, while serotonin syndrome gives clonus and hyperreflexia within hours. First step is to stop the offending agent; cooling, fluids, and dantrolene or bromocriptine follow.  [Learning objectives: LO 021, 056, 095]

wrongExplanations.0: Serotonin syndrome develops within 24 hours of a serotonergic change and produces hyperreflexia, clonus, mydriasis, and diarrhea. Her reflexes are 1+ with no clonus, her pupils are 3 mm, and the stem states she is on no serotonergic agent at all.
wrongExplanations.1: Anticholinergic toxicity produces dry flushed skin, absent bowel sounds, and mydriasis with delirium. She is profusely diaphoretic and has rigidity, which anticholinergic toxicity does not cause.
wrongExplanations.3: Malignant hyperthermia follows volatile anesthetics or succinylcholine and develops intraoperatively or shortly after. She has had no anesthetic exposure, and her syndrome evolved over days on a ward.
wrongExplanations.4: Thyroid storm causes fever, tachycardia, and agitation but produces hyperreflexia and brisk deep tendon reflexes rather than lead-pipe rigidity, and it does not generate a creatine kinase of 8,400 U/L.
wrongExplanations.5: An acute dystonic reaction is a focal, sustained muscle contraction — oculogyric crisis, torticollis, laryngospasm — occurring within hours of a dopamine blocker, WITHOUT fever, autonomic instability, or rhabdomyolysis.

questions.eli5: She never got an antipsychotic — but her anti-nausea medicine blocks the same dopamine signal. Fever, stiff-as-a-pipe muscles, and an unstable heart rate and blood pressure over several days is neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder maintained on lithium for 9 years is brought to the emergency department by her husband. She has had 4 days of profuse watery diarrhea and vomiting from a presumed viral gastroenteritis and has been unable to keep fluids down. For the past 2 days she has been increasingly unsteady, and her husband reports her speech has become slurred. She also takes hydrochlorothiazide for hypertension. Temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse is 112/min, and blood pressure is 96/58 mm Hg, falling to 78/44 mm Hg on standing. Examination shows dry mucous membranes, a coarse bilateral hand tremor, gait ataxia, and slurred speech; she is drowsy but rousable. Serum lithium concentration is 2.6 mEq/L, serum creatinine is 2.1 mg/dL (baseline 0.8 mg/dL), and serum sodium is 149 mEq/L. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?
choices: A. Discontinue lithium and begin intravenous fluid resuscitation
B. Continue lithium at half the current dose and rehydrate orally
C. Administer activated charcoal and continue lithium
D. Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate and continue lithium
E. Begin dantrolene and external cooling
questions.explanation: Lithium toxicity is managed by stopping the lithium and hydrating, with dialysis considered in severe cases. Two mechanisms converged here: volume depletion from gastroenteritis and a thiazide diuretic both drive renal sodium retention, and because lithium is reabsorbed on the same proximal tubular sodium channels, it is retained alongside the sodium. The rising creatinine confirms that reduced clearance is doing the work. Board pearl — the tremor is a built-in level meter: a FINE tremor is expected at therapeutic concentrations, whereas a COARSE tremor with ataxia and slurred speech signals toxicity, which typically begins above 1.2 mEq/L.  [Learning objectives: LO 064, 074, 085, 088]

wrongExplanations.1: Halving the dose still delivers lithium to a patient at 2.6 mEq/L with acute kidney injury, and oral rehydration is inadequate for someone vomiting with orthostatic hypotension and a creatinine of 2.1 mg/dL.
wrongExplanations.2: Activated charcoal does not bind lithium, which is a small cation. It also requires a protected airway, and she is drowsy.
wrongExplanations.3: Urinary alkalinization with bicarbonate is the strategy for barbiturate poisoning, where ion trapping of a weak acid enhances elimination. It does not meaningfully increase lithium clearance, and continuing lithium is unsafe.
wrongExplanations.4: Dantrolene and cooling treat neuroleptic malignant syndrome and malignant hyperthermia. She is afebrile with no rigidity; her findings are cerebellar and gastrointestinal.

questions.eli5: Being dehydrated and on a water pill made her kidneys hold on to salt — and lithium rides along with salt, so her level climbed until she was shaky and slurring. Stop the lithium and give fluids through an IV.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old man who has taken escitalopram 20 mg PO daily for 5 years for major depressive disorder is admitted for a diabetic foot infection. Cultures grow vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus, and the infectious disease service begins an antibiotic. Approximately 20 hours after the first dose he becomes agitated and diaphoretic. Temperature is 38.7°C (101.7°F), pulse is 126/min, and blood pressure is 162/96 mm Hg. Examination shows inducible ankle clonus bilaterally, 3+ patellar reflexes, 6-mm pupils, hyperactive bowel sounds, and moist skin; muscle tone is otherwise normal with no lead-pipe rigidity. He has received no antipsychotic and no antiemetic. Which of the following newly started medications is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Linezolid is a reversible monoamine oxidase inhibitor, and adding it to a patient already on an SSRI combines two DIFFERENT serotonergic mechanisms — which is precisely where serotonin syndrome risk climbs most sharply, far more than simply stacking additional drugs of the same class. His presentation is textbook: onset within 24 hours, the three A's of increased neuromuscular activity (clonus, hyperreflexia), autonomic instability (fever, tachycardia, hypertension, diaphoresis), and altered mental status. Board pearl — the serotonergic list runs well beyond antidepressants: tramadol, fentanyl, meperidine, ondansetron, triptans, dextromethorphan, MDMA, St. John's wort, and linezolid all belong on it.  [Learning objectives: LO 056, 102]

wrongExplanations.0: Vancomycin has no serotonergic activity. Its characteristic infusion reaction is vancomycin flushing syndrome — histamine-mediated flushing of the face and torso — without clonus, hyperreflexia, or hyperthermia.
wrongExplanations.1: Ceftriaxone is a cephalosporin with no monoamine oxidase or serotonergic activity, and it would not be selected for vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus in the first place.
wrongExplanations.2: Metronidazole carries a disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol and increases lithium nephrotoxicity, but it has no serotonergic mechanism and this patient is on neither alcohol nor lithium.
wrongExplanations.4: Daptomycin is an appropriate agent for vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus, but its signature adverse effect is myopathy with creatine kinase elevation. It produces no serotonin toxicity, and myopathy would not cause clonus and hyperreflexia.

questions.eli5: The antibiotic they picked for this resistant infection also raises serotonin, and he was already on an antidepressant that does the same thing. Two different ways of raising serotonin at once pushed him into serotonin syndrome.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man is treated in the emergency department for an acute migraine and receives intravenous prochlorperazine. Ninety minutes later he returns with his eyes deviated upward and fixed, his neck twisted forcibly to the left, and his jaw clenched. He is frightened but fully alert and oriented, and he can answer questions. Temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), pulse is 104/min, and blood pressure is 132/80 mm Hg. There is no generalized rigidity, no diaphoresis, no clonus, and no confusion. He is protecting his airway and speaking in full sentences. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
choices: A. Oral benztropine, with reassessment in 4 hours
E. Intravenous lorazepam followed by observation
questions.explanation: This is an acute dystonic reaction — oculogyric crisis with torticollis and trismus — occurring within HOURS of a dopamine-blocking agent, and prochlorperazine is a phenothiazine antiemetic that blocks D2 just as an antipsychotic does. Treatment is a parenteral anticholinergic or antihistamine: intramuscular or intravenous diphenhydramine or benztropine. The parenteral route matters, because these reactions are frightening and can progress to laryngospasm, and oral dosing is too slow. Board pearl — the EPS timeline is 4-4-4-4: dystonia in hours treated with an IM anticholinergic, akinesia in days treated with benztropine, akathisia in months treated with propranolol, and tardive dyskinesia in years treated by withdrawing or switching the agent and adding valbenazine.  [Learning objectives: LO 049, 051, 053]

wrongExplanations.0: Benztropine is the right drug class but the wrong route and timing. Oral absorption is far too slow for an acute dystonic reaction, and waiting 4 hours risks progression to laryngeal involvement.
wrongExplanations.2: Propranolol is first-line for AKATHISIA, the subjective restlessness that emerges over weeks to months. It has no role in acute dystonia, and the timeline here is 90 minutes.
wrongExplanations.3: Dantrolene treats the rigidity and hyperthermia of neuroleptic malignant syndrome and malignant hyperthermia. He is afebrile with no generalized rigidity, diaphoresis, or confusion — the stated negatives that exclude NMS.
wrongExplanations.4: A benzodiazepine may provide some muscle relaxation and anxiolysis but does not target the underlying dopamine-acetylcholine imbalance and is not the definitive treatment for an acute dystonic reaction.

questions.eli5: The anti-nausea shot he got for his migraine blocks dopamine, and a few hours later his eyes rolled up and his neck twisted. A shot of diphenhydramine reverses it quickly — a pill would work too slowly.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman with chronic low back pain has taken extended-release oxycodone 20 mg PO twice daily for 3 years. She comes to the office reporting worsening anxiety and difficulty sleeping since her husband's death 2 months ago, and she asks for "something like the Xanax my friend takes." She has no history of substance misuse. She lives alone. Her body mass index is 21 kg/m2, her serum creatinine is 1.3 mg/dL, and she has mild chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with a resting oxygen saturation of 94% on room air. Which of the following best describes the principal hazard of adding a benzodiazepine to her regimen?
choices: A. Precipitation of an acute dystonic reaction
B. Accelerated hepatic metabolism of her opioid
C. Displacement of oxycodone from plasma protein binding
D. Precipitation of a serotonergic reaction
questions.explanation: Benzodiazepines must never be combined with alcohol or opioids because the central nervous system depression is ADDITIVE and the principal risk is respiratory depression. Three features compound it here: she is 74, so increased body fat expands the volume of distribution for these lipophilic drugs and prolongs their effect; she has COPD with limited respiratory reserve; and she lives alone, so a respiratory event would go unwitnessed. Board pearl — the benzodiazepine ceiling effect is real but does NOT make them overdose-proof; that ceiling disappears in combination with another depressant, which is exactly this scenario.  [Learning objectives: LO 048, 091]

wrongExplanations.0: Acute dystonic reactions follow dopamine-blocking agents such as antipsychotics and phenothiazine antiemetics. Benzodiazepines have no D2 activity and do not cause dystonia.
wrongExplanations.1: Benzodiazepines are not hepatic enzyme inducers. Induction of a substrate's metabolism describes carbamazepine and cigarette smoke, and accelerating opioid clearance would reduce rather than compound the danger.
wrongExplanations.2: Protein-binding displacement produces transient, clinically minor changes in free drug and is not the mechanism of benzodiazepine-opioid harm. The interaction is pharmacodynamic, not pharmacokinetic.
wrongExplanations.3: Neither benzodiazepines nor oxycodone at standard doses is a strong serotonergic agent in this context. Serotonin syndrome would require hyperreflexia and clonus, and the danger here is depression of respiratory drive, not excitation.

questions.eli5: Both her pain medicine and the anxiety pill she is asking for slow down breathing, and together they slow it much more than either alone. She is elderly, has lung disease, and lives alone — so if her breathing stopped, no one would be there.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia has taken clozapine for 10 weeks with marked improvement in auditory hallucinations and a substantial reduction in suicidal ideation. He has had weekly absolute neutrophil count monitoring, with values consistently between 3,000 and 4,500/mm3. Today's laboratory studies show an absolute neutrophil count of 900/mm3, confirmed on a repeat specimen drawn the same day. He is afebrile with no sore throat, no mucosal ulceration, and no other symptoms. He has had no chest pain or dyspnea, and troponin and C-reactive protein are within normal limits. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
choices: A. Continue clozapine and increase monitoring to twice weekly
B. Continue clozapine and add filgrastim prophylactically
C. Reduce the clozapine dose by half and recheck in 1 week
D. Discontinue clozapine and monitor the neutrophil count
E. Continue clozapine, since he is asymptomatic and afebrile
questions.explanation: Clozapine causes agranulocytosis in roughly 1 to 2% of patients, and mandatory REMS monitoring exists precisely so that the drop is caught BEFORE the patient becomes septic. An absolute neutrophil count of 900/mm3, confirmed on repeat, is severe neutropenia and requires immediate discontinuation with continued hematologic monitoring — the absence of fever or sore throat is reassuring about his current state but says nothing about where the count is heading. Board pearl — do not confuse clozapine's two serious hematologic and cardiac complications: this one is caught by the ANC schedule, whereas myocarditis appears in the first several weeks with chest pain, dyspnea, and troponin elevation, and the stem clears myocarditis explicitly here.  [Learning objectives: LO 086, 095]

wrongExplanations.0: Intensified monitoring is appropriate for a mild or moderate decline that has not crossed the severe threshold. At 900/mm3 the count has already crossed it, and watching more closely while continuing the drug does not protect him.
wrongExplanations.1: Filgrastim is used to support neutrophil recovery once the offending agent has been stopped. Giving it while continuing clozapine treats the marrow while leaving the cause in place.
wrongExplanations.2: Clozapine-induced agranulocytosis is idiosyncratic rather than dose-dependent, so halving the dose does not reliably reverse it, and a week of continued exposure at a count of 900/mm3 is unsafe.
wrongExplanations.4: Being asymptomatic is expected at this stage and is the entire reason for scheduled surveillance. Waiting for fever or a sore throat means waiting for neutropenic sepsis.

questions.eli5: His white cells that fight infection have dropped dangerously low, even though he feels fine — which is exactly what the weekly blood tests are for. The medicine has to stop now, before an infection has a chance to take hold.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old man is seen on postoperative day 2 after an elective total knee arthroplasty because of new confusion. His daughter states he manages his own finances and drove himself to the preoperative visit last week. Since yesterday evening he has been intermittently agitated, has pulled at his intravenous line, and has told the nurse there are cats under his bed; at other times during the day he has been calm and appropriately conversant. Temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), pulse is 88/min, and blood pressure is 132/78 mm Hg. Urinalysis, complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, and chest radiograph are unremarkable, and oxygen saturation is 97% on room air. His postoperative orders include oxybutynin for bladder spasm, diphenhydramine at bedtime for sleep, cyclobenzaprine for muscle spasm, and scheduled acetaminophen. Which of the following is the most likely contributor to his presentation?
questions.explanation: The picture is delirium — acute onset from a documented recent baseline, fluctuating attention with lucid intervals, and visual hallucinations. The rule-out ladder puts substances and MEDICATIONS ahead of a primary psychiatric or degenerative explanation, and his order set stacks three anticholinergic agents: oxybutynin, diphenhydramine, and cyclobenzaprine. Anticholinergic burden is a leading reversible cause in older surgical patients, and the workup here is deliberately clean so no competing cause remains. Board pearl — diphenhydramine is a particularly common iatrogenic offender because it is ordered as a sleep aid on exactly the patients least able to tolerate it, and it is also why an antihistamine is the wrong choice for agitation in delirium.  [Learning objectives: LO 032, 093]

wrongExplanations.0: His daughter documents independent finances and driving one week ago, which establishes a normal recent baseline. Major neurocognitive disorder develops insidiously over months to years and does not produce fluctuating attention with lucid intervals.
wrongExplanations.1: Urinary tract infection is the classic reversible cause in an older adult, which makes it the reflexive answer — but the stem reports a normal urinalysis, a normal white blood cell count, and no fever.
wrongExplanations.3: Hypoxemia is a genuine postoperative cause of delirium, and it is excluded here by an oxygen saturation of 97% on room air and an unremarkable chest radiograph.
wrongExplanations.4: Alcohol withdrawal peaks around days 2 to 3 and would fit the timing, but it produces tremor, diaphoresis, and autonomic hyperactivity. He is afebrile with a pulse of 88/min and a normal blood pressure, and no alcohol history is given.

questions.eli5: He was sharp enough to drive himself to his appointment last week, and now he drifts in and out of confusion and sees cats. Three of his new hospital medicines all dry out the same brain chemical, and together they tipped him over.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man with bipolar I disorder is admitted with 9 days of decreased need for sleep, pressured speech, grandiosity, and reckless spending that has required hospitalization. He has no psychotic symptoms. He is not currently taking any medication, having stopped his previous regimen 4 months ago. Serum creatinine is 0.8 mg/dL, thyroid-stimulating hormone is 1.8 μU/mL, aminotransferases are within normal limits, complete blood count is normal, a pregnancy test is not applicable, and electrocardiography shows normal sinus rhythm with a QTc of 420 ms. He has no history of rash with any medication. Which of the following would be the LEAST appropriate agent for this acute episode?
questions.explanation: Bipolar treatment is phase-specific, and lamotrigine is the one agent on this list that fails at this pole: it is first-line for bipolar DEPRESSION and maintenance but weak for acute mania. Everything else listed is a legitimate first-line option for an acute manic episode — lithium, valproate, and carbamazepine, plus second-generation antipsychotics such as olanzapine and quetiapine, frequently with a short benzodiazepine bridge for 7 to 10 days while the mood stabilizer loads. Board pearl — lithium is the overall gold standard precisely because it is the only agent effective across mania, depression, AND maintenance; lamotrigine covers the opposite half of the illness, which is why memorizing one mood stabilizer for bipolar disorder reliably produces wrong answers on phase-specific questions.  [Learning objectives: LO 084, 096]

wrongExplanations.0: Lithium is first-line for acute mania and is the classic answer for euphoric mania, especially in a hospitalized patient. His renal function, thyroid studies, and ECG are all clean, so none of the four exceptions to lithium applies.
wrongExplanations.1: Valproate is first-line for acute mania and mixed episodes. His normal aminotransferases clear the hepatic contraindication, and pregnancy is not applicable.
wrongExplanations.2: Carbamazepine is first-line for acute mania. His normal complete blood count clears the bone marrow suppression concern, though its autoinduction and oral contraceptive interaction remain practical considerations.
wrongExplanations.3: Olanzapine is a second-generation antipsychotic with FDA approval for bipolar mania and maintenance. Its liability is metabolic burden, not lack of antimanic efficacy.
wrongExplanations.4: Quetiapine carries the broadest bipolar labeling of the group — mania, depression, and maintenance — and is an entirely appropriate choice for an acute manic episode.

questions.eli5: Almost every drug on this list calms mania. Lamotrigine is the odd one out — it is excellent for the depressed side of bipolar and weak for the manic side.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old woman is brought to the office by her son. For the past 7 weeks she has had depressed mood, has stopped attending the quilting group she had led for a decade, has lost 22 lb without dieting, sleeps 3 hours nightly with early-morning awakening, and moves and speaks noticeably slowly. Over the past 2 weeks she has additionally become convinced that her body is "hollowed out and rotting" and that she deserves to be punished for a minor tax error she made 20 years ago. Her son states that before this episode began she had no unusual beliefs of any kind, and that during a prior depressive episode 6 years ago she had similar low mood but no such beliefs, with complete return to normal afterward. She has never had elevated mood or decreased need for sleep. Urine toxicology screening is negative and thyroid-stimulating hormone is normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
choices: B. Major depressive disorder, severe, with psychotic features
E. Bipolar I disorder, with psychotic features
questions.explanation: Ask what the BASELINE symptom is. Here depression came first and the psychotic features arrived 5 weeks into the episode, on top of it — and her son documents that she had no unusual beliefs before the episode and none during a prior depressive episode that resolved completely. Psychosis confined entirely to the mood episode defines a mood disorder with psychotic features. Her delusions are also mood-congruent, involving bodily decay and deserved punishment. Board pearl — the discriminator against schizoaffective disorder is the requirement of at least 2 weeks of hallucinations or delusions in the ABSENCE of a mood episode, and this history explicitly rules that window out in both directions.  [Learning objectives: LO 017, 063]

wrongExplanations.0: Schizoaffective disorder requires a period of 2 weeks or more with psychosis but no mood episode. Her son reports no unusual beliefs before this episode and none during her prior episode, so that window has never occurred.
wrongExplanations.2: Delusional disorder requires the delusion to be essentially the only psychotic feature, with preserved functioning and without a prominent mood episode driving it. She has a full major depressive episode with a 22-lb weight loss and psychomotor retardation.
wrongExplanations.3: Schizophrenia requires 6 months of disturbance with active-phase symptoms not substantially accompanied by a concurrent major mood episode. She has 7 weeks of illness, entirely within a depressive episode, and a documented return to normal after a previous one.
wrongExplanations.4: Bipolar I requires at least one manic episode. She has never had elevated mood or decreased need for sleep — this is a stated negative rather than an omission.
wrongExplanations.5: Persistent depressive disorder is chronic milder depression lasting 2 or more years. Her episode is 7 weeks long, meets full major depressive episode criteria, and includes psychosis, which PDD does not accommodate.

questions.eli5: The sadness came first and the strange beliefs showed up weeks later, on top of it — and when she was depressed years ago she had no strange beliefs at all. When psychosis only lives inside the depression, it is depression with psychotic features.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman is seen 14 months after she was assaulted during a home invasion. She has intrusive memories several times weekly, avoids the neighborhood where she previously lived, feels persistently detached from her friends, and startles violently at unexpected sounds. She reports no nightmares and states she sleeps through the night without difficulty. She has no psychotic symptoms, denies suicidal ideation, and has never had a manic episode. She has completed 4 months of trauma-focused psychotherapy with partial benefit and now wishes to add medication. She takes no other medications, has no cardiac disease, and blood pressure is 114/72 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
questions.explanation: The PTSD algorithm branches first on the sleep complaint, and this stem deliberately closes that branch: she has NO nightmares and sleeps through the night, so neither prazosin nor trazodone has a target.
