What remains is the core syndrome — intrusion, avoidance, negative alterations in mood, and hyperarousal — for which an SSRI is first-line, with sertraline and paroxetine carrying FDA approval specifically for PTSD. Board pearl — this is the mirror image of the prazosin question: the drug you choose depends on which symptom cluster is actually in front of you, and the absence of nightmares is doing as much diagnostic work here as their presence would elsewhere.  [Learning objectives: LO 076]

wrongExplanations.0: Prazosin is the alpha-1 blocker indicated specifically for trauma-related nightmares and nighttime hyperarousal. She explicitly has no nightmares and sleeps through the night, so there is nothing for it to treat.
wrongExplanations.1: Benzodiazepines are generally avoided in PTSD — evidence suggests they do not meaningfully improve core symptoms and may worsen outcomes, alongside dependence risk.
wrongExplanations.2: Trazodone occupies the sleep-ONSET branch of the algorithm, for patients whose difficulty is falling asleep without nightmares. Her sleep is intact.
wrongExplanations.4: Quetiapine is an augmentation option for the hyperarousal cluster and is added only if psychosis is present or after a second SSRI or SNRI trial. She is antidepressant-naive and has no psychotic symptoms.

questions.eli5: She has flashbacks, avoids reminders, feels cut off from people, and jumps at noises — but she sleeps fine and has no nightmares. That rules out the nightmare medicine and leaves the standard first-choice antidepressant for PTSD.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman with obsessive-compulsive disorder has completed a 14-week trial of fluvoxamine titrated to 300 mg PO daily (maximum dose), which she has tolerated without adverse effects. Her symmetry obsessions and ordering compulsions have decreased only marginally and still consume approximately 3 hours daily. Before this she completed a 12-week trial of sertraline at 200 mg PO daily (maximum dose) with no meaningful benefit. She has been engaged in weekly cognitive behavioral therapy throughout. She has no cardiac disease, no history of myocardial infarction or arrhythmia, and electrocardiography shows a QTc of 414 ms with normal potassium and magnesium. She takes no other medications. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in pharmacotherapy?
questions.explanation: She has now failed TWO adequate SSRI trials, each at maximum dose for at least 12 weeks, with concurrent psychotherapy throughout — so this is genuinely SSRI-refractory obsessive-compulsive disorder rather than an underdosed or undertreated one. Clomipramine, a tricyclic with potent serotonergic activity, is the established next agent and has historically shown some of the best single-agent efficacy in OCD. Board pearl — the two things that make an OCD medication trial adequate are dose and duration: OCD requires substantially HIGHER SSRI doses than depression does, and the stem documents maximum doses on both trials so you cannot fall back on the underdosing explanation.  [Learning objectives: LO 081]

wrongExplanations.1: A third SSRI offers diminishing returns after two adequate maximum-dose trials of the same mechanism, and citalopram specifically carries a dose-dependent QTc warning — a poor choice when OCD requires high doses.
wrongExplanations.2: Benzodiazepines have limited benefit in OCD and do not treat obsessions or compulsions. Adding one exposes her to dependence risk while leaving the core illness untreated.
wrongExplanations.3: Lithium is a mood stabilizer with antisuicidal properties in bipolar disorder. It is not an established augmentation strategy for OCD, and she has no mood disorder.
wrongExplanations.4: Bupropion has no serotonergic activity at all — it inhibits norepinephrine and dopamine reuptake — which makes it ineffective for OCD, and its activating profile can worsen anxiety.

questions.eli5: She has now taken two different antidepressants at the highest allowed dose for months each, and the rituals still eat three hours a day. Clomipramine is the older, stronger option that works when the usual ones do not.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman with anorexia nervosa was admitted 3 days ago for medical stabilization at a body mass index of 13.8 kg/m2 and has been receiving nutritional repletion. On hospital day 3 she reports new generalized weakness and shortness of breath. Temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F), pulse is 116/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 98/62 mm Hg. Examination shows bibasilar crackles, new peripheral edema, and diffuse proximal weakness with intact sensation. Serum studies show phosphate 1.1 mg/dL (admission 3.2 mg/dL), potassium 2.8 mEq/L, magnesium 1.2 mg/dL, and glucose 104 mg/dL. Electrocardiography shows sinus tachycardia with new T-wave flattening. Which of the following best explains her deterioration?
choices: A. Sepsis from an occult infection
C. Congestive heart failure from pre-existing cardiomyopathy
questions.explanation: Refeeding syndrome is the danger that governs how anorexia is treated. Carbohydrate reintroduction triggers an insulin surge that drives phosphate, potassium, and magnesium INTRACELLULARLY, and the resulting hypophosphatemia impairs ATP production and produces weakness, respiratory failure, arrhythmia, and cardiac decompensation. Her phosphate fell from 3.2 to 1.1 mg/dL over 3 days of feeding — the single most important number in the stem. Board pearl — this is precisely why weight restoration proceeds at roughly 1 pound per week with electrolyte monitoring rather than aggressive caloric loading, and why patients at very low BMI with already-low phosphate and magnesium are the highest-risk group.  [Learning objectives: LO 023, 067]

wrongExplanations.0: Sepsis would be expected to produce fever or hypothermia with a leukocyte abnormality and a source. She is afebrile, and the derangement is a specific, explicable electrolyte shift rather than an inflammatory picture.
wrongExplanations.1: Untreated malnutrition does not produce an abrupt 3-day fall in phosphate. She is being fed, and it is the feeding itself — not its absence — that precipitated this.
wrongExplanations.2: Cardiac decompensation in anorexia is real, but the crackles and edema here are a downstream consequence of the electrolyte shift and fluid handling during refeeding, not evidence of a pre-existing cardiomyopathy that was previously silent.
wrongExplanations.3: Superior mesenteric artery syndrome is a mechanical complication of severe weight loss causing postprandial vomiting and abdominal pain from duodenal compression. She has neither, and it does not produce hypophosphatemia.
wrongExplanations.5: Thiamine deficiency can cause high-output cardiac failure and is a genuine consideration in malnutrition, but it does not explain the dramatic fall in phosphate, potassium, and magnesium, which is the defining and treatable abnormality here.

questions.eli5: Once she started eating again, her body pulled key minerals out of the blood and into her cells all at once. Her phosphate crashed, and without it her muscles and heart cannot make energy — that is why feeding has to be slow.

questions.stem: Severity in bulimia nervosa and severity in anorexia nervosa are graded using different variables. Which of the following correctly identifies the variable used for each?
choices: A. Bulimia by body mass index; anorexia by binge episodes per week
B. Bulimia by binge episodes per week; anorexia by duration of illness
C. Bulimia by compensatory behaviors per week; anorexia by body mass index
D. Both are graded by body mass index
E. Both are graded by the frequency of binge episodes per week
questions.explanation: The two disorders are graded on different axes because their defining pathology differs. Anorexia nervosa severity is set entirely by BMI: mild 18.5 to 17, moderate 16.99 to 16, severe 15.99 to 15, and extreme below 15. Bulimia nervosa severity is set by the number of COMPENSATORY behaviors per week: mild 1 to 3, moderate 4 to 7, severe 8 to 13, and extreme 14 or more. Board pearl — this reflects the diagnostic logic overall, where BMI is the fastest way to narrow the differential: a low BMI points to anorexia, while a normal-to-high BMI moves you toward bulimia or binge eating disorder, and you then ask what the behavior is FOR.  [Learning objectives: LO 008]

wrongExplanations.0: This reverses both variables. BMI cannot grade bulimia, in which patients characteristically present at a normal-to-elevated weight, and anorexia is not graded by binge frequency since many patients never binge at all.
wrongExplanations.1: Bulimia is graded by compensatory behaviors rather than binges, and duration of illness is not a severity specifier for anorexia — or for either disorder.
wrongExplanations.3: Grading bulimia by BMI would leave nearly all patients in one band, since bulimia typically occurs at a normal-to-high BMI, which is exactly why the specifier uses behavior frequency instead.
wrongExplanations.4: Anorexia severity does not use binge frequency; the restricting subtype by definition involves no recurrent binge or purge behavior in the past 3 months, so the variable would not apply.

questions.eli5: Anorexia severity is measured by how low the weight is. Bulimia severity is measured by how many times a week the person purges or compensates, because their weight is usually normal.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman with borderline personality disorder is on hospital day 4 of an inpatient admission. She tells the day nurse that she is "the only person here who has ever actually listened to me" and that the rest of the staff are "cruel and incompetent." She tells the night nurse the reverse. Over 48 hours the treatment team becomes divided, with some members advocating for early discharge and others arguing she is being mistreated; two staff members have a heated disagreement at the nursing station. The patient's own reported distress has not changed. Which of the following defense mechanisms best accounts for the team's division?
questions.explanation: Splitting is the categorization of people as all-good or all-bad with no capacity to integrate positive and negative qualities in the same person — the cardinal defense of borderline personality disorder, captured by the phrase borders split countries. Its signature on an inpatient unit is that the division reproduces itself in the TEAM: staff members find themselves in genuine conflict with one another while the patient's own distress is unchanged. Board pearl — the therapeutic response is a consistent, unified team approach with open communication among staff, and the definitive treatment for the underlying disorder is dialectical behavior therapy.  [Learning objectives: LO 029, 058, 089]

wrongExplanations.0: Projection attributes one's own unacceptable feelings or impulses to another person — a patient seeking compensation accusing others of manipulating the system. She is not disowning an impulse; she is dividing people into camps.
wrongExplanations.2: Displacement redirects an emotion from its true target onto a safer one, such as anger at a driver landing on a surgeon. Her idealization and devaluation are aimed at the actual people in front of her, not redirected from elsewhere.
wrongExplanations.3: Reaction formation converts an unacceptable feeling into its opposite, producing conspicuous over-the-top warmth toward someone resented. She expresses both poles openly to different people rather than masking one.
wrongExplanations.4: Passive aggression expresses hostility indirectly through inaction or subtle resistance. Her devaluation of staff is direct and explicit, not covert.

questions.eli5: She tells the day nurse everyone else is terrible and tells the night nurse the opposite, and soon the staff are arguing with each other. Seeing people as all good or all bad is called splitting.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man is evaluated in a correctional facility. Records document that between ages 11 and 14 he set fires, was repeatedly truant, stole from neighbors, and was cruel to animals. Since turning 18 he has been arrested four times for assault and fraud, has been fired from six jobs for theft and for failing to appear, has fathered three children he does not support, and has defaulted on several loans taken in his brother's name. He is initially charming and articulate, then becomes irritable when questioned about his record, stating that his victims "had it coming" and that he does not see why any of it is a problem. He has never had a manic episode, has no hallucinations or delusions, and urine toxicology screening is negative. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Antisocial personality disorder requires two things simultaneously: the person must be at least 18 years old, AND there must be evidence of conduct disorder with onset before age 15. Both halves are documented here — fire-setting, truancy, theft, and animal cruelty from ages 11 to 14, and a pervasive adult pattern following the CALLOUS MAN framework of arrests, deceit, unmet obligations, financial irresponsibility, and aggression. The absence of remorse and the externalization of blame complete the picture. Board pearl — this is the same behavioral pattern as conduct disorder read at a different age; the diagnosis converts at 18, which is exactly the discrimination that traps students on adolescent vignettes.  [Learning objectives: LO 041]

wrongExplanations.0: Conduct disorder is the childhood and adolescent form of this pattern. He is 28, and once a person reaches 18 with a documented pre-15 history, the adult diagnosis applies instead.
wrongExplanations.1: Narcissistic personality disorder centers on grandiosity, entitlement, envy, and a need for admiration. His superficial charm is instrumental rather than a bid for admiration, and narcissism does not require a childhood conduct history or explain the arrests and fraud.
wrongExplanations.2: Intermittent explosive disorder involves recurrent impulsive aggressive outbursts grossly out of proportion to provocation, WITHOUT the planned deceit, theft, and fraud described here. His fraud and loans in his brother's name are premeditated and instrumental.
wrongExplanations.4: Borderline personality disorder centers on abandonment fear, unstable identity and relationships, chronic emptiness, and self-harm. None is described; his pattern is disregard for others' rights rather than instability of self.
wrongExplanations.5: Bipolar I requires at least one manic episode, which the stem explicitly negates. Reckless behavior confined to a discrete mood episode would look nothing like a 17-year continuous pattern.

questions.eli5: He broke rules and hurt animals as a kid, and as an adult he lies, steals, gets arrested, and feels no guilt about any of it. That lifelong pattern, once someone is over eighteen, is antisocial personality disorder.

questions.stem: An 8-year-old boy meets full criteria for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, with symptoms documented before age 12, present at home and at school, and causing clear functional impairment. His parents have agreed to a trial of a long-acting stimulant. He was born at term with no complications, and his growth has tracked along the 50th percentile. Which of the following is most important to obtain before initiating the medication?
choices: A. A cardiovascular review of systems and family history of sudden cardiac death
C. Baseline serum thyroid-stimulating hormone and free thyroxine
D. Baseline liver function tests and a complete blood count
E. Formal neuropsychological testing of processing speed
questions.explanation: Stimulants block dopamine and norepinephrine reuptake and enhance their release, producing tachycardia, palpitations, and elevated blood pressure as expected effects — so a cardiovascular review of systems, including a family history of sudden cardiac death or structural heart disease, is the pre-treatment assessment specifically called for. Board pearl — the rest of the stimulant monitoring profile is worth holding alongside it: appetite suppression and weight loss, insomnia (dose after meals rather than at night), growth effects of roughly 2 to 3 cm addressed with drug holidays, gastrointestinal upset and headache, and tics, which are especially associated with the amphetamine family. Extended-release stimulants are not used in children under 6 years.  [Learning objectives: LO 075, 100]

wrongExplanations.1: EEG is not part of routine ADHD evaluation or stimulant initiation. It would be considered only if the history suggested absence seizures, which can mimic inattention but produce discrete staring spells with abrupt onset and offset.
wrongExplanations.2: Thyroid studies are reasonable when the history suggests thyroid disease, but they are not a routine prerequisite for stimulant initiation, and his history gives no such indication.
wrongExplanations.3: Liver function tests and blood counts are not required before stimulants. Hepatic monitoring concerns attach to atomoxetine, and mandatory blood count monitoring belongs to clozapine.
wrongExplanations.4: Neuropsychological testing can characterize a learning profile but is not required to diagnose ADHD or to start medication, and no test result is diagnostic of the condition.

questions.eli5: Stimulants speed up the heart a little, so before starting one the doctor asks about heart symptoms and whether anyone in the family died suddenly and young. That is the safety check that matters most.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man with schizophrenia, stable on paliperidone for 3 years, tells his psychiatrist during a routine visit, "Some days I get so angry at my landlord I could kill him. I would never actually do anything — I just get furious when the heat goes out again." He names no plan, no method, and no timeframe, has never been violent, owns no weapons, and has no history of arrest. His mental status examination shows no delusions involving the landlord, organized thought process, and no command hallucinations. He is adherent to medication and his psychotic symptoms remain in remission. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
choices: A. Notify law enforcement of a threat against the landlord
B. Contact the landlord directly to warn him
D. Contact the patient's family and ask them to monitor him
E. Document the assessment and continue routine outpatient care
questions.explanation: The Tarasoff duty fires only when a specific, identifiable victim is in IMMINENT and PROBABLE danger. Fantasies and rhetorical anger are explicitly not reportable when clinical judgment holds that the patient does not intend to act — the lecture's own example is that "I could kill my brother, I just hate him" does not meet the bar, whereas naming a victim with a method and a timeframe does. He supplies no plan, no method, no timeframe, no history of violence, no weapon access, and no delusion or command hallucination involving the landlord. The correct action is a documented risk assessment and continued care. Board pearl — when a statement genuinely sits on the line, obtain a second clinician's opinion before deciding not to report; and remember that breaching confidentiality unnecessarily damages the alliance that makes future disclosure possible.  [Learning objectives: LO 052]

wrongExplanations.0: Notifying law enforcement is the correct discharge of the duty when it is triggered, but triggering requires imminent and probable danger to an identifiable victim. Reporting rhetorical anger with no plan would breach confidentiality without a legal or ethical basis.
wrongExplanations.1: Even when the duty IS triggered, warning means contacting the police and letting them notify and protect the victim — the physician is not expected to call the intended victim directly. Here the duty is not triggered at all.
wrongExplanations.2: Involuntary hospitalization requires danger to self or others or grave disability. He is medication-adherent, in remission, organized, and describes frustration rather than intent.
wrongExplanations.3: Family involvement is a legitimate rung on the least-restrictive ladder when escalating risk warrants it, and a family's promise to monitor never transfers physician responsibility. Neither consideration applies to a patient whose risk assessment is reassuring.

questions.eli5: Saying you are so angry you could kill someone is not the same as planning to. He named no plan, no weapon, and no date, so the doctor writes down the careful assessment and keeps treating him.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man with schizophrenia is admitted with necrotizing fasciitis of the left lower leg. The surgical team recommends urgent debridement, explaining that without it the infection will spread and is likely to be fatal. He is able to repeat back the proposed operation, its risks, and its benefits accurately. He refuses, stating that his leg is not infected but has been "replaced with a device by the government to track me," and that surgery would allow the transmitter to be reinstalled. He states this belief with fixed conviction and does not accept photographs of the wound as evidence against it. He is alert, oriented, and his attention does not fluctuate. Which of the following best describes his decision-making capacity?
choices: A. He has capacity, because he can accurately describe the procedure and its risks
B. He has capacity, because a psychiatric diagnosis does not remove decisional ability
C. He lacks capacity, because he cannot appreciate how the facts apply to himself
D. He lacks capacity, because refusing life-saving surgery is inherently irrational
E. Capacity cannot be assessed while an active psychotic disorder is present
questions.explanation: Capacity is judged against four standards, often remembered as CARD: Communicate a choice, Appreciate the facts as they apply to oneself, Reason through the options, and Demonstrate understanding. He clears communication and understanding — he can recite the procedure and its risks accurately — but he fails APPRECIATION, because a fixed delusion prevents him from accepting that the facts describe his own body. That single failed element is enough. Board pearl — capacity is decision-SPECIFIC and clinical, made by a physician, whereas competence is a global legal status decided by a court; and a psychiatric diagnosis by itself never establishes incapacity, which is why the reasoning must be tied to a named failed standard rather than to the diagnosis.  [Learning objectives: LO 057, 079]

wrongExplanations.0: Accurate recitation satisfies the understanding standard only. Appreciation is a separate and higher requirement — the patient must accept that the information is true OF HIM — and his delusion prevents exactly that.
wrongExplanations.1: The general principle is correct and important: a psychiatric diagnosis never by itself removes capacity. But it does not settle this case, where a specific delusion is directly blocking one of the four standards.
wrongExplanations.3: Refusing recommended treatment is not itself evidence of incapacity — patients with capacity may decline life-saving care for reasons grounded in their own values. What disqualifies him is the delusional premise, not the choice.
wrongExplanations.4: Capacity is assessed in patients with active psychiatric illness routinely, and many such patients retain it. Declining to assess would improperly equate diagnosis with incapacity.

questions.eli5: He can repeat back everything the surgeon told him, so he understands the words. But he believes his leg was swapped for a government tracking device, so he cannot accept that any of it is really about him — and that is the part he fails.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old graduate student is brought to the emergency department by her roommate 19 days after her father died unexpectedly. Beginning about 3 days after the death she became convinced that her academic department was reviewing her private messages and planning to expel her, and for the past week her roommate has heard her speaking to someone who is not present. Her speech is at times difficult to follow, with answers that trail off mid-sentence. She has continued to shower and eat, and her roommate states she was "completely herself" until her father died. She has no personal or family psychiatric history. Temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F) and vital signs are otherwise normal; physical and neurologic examinations show no abnormalities. Urine toxicology screening is negative, thyroid-stimulating hormone is normal, and noncontrast CT of the head shows no abnormality. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
choices: C. Major depressive disorder with psychotic features
questions.explanation: Brief psychotic disorder requires at least one core psychotic symptom — delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, or grossly disorganized behavior — lasting from 1 day to less than 1 month, with an expected full return to premorbid functioning. She has all three of delusions, hallucinations, and disorganized speech, beginning 16 days ago, with a marked stressor (her father's sudden death) and preserved self-care. Board pearl — the duration ladder is the whole game in psychotic disorders: under 1 month is brief psychotic disorder, 1 to 6 months is schizophreniform disorder, and more than 6 months is schizophrenia. Her normal toxicology, thyroid studies, and head CT close the secondary causes before a primary diagnosis is assigned.  [Learning objectives: LO 063]

wrongExplanations.0: Schizophrenia requires continuous signs of disturbance for at least 6 months including prodromal and residual phases, with characteristic functional decline. She is 16 days into her first-ever symptoms and was entirely well before.
wrongExplanations.1: Schizophreniform disorder requires symptoms lasting 1 to 6 months. At 16 days she has not reached the 1-month threshold, which is the single criterion separating it from the correct answer.
wrongExplanations.2: A major depressive episode requires depressed mood or anhedonia plus additional symptoms for at least 2 weeks. No depressive syndrome is described — grief following a death is not itself a mood episode, and her psychosis is not mood-congruent.
wrongExplanations.4: Delusional disorder requires at least 1 month of a delusion as essentially the only psychotic feature, without prominent hallucinations or disorganized speech. She has both, and she is under a month.
wrongExplanations.5: Schizoaffective disorder requires a major mood episode concurrent with psychosis PLUS at least 2 weeks of psychosis in the absence of a mood episode. She has neither a mood episode nor the required longitudinal history.

questions.eli5: Two and a half weeks after her father died suddenly, she became paranoid, started hearing voices, and her speech got hard to follow — and she was completely fine before. Psychosis lasting under a month is brief psychotic disorder.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 5-month history of episodes of racing heart, trembling, sweating, and a sense of impending doom, occurring several times weekly and lasting 20 to 40 minutes. She also reports that she has lost 18 lb over the same period despite an increased appetite, feels uncomfortably warm when others are cold, and has had looser stools. She attributes all of it to stress at work. Temperature is 37.4°C (99.3°F), pulse is 118/min and regular, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 142/72 mm Hg. Examination shows a fine resting tremor of the outstretched hands, warm moist skin, brisk deep tendon reflexes, and lid lag on downward gaze. She takes no medications, urine toxicology screening is negative, and electrocardiography shows sinus tachycardia. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
choices: C. Begin a trial of sertraline and reassess in 6 weeks
E. Refer for cognitive behavioral therapy for panic disorder
questions.explanation: The panic-like surges are the dramatic decoy; the buried clues are everywhere else in the vital signs and examination. Weight loss despite increased appetite, heat intolerance, loose stools, a widened pulse pressure, fine tremor, warm moist skin, brisk reflexes, and lid lag together describe thyrotoxicosis, and a thyroid-stimulating hormone level is the appropriate first test. Board pearl — the rule-out ladder puts substances and then MEDICAL conditions ahead of a primary psychiatric diagnosis, and thyroid disease is the classic secondary cause; treating this as panic disorder would leave a treatable endocrine illness to progress while an SSRI is titrated over 6 weeks.  [Learning objectives: LO 032, 099]

wrongExplanations.0: The GAD-7 screens for generalized anxiety disorder and would simply score the symptoms she already reports. It cannot distinguish a primary anxiety disorder from a secondary one, which is the entire question here.
wrongExplanations.2: Starting an antidepressant accepts the psychiatric label before excluding a medical cause, and it would delay diagnosis by 6 weeks while thyrotoxicosis continued — the exact failure mode the rule-out sequence exists to prevent.
wrongExplanations.3: Ambulatory monitoring is appropriate when a paroxysmal arrhythmia is suspected, but her tachycardia is sustained and regular rather than paroxysmal, and it does not explain the weight loss, heat intolerance, or lid lag.
wrongExplanations.4: Referral for psychotherapy commits to a primary psychiatric diagnosis before the medical workup is complete, and CBT will not treat the underlying endocrine disorder.

questions.eli5: Her heart races and she feels doom, which sounds like panic — but she is also losing weight while eating more, always hot, and has a tremor and a telltale eyelid sign. That points at an overactive thyroid, so check the thyroid blood test first.
